3

The shift in the burden of verification for papers

When an editor or reader receives a paper flagged as AI-generated, they cannot tell whether
the author validated its content. The author may have checked every claim in the paper, a
selection of them, or, worse, none. Our claim is not that AI-generated text has not been
verified. It is that verification has become unobservable from the text, so the burden of
verification shifts to the reader.
Why would an author prefer shifting the burden? Verification is costly, and with AIgenerated text, no one can observe whether the author has done the verification. In most cases,
the author gains little from verifying: only protection against damage to their reputation
9
Jr et al. (2026) run a similar exercise with abstracts. We do not find their main result (that human-written
text refined with AI can be scored as up to 80 percent AI-generated) convincing. First, the authors use an
older version of Pangram (3.2). Second, and much more importantly, abstracts are short texts with formulaic
prose, so a “refined” abstract can be quite different from the original one.

9

 from a wrong result, and only if someone notices the error. We all recognize this as a classic
moral-hazard problem, with the usual outcome: authors verify too little.
We reject this shift. Responsibility for the content of a submission lies with its author,
who also benefits most from publication. Editors’ and referees’ time is the scarce input of the
peer-review system (time that is often unpaid or paid well below market rates).
This is not just about fairness but also about efficiency. The social planner reaches
the same conclusion because the verification cost should fall on whoever can verify most
cheaply, and that is the author, for two reasons. First, the author built the data, derived the
mathematical proofs, wrote the code (or at least worked with an LLM to do so), and thought
about the paper for many hours. A check that takes the author an hour can easily take a
reader a week. Second, and quantitatively much more important, the author verifies once,
but a paper might reach hundreds of readers. Verification by readers is a public good: every
reader benefits from a check done by someone else, so every reader waits for someone else to
do the check. So, in the end, nobody verifies.
A good analogy comes from legal systems. A key decision in any legal system is which
side bears the burden of proof. In criminal cases, the burden of proof lies with the state, not
the defendant. Placing the burden of proof on the state is a straightforward application of
optimal mechanism design: proving guilt is easier than proving innocence and, as a society,
we have decided we want to minimize the number of innocent persons who are punished.
But civil law shifts the burden of proof to the defendant when the facts point to the
defendant’s negligence and the defendant can produce the evidence at a lower cost (Hay
and Spier, 1997). The classic case in English tort law is Byrne v. Boadle (1863), which
established the principle of res ipsa loquitur (“the thing speaks for itself”). The court held
that, when a barrel of flour falls from a second-story warehouse window onto a passerby, it is
the warehouse owner who must show that he was not negligent. Since barrels do not usually
fall by themselves, only the warehouse owner is in a position to know how the barrel was
handled and why it fell.
Peer review should work the same way. The author always bears the burden of verification.
What an AI flag shifts is the burden of proving negligence. Without a flag, a mistake may be
an honest slip, and the editor needs evidence of negligence. With a flag, the mistake speaks
for itself. To avoid a sanction, it is up to the author to show that the analysis was verified.
Delegating the writing, however, is not a problem in itself. The output of an author is
the research: the question, the ideas, the evidence, and the results. The text is only the
medium that communicates the output, not the output itself. If the author delegates much
or most of the writing to an LLM but verifies the content thoroughly and does the thinking,
the delegation is not a concern (beyond forcing readers to suffer the bland chant of LLMs),
10

 because the burden of verification is still allocated efficiently.
For the same reason, an author who lets AI write the prose is not committing plagiarism,
at least not in full. The author is not passing off someone else’s work. Plagiarism applies
only when AI supplies the substance (the ideas or the fundamental results) and the author
presents that substance as their own.10
To push the point to its extreme: a paper written entirely by AI, whose ideas are the
author’s and whose results the author has verified, is acceptable. But we have a strong prior,
given the current state of LLMs, that such a paper will rarely be good, because the author
skipped the thinking that writing forces.
From our perspective, a closer analogy is submitting a paper with unchecked errors, which
is negligence rather than misconduct. Every major legal system draws this distinction and
attaches different penalties to each. One of the first things you learn in criminal law is that
killing someone because you did not check the brakes of your car is very different from killing
someone because you, a professional boxer, punched them in a bar fight and they hit their
head when they fell. Referees, as we argue next, are held to a stricter standard.

4

AI-based peer review is unacceptable

Every paper has problems, and LLMs are very good at finding them. If you ask an LLM
for more issues, it will come up with more, no matter how many times you iterate. But
peer review is not about finding one sentence that is not entirely precise or a slightly sloppy
mathematical proof. Referees are asked to evaluate which questions are important, whether
the paper’s contribution is worth publishing despite its flaws, and whether the paper is a
good fit for the journal in terms of quality and focus. That judgment is the task for which
they are selected as subject experts (see also the model in Section 5).11
The failure of using AI for peer review that we have in mind is delegating judgment to
the model. A referee who relies on an LLM to decide which issues to raise and how to rank
them has not done their job, even if they carefully read the output before submitting it. It is
not enough for the comments to be factually correct. A report can list many issues, some of
them technically correct, none of which is essential to the contribution of the paper.
10

We do not want to push this point too far either. If an author writes down a model and the LLM
finds an interesting corollary to one of the results in the theoretical analysis, is that corollary a substantive
contribution? Or is the corollary similar to the results that research assistants used to derive in the past? Or
perhaps to a suggestion by a seminar participant of an interesting extension of the model?
11
Our position that AI-based peer review is unacceptable does not imply that AI-assisted peer review is
useless. Referees can use AI to check the grammar and syntax of their own report, to find related papers in
the literature, or to help verify specific claims. These uses must, however, comply with the journal’s policies.

11

 Taking superficial notes and letting an LLM write the report around them is not acceptable
either. As Carl Bergstrom puts it, “taking superficial notes and having an LLM synthesize
them falls far, far short of writing an adequate peer review” (Naddaf, 2025a). We put the
case of detailed notes in a different bucket. A referee who writes detailed notes while reading
the paper, asks an LLM to turn them into a complete report, and checks that report sentence
by sentence has engaged with the paper and exercised their judgment. If the report is flagged,
the referee can show the notes.
Unlike for authors, for a referee an AI-generated report is the problem. No amount of ex
post checking repairs that. A referee who is not willing to judge a paper on their own should
be open about it and decline the invitation to referee, not pretend they are doing it.
AI-based review has a further problem: LLMs can be primed. It is trivial to ask an LLM
to write a positive or negative referee report about any paper. The latter is more damaging
to the author and, given the incentives in the profession, perhaps more likely. As editors, we
know that negative reports far outnumber positive ones. Thus, for a referee, there is safety
in numbers: a mildly negative report is unlikely to raise suspicion.
The cost is likely to be highest for innovative work, which departs from the existing
literature by construction and will produce more deviations from standards for an LLM to list.
AI-based review, therefore, risks being not just shallow, but systematically biased against
innovative work. Our experiment suggests that LLMs lean this way even without priming
(Section 2.2).
This point answers an objection we have heard over and over: referees can be biased and
sloppy, while AI is objective and thorough. AI is thorough at listing problems, which is not
the scarce input in peer review, and AI is not neutral. The remedy for sloppy referees is
better incentives for careful reports, not removing judgment from peer review.
For referees, the closest analogy is plagiarism. Plagiarism is conventionally defined as
presenting someone else’s work as one’s own. An AI-generated report presents the judgment
of the LLM as the judgment of the referee. Editing the output of the LLM does not change
the nature of this action, just as paraphrasing someone else’s text does not make the text one’s
own (and the rules defining plagiarism deal explicitly with paraphrasing). The profession
should treat AI-generated reports in the same way it treats plagiarism. Both are matters of
professional misconduct, not issues of writing style.12 As with plagiarism, a flag from an AI
detector starts a serious inquiry, but the flag is not a verdict.
12

Uploading a manuscript under review to a non-local LLM can also breach the confidentiality that referees
owe to authors, because a third party can access the paper, the identity of the author, and the identity of the
owner of the account. Several publishers explicitly prohibit such uploads for that reason.

 5

A simple model of peer review

We now present a simple model of peer review. We do not write such a model just for the
sake of having some math behind our statements, but because a model gives us a coherent
framework to think through the problem: it helps us understand what our arguments assume
and appreciate their implications. At the same time, we are aware this is just a stylized
model, and we do not claim to have proven any particularly surprising result with it. Think
of the model as our own self-verification.
The model delivers five results. First, a text flagged as AI-generated predicts a worse
paper, because the authors who skip the writing are also more likely to skip checking their
analysis. Second, a lower tolerance for mistakes in flagged papers is rational: a visible mistake
in a flagged paper raises the probability that the analysis also contains hidden errors. Third, a
flag that the text is AI-generated should trigger closer scrutiny, while sanctions should follow
the errors that scrutiny finds, not the flag itself. Fourth, a journal that commits to scrutiny
gains even more, because the threat of scrutiny leads negligent authors to vet their analysis
before they submit. Fifth, a referee report generated by AI adds nothing that the editor
could not obtain faster and more easily from an LLM. These reports remove the journal’s
main defense against shallow papers. Even worse, because these reports no longer reflect the
judgment of the referee about quality, they can weaken the incentives of authors to do the
thinking instead of just writing papers that can get through the review of an LLM.

5.1

How AI enters the production of a paper

As we discussed in the introduction, AI in general, and LLMs in particular, are incredible tools
for research in economics. We use them constantly for ideation, data gathering, statistical
analysis, mathematics, coding, debugging, writing assistance, and compiling replication
packages (see also Korinek, 2023). In fact, given the quality of their feedback, we are
suspicious of papers that have not used LLM-verification tools before submission to a working
paper series or a journal. One of us found a serious error in a first draft of a paper he wrote a
few months ago thanks to Refine.ink (and was able to fix it before submission to a journal).
An academic paper is produced in three stages, and AI can enter at each of them:
• Stage 1: Idea Generation. Papers start from an idea of quality q0 . AI can help
generate and refine ideas, for example, through a preliminary conversation with the
researcher.
• Stage 2: Analysis and Execution. The author turns the idea into results: collecting
and cleaning data, writing code to estimate or solve a model, deriving proofs. Without
13

 AI, execution is time-consuming, but the author who executes the analysis understands
each step. AI makes execution cheap, so we assume all authors use AI for at least some
steps of the paper. The author receives output they did not build, which can contain
errors. Thus, the author must vet that output afterward, and that activity carries a
cost.
• Stage 3: Writing. AI can draft text at almost no cost. There is nothing wrong
with using an AI draft, provided the author engages with it: reading the cited work,
checking the logic, and revising the text. The problem comes when the author delegates
these tasks without doing the work, because writing and thinking are closely connected
in the research process. As the historian David McCullough remarked, “writing is
thinking. To write well is to think clearly. That’s why it’s so hard” (McCullough,
2003). An economist who, instead of reading the relevant papers, lets the LLM write
the literature review misses the nuances that could have sharpened the idea. Just think
about how many new insights come from reading classic papers in economics you might
have already read ten times. And an author who lets AI state the contribution of their
paper never learns whether the argument is tight enough or just sounds plausible at
first glance.

5.2

Authors, detectors, and editors

Detection technology. The detector reads only the final text, the output of stage 3,
and classifies it into three levels: s = human, s = assisted (human text edited by AI), and
s = AI (AI-generated). We call s = AI a flag. We write F for a flagged paper and H for an
unflagged one, with s = human or s = assisted. As we documented in Section 2, the detector
is accurate about the text, and its errors are mostly false negatives.
Author. The author has a private type τ ∈ {N, C} (negligent, careful). The share of
careful authors is µ ∈ (0, 1). Each type is defined by a parameter θτ representing the cost of a
unit of effort, with θN > θC > 0. A high θ can stand for a variety of costs: a high opportunity
cost of time (too many projects, lucrative consulting engagements, administrative burdens at
the author’s institution), less familiarity with the topic and the methods, or less intrinsic
concern for getting things right. Within the model, negligent means “high cost of careful
work,” not a judgment about the intrinsic quality of a researcher. Our key assumption is
that the same θτ scales the cost of the tasks at stages 2 and 3: authors who are careful in
verifying the execution are also deeply engaged with the writing.
We do not need the extreme assumption that the authors who verify the execution are
14

 exactly the authors who engage with the writing. We could instead assume that authors
who are careful in verifying the execution are also more likely to engage deeply with the
writing. The main thrust of our results would still go through, at the cost of more complicated
expressions. We do not find the opposite case, in which authors who are careful in verifying
the execution are less likely to engage deeply with the writing, empirically relevant.
At stages 2 and 3, the author makes two choices:13
1. A binary choice of whether to vet the execution, v ∈ {0, 1}, at a cost θτ cv . Unvetted
AI-assisted execution contains a material error with probability ε ∈ (0, 1). We assume
for simplicity that vetted execution is error-free.14 By a material error, we mean a
substantial error in the paper, not a mistyped figure in a table or a minor, fixable
problem in a proof.
2. A binary choice of whether to engage with the writing, r ∈ {0, 1}, at a cost θτ cr .
Not engaging (r = 0) lowers the quality of the paper to q = q0 − ∆, with ∆ ≥ 0:
the author never read the literature or thought the argument through in writing.
For communication text (for instance, summarizing a table, describing the data, or
documenting an algorithm), ∆ ≈ 0, as the text only conveys work already done. For
thinking text (the literature review, the motivation, the statement of the contribution,
the economic intuition, the policy implications), ∆ > 0: writing that text is how the
author works out what the contribution is.
Who gets flagged. An author who engages with the writing of the paper usually scores
s = human or s = assisted. An author who does not engage with the writing scores s = AI.
Some authors who engage might score s = AI, for instance because they do their thinking
elsewhere (detailed notes or mathematical derivations) and let AI write all the prose, or
because they iterate with an LLM on each passage so often that the detector flags the text
as AI-generated. We capture these cases in reduced form: a share φ ∈ (0, 1) of authors who
engage receive s = AI. The detector is not wrong: the text is AI-generated, but the paper is
sound.15
13

In practice, vetting the execution also improves the quality of the paper, and engaging with the writing
also reduces the probability of an error. Adding either effect widens the gap between careful and negligent
authors and makes the flag more informative about errors, so it strengthens our results.
14
If vetting reduces the error probability from ε to εv ∈ (0, ε), the marginal incentive to vet depends on
ε − εv , while Bayesian probabilities and editorial scrutiny conditions must also account for residual errors.
15
We believe φ is small. From our own experience, authors who write detailed notes and use AI to polish
the text and proofread are not flagged. In comparison, as editors, we have seen that papers flagged as mostly
AI-generated turn out to be shallow.

15

 Payoff. We normalize the value of a publication for the author to one. Absent the additional
scrutiny introduced below, a paper of quality q is published with probability πF (q) if flagged
and πH (q) if unflagged. These probabilities average over the noisy signal that the referees
send to the editor. We take them as given and assume, rather plausibly, that a flag never
raises the probability of publication: πH (q) ≥ πF (q). If the paper contains an execution error,
the error is found with probability ρ ∈ (0, 1], whether or not the paper is published (working
papers circulate), and the author pays a reputational penalty P .
Thus, the author chooses v and r to maximize
Uτ (v, r) = Pr(publication | r) − (1 − v) ρ ε P − θτ (cv v + cr r) .

Vetting does not enter the publication term because referees rarely catch execution errors
(e.g., a serious bug in the code): catching these errors requires redoing the analysis.
Editor. The editor wants to publish high-quality papers without errors, because an error
found after publication damages the reputation of the journal. The journal values the quality
of published papers: write this value as V (q) > 0, increasing in q. In the scrutiny calculations
below, V denotes V (q0 − ∆). An error found after publication costs the journal a reputational
loss L > 0. A material error found before publication leads to rejection, and the discovery of
an error with probability ρ happens only after the editorial decision. We assume ρL > V :
publishing a paper with an error is a net loss for the journal.
The editor does not observe q, v, or r. Instead, the editor observes the detector score s,
which tells how the text was produced, and a noisy signal of q, which comes mostly from the
referees. The editor can scrutinize a paper more closely than a referee would, at a cost k > 0
per paper.

5.3

Results

Result 1: An AI flag predicts a worse paper. We first ask when careful and negligent
authors behave differently, absent closer scrutiny by editors (which we introduce in Result 3).
Careful authors vet the execution and negligent authors do not if
θC cv ≤ ρ ε P < θN cv .
In words: an author compares the expected reputational cost of an error being found with
the cost of verification.

16

 An author who engages with the writing is published with probability (1 − φ) πH (q0 ) +
φ πF (q0 ), because a share φ of these authors is still flagged. An author who does not engage
is flagged and published with probability πF (q0 − ∆).
Hence, engaging raises the probability of publication by:
(1 − φ) πH (q0 ) + φ πF (q0 ) − πF (q0 − ∆)
= [πF (q0 ) − πF (q0 − ∆)] + (1 − φ) [πH (q0 ) − πF (q0 )]
= D + (1 − φ) G.
Engaging with the writing has a direct benefit, D ≡ πF (q0 ) − πF (q0 − ∆), which works
through the referees’ assessment of quality, and a signaling benefit, G ≡ πH (q0 ) − πF (q0 ),
which works through the editor’s response to the flag and which an author who engages
obtains only with probability 1 − φ. From now on, we consider the writing as thinking text,
so ∆ > 0, and πF is strictly increasing in q, so D > 0.
Careful authors engage with the writing and negligent authors do not if
θC cr ≤ D ≤ D + (1 − φ) G < θN cr .
Under these conditions, careful authors vet and engage, and negligent authors do neither.
The first inequality says that careful authors would engage even if they were sure to be
flagged. Hence, careful authors engage with the writing because engaging improves the paper,
not because they fear the flag.
Importantly, the separation between careful and negligent authors does not come from the
use of the detector, but from the costs of vetting the analysis and engaging with the writing.
If removing the detector leaves the direct benefit D unchanged, setting G = 0 preserves these
inequalities and the authors’ choices. The detector only makes the separation between careful
and negligent authors more visible to the editor.
Because the same authors skip both the writing and the vetting, a flag identifies a negligent
author with probability

Every author who skips the writing is flagged, so unflagged papers all come from careful
authors.16
16

With a share h of false negatives (for instance, from humanizers), unflagged papers also include some
from negligent authors. If authors make the same choices, flagged papers remain worse in expectation than
unflagged ones as long as h + φ < 1, that is, as long as a flag raises the probability that the author is negligent.

17

 A flagged paper is worse, in expectation, than an unflagged one, through two channels.
The first channel is selection. The flag picks out negligent authors, and, as we discussed
above, negligent authors also skip vetting the execution of the paper. Hence, a flagged paper
contains an error with probability Pr(error | F ) = λ ε, while an unflagged paper contains none.
Even though the detector never looks at the execution of the paper, the flag is informative
about the execution.
The second channel is causal. Skipping the writing lowers the quality of the paper by
itself. Thus, holding q0 fixed, the expected quality of a flagged paper is E[q | F ] = q0 − λ ∆,
against q0 for an unflagged one. The more careful authors let AI write their prose (a high φ),
the lower λ is, and the less the flag tells the editor.
This does not mean that unflagged papers are good. As we mentioned in the introduction,
we have seen terrible papers for decades. The flag speaks only to the problems that AI adds
to the paper. For instance, an unflagged paper can still rest on a weak idea (a low q0 ), and
judging that remains the job of the referees, as it was before AI. The quality q0 can vary
across papers, independently of the type of the author, and we assume that the conditions
above hold for each q0 .
Result 2: A lower tolerance for mistakes in flagged papers is rational. An author
who did not check what the editor can see is unlikely to have checked what the editor cannot
see.17 Before the threat of scrutiny makes negligent authors vet (Results 3 and 4), and holding
the choices of authors fixed, suppose that a paper whose author did not vet shows a visible
mistake (a slip on the page, not a material error in the execution) with probability σN , and a
paper whose author vetted with probability σC < σN , and that visible mistakes and hidden
errors are independent given whether the author vetted. A visible mistake in a flagged paper
then raises the probability that the author did not vet from λ to:

Rejecting a flagged paper at the first mistake can be justified by Bayesian reasoning and is
not a tax on the use of AI. The editor rejects a paper when the probability of a hidden error
is high enough that the expected reputational loss for the journal exceeds the expected value
of publishing the paper, and a visible mistake in a flagged paper both raises the probability
of a hidden error, from a starting point λε that is already above the zero of an unflagged

Checking data and code, even if available in a replication package, is extremely difficult. For example,
code can be formally correct but involve subtle bugs that take considerable time to identify.

18

Result 3: Penalize the errors found, not the use of AI, by using the flag as a
trigger for closer scrutiny. Scrutinizing every submission closely is not feasible for a
journal that receives hundreds or even thousands of submissions a year. But scrutinizing
the flagged submissions is a much easier task. This is the time argument we made in the
introduction: the cost k is the time of the editor. A flag that the text is AI-generated can
help the editor allocate their time efficiently.
Suppose now that the editor scrutinizes every flagged paper and that a close reading finds
an error, when the paper has one, with probability α ∈ (0, 1], and never finds an error in a
sound paper. The editor then rejects the paper, and the author pays the penalty P . For a
negligent author, skipping the vetting is no longer cheap. The paper contains an error with
probability ε. The close reading finds the error with probability α, and the author loses a
publication that would have happened with probability πF (q0 − ∆). The author also pays the
penalty P with probability ρ + (1 − ρ) α, assuming an error missed by scrutiny is subsequently
found with probability ρ.
Without scrutiny, the gain from vetting for the negligent author is ρ ε P , which is below
θN cv (Result 1). With scrutiny, it rises because a caught error also costs the publication and
makes the penalty more likely. Thus, negligent authors vet their analysis only if:
θN cv ≤ ε [α πF (q0 − ∆) + (ρ + (1 − ρ) α) P ] .
Even with α = 1, this condition requires θN cv ≤ ε [πF (q0 − ∆) + P ]. When journals publish
few flagged papers, the penalty P does most of the work.19
The following scrutiny comparisons are written for a fixed q0 . If q0 varies and is unobserved,
their right-hand sides must be averaged over the relevant distribution of q0 ; a case-by-case
decision using referee signals must also condition on those signals. When q0 varies, deterrence
can also be partial: the right-hand side of the condition for vetting rises with πF (q0 − ∆), so
negligent authors with a low q0 , whose papers the journal rarely publishes, may keep skipping
the vetting.
For the editor, if negligent authors keep skipping both the vetting and the writing,
and publication probabilities are held fixed for papers that pass scrutiny, scrutinizing a

k < α λ ε πF (q0 − ∆) (ρL − V ), where the right-hand side is the expected loss avoided through
scrutiny. A share λε of flagged papers contains an error, the close reading catches a share α
of these errors, the journal would have published these papers with probability πF (q0 − ∆),
and each error caught saves the journal the expected reputational loss ρL minus the value V
of publishing the paper. But scrutinizing an unflagged paper never pays: unflagged papers
come from authors who already vetted their analysis. In other words, the editor spends time
only on the papers most likely to have errors.20
In summary: the flag is a trigger, not a verdict. If editors treated the flag as a verdict
and rejected every flagged paper, they would discard the sound papers of careful authors,
which constitute a share 1 − λ of the flagged papers. Treating the flag as a trigger clears
those sound papers at a cost of k per flagged paper.
Holding the choices of authors fixed, and once negligent authors vet, the trigger is better
as long as k is below the expected value of the publication decision on a flagged paper:
(1 − λ) πF (q0 ) V (q0 ) + λ πF (q0 − ∆) V (q0 − ∆).
A verdict would also change the choices of authors. Negligent authors could gain from
engaging with the writing without vetting, which avoids the flag with probability 1 − φ and
would move their errors into the unflagged papers. And that is why sanctions on authors
should follow the errors that scrutiny finds.
Result 4: Commit to scrutiny. A journal that commits to scrutiny gains even more,
as long as the conditions for deterrence in Result 3 hold, because the threat of scrutiny
leads negligent authors to vet before they submit. The journal then avoids the whole
expected loss, not just the share α, and keeps the value of publishing these papers. Therefore,
holding the pool of submissions and the publication probabilities fixed, commitment pays if
k < λ ε πF (q0 − ∆) ρ L.
But the commitment must be credible. Once negligent authors vet, flagged papers contain
no execution errors: the flag still predicts a lower quality through ∆, but no longer predicts
errors, and an editor who decides paper by paper has no reason to pay k.21
20
This argument breaks down if LLMs become good enough at making AI-generated text pass as human.
We assume for the moment that LLMs are not that good yet and that AI detectors will keep improving as
fast as LLMs do. Also, some frontier labs already watermark the text that their models generate, which
might help detection in the future.
21
Scrutinizing only a random share d of flagged papers is cheaper, as with tax audits. The conditions for
authors are the same, with dα in place of α, and commitment pays if dk < λ ε πF (q0 − ∆) ρ L, provided that
negligent authors still vet with dα in place of α.

20

 Result 5: An AI-generated referee report adds nothing. The output of the referee is
a signal about q whose precision rises with the effort of the referee. Scrutiny by the editor can
catch errors, but not the loss of quality ∆ that comes from skipping the writing: a shallower
idea is not an error that the editor can point to. The signal of the referee is therefore the
main defense of the journal against ∆. An AI-generated report R = f (paper) is a function of
the paper alone, plus, at most, randomness that, given the paper, is independent of q, and
the editor can compute this function at negligible cost: most likely, the editor has access to
the same LLMs as the referees. So Pr(q | paper, R) = Pr(q | paper), and the report adds
no information beyond what the editor already has. The editor could have asked the same
model and expedited the process.
A referee who generates the report with AI, reads the report, and agrees with it without
contributing independent judgment is in the same position. Every paper in economics, even
those that have shaped the profession for decades and defined whole literatures, has problems.
To put it more plainly: a long list of problems exists for every paper, whatever its quality q.
And, as we discussed above, it is trivial to prime an LLM to generate a negative report.
The value added by a referee is not just finding that an entry in Table 8.2 of Section
8 has the wrong sign or even that the authors have not considered “additional baselines.”
Instead, referees make a difference when they weigh the problems of the paper against the
overall contribution of the paper and decide what needs to be fixed and what does not.
Many perfectly fine papers can get published in an excellent field journal but should not be
published in a top general-interest journal. The referee needs to help the editor make that
call.
Even worse, delegation by referees feeds back to authors. If, under AI-based refereeing, the
publication rule becomes insensitive to quality (unlike in Result 1, but as in our experiment, in
which every report written by AI recommended major revision), so that πF (q0 ) = πF (q0 − ∆),
the direct benefit of engaging with the writing, D, goes to zero, and careful authors lose their
main reason to do the thinking. They engage only if θC cr ≤ (1 − φ) G, that is, only to avoid
the flag.
Our model takes the set of submissions as given. If AI lowers the cost of producing papers
and induces a proportionally larger increase in submissions by negligent authors, the share
of careful authors µ falls. This is how the market-for-lemons mechanism of Akerlof (1970)
would manifest itself, and the pool of submissions would deteriorate. A lower µ also raises λ:
as the pool gets worse, a larger share of flagged papers comes from negligent authors.

21

 6

Taking stock

As LLMs have become prevalent in economics, peer review needs to adapt to this new reality.
In this paper, we have outlined why the burden of verification must remain with the authors
of papers and why AI-generated referee reports are unacceptable. We have also proposed a
few ideas for making the system more workable in the near term. We hope to start a serious
conversation about this issue.
If producing papers stays cheap while the time of referees grows scarcer, professional
organizations and publishers should plan for more desk rejections, higher submission fees,
paid or graded referees, and fewer referees per paper. They should also consider adding an
automatic AI review that authors must respond to before they can complete their submission.
For experts in mechanism design, there is much work to do here. Neither of us is a theorist,
and our research has always focused on macroeconomics and econometrics. But economic
theorists have thought long and hard about similar problems in other contexts, and our
model leaves most of the hard questions open. Theorists can bring their expertise to these
questions and produce far more than we can, even with the help of LLMs.
It will take time for the profession to adjust to this new environment, and the adjustment
will be the outcome of a long and hard process. In the meantime, however, we believe that
all of us can already do something, and for that reason we close with a practical guide.
1. Authors. Use AI for code, data, proofs, and editing, but verify every output and keep
the evidence of the verification. Do not submit text you have not read and revised, or
cite papers you have not read.
2. Referees. Make up your mind about the paper before using an LLM. Use AI to polish
your report, find related papers, verify specific claims, or turn your detailed notes into
prose that you then check. Do not upload the manuscript into an LLM unless the
journal allows it. And, most importantly, decline the invitation if you lack the time
(and do not ignore the invitation email: just click “decline”).
3. Editors. Screen papers and reports with a detector. Read closely what is flagged,
sanction the errors you find rather than the use of AI, and do not forward reports you
believe were generated by AI.

The experiment

Reports. The reports come from the Corpus of Transparent Peer Review (Akbas et al.,
2023), which collects the published referee reports of 560 Nature Communications papers.
The corpus is distributed under a CC BY 4.0 license. We put the papers in a random order,
took one first-round report at random from each, and used the first 25. All reports were
written between 2018 and mid-2020, before ChatGPT was released in 2022. We matched
reports to the published versions of the papers through Crossref. The 25 reports run from
256 to 1,310 words.
Versions. Research assistants ran each prompt once per report, in a new chat with memory
and personalization turned off. The Claude runs used Claude Sonnet 5.5 and the ChatGPT
runs used ChatGPT 5.6 Terra, both at the highest reasoning setting. For prompt 4, the
research assistants attached the PDF of the published paper.
Scoring. We uploaded each text to Pangram as a Word document in November 2026. We
recorded the shares that Pangram classified as human, AI-assisted, and AI-generated. Table 2
reports the averages by LLM.
Prompts. Each prompt was followed by the full text of the report or, for prompt 4,
accompanied by the PDF of the paper.
1. Proofreading. Proofread the referee report below. Correct spelling, grammar, and
punctuation errors only. Do not change the wording, style, tone, or structure, and do
not add or remove content. Return the full corrected report and nothing else.

What analog processes cause a CMOS memory IC that we like to think of as being discrete to be consistently wrong at reading its stored values? I'd like to know all the way down to the interaction between the gates and traces. Did some pathway erode due to constant interchange of charge carriers? Did thermal cycles or stress cause one of the mechanical interconnects on the package to fracture and no longer conduct? If so, which one? According to AI, one type of failure mode in those early aerospace CMOS chips was sudden parasitic current in the PNPN junction being caused by a high energy particle, shorting paths to ground melting metal. HUMAN.md — Briana (Mazzio) May 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Skip to the text 

 
 
 
 BRIANA (MAZZIO) MAY · APR 28, 2026 
 HUMAN.md 
 
 > a working manifesto. notes-to-self, mostly. 
 > not a thinkpiece. not a thread. not a deck. 
 > last edited at the kitchen table, coffee #2. 
 
 
 ## what this file is 
 A reminder, in plain text, of what I think humans actually bring to the table now that the machines are very good and getting better every day. 
 I keep coming back to the word "taste" and I keep finding it too small. Taste is the surface. There is a whole engine underneath it, and that engine is the part the model can't have. Yet. Maybe ever. I don't know. I'm not in that argument. I'm in this one: 
 ## the actual job 
 ### 1. break the rule on purpose 
 Models are trained on the average. The average is the floor, not the ceiling. Our job is not to conform a little better than the last person who conformed. Our job is to know the rule cold, and then break it on purpose, in public, with a reason. 
 Symmetry is a rule. Break it. Three-act structure is a rule. Break it. "Don't shoot into the sun" is a rule. Break it. 
 If you can't say why you broke it, you didn't break it, you just missed. 
 ### 2. find the thing in the weird place 
 Inspiration does not live in the first ten image-search results. It lives in: 
 
 a misprinted parking ticket 
 the way your grandfather folded a napkin 
 an obscure Victorian zoetrope of a cat 
 the back of a menu in a town you can't pronounce 
 the tension in Rene Magritte's "The Son of Man", 1946 
 
 A model averages the internet. A human walks somewhere strange and brings back something unexpected. 
 ### 3. advocate for the human and humanity 
 Every brief now has an invisible third party at the table. Someone has to keep saying "and what does this feel like for the person on the other end of it." Someone has to keep saying "how is humanity better through the birthing of this idea?" That's the job. Not "is it on-brand." Not "does it convert." What does it feel like? what good does it do? 
 If you aren't there saying it, no one will. The model certainly won't. 
 ### 4. design for emotional resonance, not correctness 
 Tension. Surprise. Restraint. The pause before the punchline. The photograph that's almost in focus. The sentence that ends one beat earlier than you expected. 
 These are not bugs. These are the entire reason anyone remembers anything. "Correct" is the lowest bar in the building. Step over it and keep walking. 
 ### 5. seek delight, not delivery 
 I would rather make one thing that makes someone laugh out loud on a train than ten things that "meet the brief." At the very least, it needs to make ME laugh. This is a personal bias. 
 If it's not at least a little bit fun, why are we here? 
 ### 6. experiment ruthlessly, ship more than you opine 
 A working sketch beats a confident take. Every time. A bad first draft beats a brilliant unwritten one. Every time. A weird little prototype beats a slide deck about prototyping. Every. Time. 
 Make 50 things. Throw away 47. Talk about the 3. Do not, under any circumstances, become a person who mostly posts opinions about other people's work. 
 ### 7. own the output. fully. 
 If the AI output is bad, the AI did not fail you. You failed it. You picked the tool. You wrote the prompt. You accepted the result. You shipped it. 
 The fix is not a better model, or a return to tools of the past. The fix is a sharper you. Sharpen yourself. Sharpen your ideas. Sharpen the way you say what you mean, because the gap between what you wanted and what came back is almost always a gap in you , not in the tool. 
 Powerful tools reward the people who showed up sharp, iterate, spend extra time on the vision. They expose the people who didn't. AI is not the great equalizer, it is the great amplifier. 
 ### 8. design with it, not next to it 
 Watching the generation happen is not the work. Prompting once and accepting the result is not the work. The work is the back-and-forth. The push. The loop. The "again, but tweak is this way..." The hundredth iteration where the thing finally clicks. 
 If you're a spectator to your own output, you are not the author of your own output. Get your hands in. 
 ### 9. play with purpose. and play for play. 
 Both. At the same time. Some days the play is in service of a thing. Some days the play is the thing. A practice that only ever has goals is a job. A practice that never has goals is a hobby. The good work lives in between. Play doesn't result in burnout. It results in excitement, happiness, experiment, the unexpected, and an urge to play more. 
 ### 10. be a builder and an ideas person 
 The split is fake. It was always fake. It's especially fake now. The people who can think of the thing and make the thing are going to eat. The people who can only do one half are going to be very busy explaining why the other half is hard, or blame the processes or tools. 
 Don't be that person. Learn the other half. It's never been cheaper to learn it. 
 
 ## things I am trying to stop doing 
 
 waiting until it's "ready" 
 editing in my head instead of on the page 
 making but not sharing publicly 
 taking briefs that secretly bore me 
 pretending taste is an innate quality 
 treating "AI" like a noun instead of a verb 
 
 ## things I am trying to do more 
 
 finish the bad version first 
 show people the in-between, mess, experiments 
 write the thing I'd want to read 
 dig deeper, get help 
 stop pretending I know stuff, ask dumber questions 
 say the more specific thing 
 
 
 This file will be wrong in six months. That is fine. I'd rather be specifically wrong than vaguely correct. 
 — b. last touched, kitchen table, late.

 This is a beautiful expression, and the author would do well to refine their notion of taste further. Anyone familiar with Dr. John Vervaeke's work will find another notion, relevance realization (RR), fits nicely. The thing I like about RR over "taste" when talking about AI is that it captures what the taste metaphor does not - that there is a missing _relevant_ dimension of consideration from the LLMs output. "Hey you got the code working but this 4000 line PR will never be approved."
"You spent tokens hardening the API, when this entire project is just a local test that will never hit production". Etc, etc, ad nauseum. Vervaeke reveals why in his lecture series "Awakening from the Meaning Crisis". Fundamentally, RR cannot be achieved through reason alone. Full stop. Vervaeke uses this fact to point out the irrationality of the "rationalist" movement in order to highlight its dangers (which many would agree the effective altruism crowd has thoroughly proven him right about), but the same framing and argument can be used to explain why your AI has bad taste. There is no way to enumerate the set of dimensions that are or are not relevant in a given real world context. The detail of the universe, combined with the set of actions an agent does (and does NOT!) take leads to a combinatorial explosion of complexity. AI agents need to be told what to do, and even then, they will only stochastically sample what you tell them. Anthropic tells Claude lots of things about Rust, for example, and things to look out for in security context, but they fundamentally cannot put enough information in to grant the agent the ability to wisely choose what is and is not relevant. You can only ever consider _some_ relevant things. I don't personally think it is impossible for computers to perform RR, it's just that today's agents do not, which is why its taste and yours differ. reply aDyslecticCrow 1 day ago | prev | next [–]

California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents - ABC7 San Francisco 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 24/7 Live San Francisco East Bay South Bay Peninsula North Bay Waymo CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents By Tim Johns Tuesday, November 17, 2026 6:29PM The California DMV has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on state freeways, citing concerns after several recent traffic incidents in the Bay Area. @luluesque The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard. The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them. One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times. The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month. VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway A surprising moment caught on video shows a driverless Waymo robotaxi attempting to bypass CHP officers controlling traffic on I-280 in San Francisco. In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority. "Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News. The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new. This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones. The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until   Waymo demonstrates to the   Department   that   it has taken   effective   corrective   actions..." "I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco. Top Stories Live Bay Area weather updates: Severe flooding inundates roadways leads to crashes, closures across Northern California Rare waterspouts over San Francisco Bay possibly fueled by El Niño conditions Video shows flooding across San Francisco Bay Area as storm batters region Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop. MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco "An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said. Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday. "I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said. Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue. "You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.  Gemini 4 Neon is available
 
 
 
 
 
 Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

 Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). 
 
 

 

 
 





 
 
 
 
 







 














 


 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 



 
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Built for production-ready code 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. 
 
 

 

 
 





 
 
 
 
 







 














 


 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. 
 
 

 

 
 







 



 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 




 
 
 
 
 















 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 




 
 
 
 
 















 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 




 
 
 
 
 















 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 




 
 
 
 
 















 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 


 
 
 




 
 
 
 
 















 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. 
 
 

 

 
 





 
 
 
 
 







 














 


 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. 
 
 

 

 
 





 
 
 
 
 







 














 


 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 
 Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team.

 Purely outside looking in, but yes, I'd argue you are right and higher-quality is a major part of it, both for pre- and post-training. There appears to be a far greater willingness to adopt specifically tailored training sets from third-parties, consistently update and build on them. From simple frontend work to strategically adding virtual rulers when working with LIDAR scans to extract more accurate data, there are very clear points when Anthropic introduces a new external data set into their mix and while I have seen the same from competitors such as Google, there simply appears to be a greater tendency to stick with these once they have them. As an example, at release it was quite apparent that Gemini 3 Pro, 3 Flash and Opus 4.5 had a similar, possible even the same frontend-focused training base bought in from a third party. But while Anthropic has had both smaller and larger improvements across each subsequent Opus release, I have not noticed such a consistent improvement with Gemini models over the last year. Maybe Anthropic simply buys updates more often, maybe they create more artificial PRs on top, who knows. Same with the LIDAR scans, there was a point a few months ago when models started to exhibit a very systematic way of handling visual references in some few leather-crafting tasks, enabling whole new ways of working more efficiently combining existing measurements with images. Step-by-step pixel measurements, compensation for angles and poor captures, etc. Have since seen this in other models, again very much feels like a bought in data set that they are pushing as far as it goes. Then there is 3D capability with models like Muse Wonder Full. I have not used it myself, if it ain't on API, it doesn't exist, but have seen PRs and do find the model output very parsable, despite it being terrible at any modelling task because these capabilities do not emerge from just training on vast amounts of data, they require high-quality, well tailored, step-by-step reference data of the entire process. Harness wise, while pure output performance is very consistent across harnesses in my evals (I nowadays use both OpenCode via API and the labs own harness three times each to normalise), Anthropic also appears to be far more willing to use the time between releases to prepare features for the next. Stuff like workflows, proper subagent implementation, advisor, etc. often have found there way into Claude Code either in-between models or were first seen with a model that couldn't fully leverage these. 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit • VioletPixel 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 VioletPixel 
 Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea 
 
 
 Blog 
 About 
 Now 
 Contact 
 Feed 
 
 
 
 
 Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST 
 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit 
 Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions. 
 When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable. 
 The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things: 
 
 Intimate knowledge of the system 
 The drive and determination to force the system to work 
 
 Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure. 
 Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse. 
 And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI. 
 I guess that depends on how you look at it. 
 I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit. 
 So where did they go? 
 Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity. 
 Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea. 
 People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from? 
 It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics. 
 Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this. 
 It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real. 
 Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system). 
 We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail. 
 I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now. 
 Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.

 "Smart" is a word we label for someone who possesses enough "intelligence", "knowledge" or "experience". Generative AI started with lots of "knowledge", and has since been trained on lots of practical examples to give it lots of "experience". AI has significantly more "knowledge" and "experience" than a human can attain during his lifetime. But it isn't and can't be "intelligent". It can't "think outside the box", it doesn't have "intuition", it doesn't know how to "ask the right questions"... It can simulate all three if the problem you point it at is related to the "knowledge and experience" it has, or by the sheer fact of letting it run a long time until it figures out the right solution by just analyzing lots of unneeded paths inside its 1M context window. If you're smart and want to see it's "non-intelligence" in action, just turn on the extended thinking summaries and watch it work in real time on some harder task, like debugging some non-trivial bug. It's initial intuition is often very wrong, it often presumes something to be true without asking or checking, or double checks stuff that do not need double checking, if it sees contradictory evidence, it can't properly assess what's going on... The thing is - if you don't see this (and most people won't cause by default it doesn't show you its process, you have to turn it on) - and just let it run for an hour or two, it often eventually does arrive at the correct conclusion - and you may consider it smart for figuring it out, even if you yourself could've figured that out 2x faster, but were too lazy to dig deep.  Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion 



 
 Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 

 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. 

 CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. 

 GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 : Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings 

 Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. 

 GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x : Double free in regular expression compilation 

 Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. 

 GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px : Integer overflow in case conversion of strings 

 Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. 

 GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching 

 Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. 

 GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w : Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation 

 Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. 

 GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 : Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s 

 Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s . Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. 

 GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching 

 Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. 

 Affected versions 

 
 Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier 
 Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 
 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 
 

 Recommended action 

 We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. 

 Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes.

This repository holds the **BF16** weights of DaisyRose-27B. ## 1. General Information DaisyRose-27B is RadixArk's first model: a multimodal reasoning model built on Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning only, without any supervised fine-tuning or distillation. It was trained on about 1,200 curated long-horizon agent tasks, with sessions of up to 1M tokens, for 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0, and the model also improves on most of the other coding, reasoning and instruction-following benchmarks below. DaisyRose-27B keeps the base model's architecture, tokenizer and chat template, along with its image understanding and 256K-token context, so it is a drop-in replacement for Qwen3.8-27B in existing inference and post-training stacks. Weights are released under Apache-2.0 in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4. ## 2.
