## 3. Getting Started ### Serving with SGLang We strongly recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding, using the official `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` Docker image (DSpark is included). The [SGLang cookbook for DaisyRose-27B](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/RadixArk/DaisyRose-27B) generates the launch command for each GPU and precision. BF16 on a 4-GPU node, one replica per GPU: ```bash docker run --gpus all --ipc=host --shm-size 32g -p 30000:30000 \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \ lmsysorg/sglang:latest \ python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path RadixArk/DaisyRose-27B \ --served-model-name DaisyRose-27B \ --tp-size 1 --dp-size 4 \ --context-length 262144 \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \ --trust-remote-code \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \ --chunked-prefill-size 2048 \ --mamba-full-memory-ratio 11.01 \ --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \ --mamba-ssm-dtype float32 \ --speculative-algorithm DSPARK \ --speculative-draft-model-path RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark \ --speculative-draft-attention-backend flashinfer \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 ``` ### Supported hardware DaisyRose-27B runs on a single GPU, from data-center cards (H200, B200, GB300) to local hardware such as RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090 and DGX Spark. The weights take about 52 GB in BF16, 29 GB in FP8 and 23 GB in NVFP4; NVFP4 needs a Blackwell GPU. See the [SGLang cookbook for DaisyRose-27B](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/RadixArk/DaisyRose-27B) for per-GPU launch settings. ### Quickstart The example uses the `openai` Python client against the server above. The model thinks before answering by default; the thinking comes back in `reasoning_content` and the answer in `content`. ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1", api_key="none") SAMPLING = dict(temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, extra_body={"top_k": 20, "min_p": 0.0}) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="DaisyRose-27B", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How many positive divisors does 360 have?"}], **SAMPLING, ) print(resp.choices[0].message.reasoning_content) # thinking print(resp.choices[0].message.content) # final answer ``` - Use `temperature 1.0`, `top_p 0.95`, `top_k 20`, `min_p 0` in thinking mode. - Leave `max_tokens` unset for hard problems; long thinking runs to tens of thousands of tokens. - In multi-turn chats, send earlier turns back with their `reasoning_content`; the chat template keeps it by default. ## 4. Model Properties | Property | Value | | --- | --- | | Model type | Multimodal causal language model with a vision encoder; thinking model | | Architecture type | Qwen3.8-27B (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`): 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern of linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) and full-attention layers, hidden size 5,120, a 27-layer vision encoder, and one multi-token-prediction layer | | Parameters | 27.8B in total, including a 0.46B vision encoder and a 0.42B multi-token-prediction head | | Context length | 262,144 tokens | | Numerics support | BF16, FP8, NVFP4 | | Input modalities | Text, images | | Output modalities | Text | ## 5. Training DaisyRose-27B is trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning only. The vision encoder and the multi-token-prediction head are the base model's, unchanged. **Training data.** We built the tasks with [Eigent AI](https://www.eigent.ai), starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science and other fields. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. Each task targets a mistake the base model makes and is tuned until its solve rate is neither too easy nor too hard to learn from. Each is a long job of several interdependent problems: an attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox, with more than 100 tool calls and more than 256K output tokens. We reviewed every task together with the model's attempts, and fixed or removed any that could be passed without really solving it. **Training infrastructure.** Training ran fully asynchronously with [Miles](https://github.com/radixark/miles), our open-source reinforcement-learning framework, on RadixArk's internal training backend. 128 H200s ran the agent on its tasks, served by [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang), while 16 more trained on the finished trajectories; after every step the updated weights went back to the 128. Each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens. The run took 18 days on 144 H200s, about 63,000 GPU-hours. Every attempt ran in a sandbox on our own sandbox service, built on [AgentENV](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/AgentENV). ## 6. Acknowledgements We thank Eigent AI for building the training data with us, and the Qwen team for Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities and other open-source projects, including AgentENV and Harbor. ## 7. License **GOVERNING DOWNLOAD TERMS:** Use of the model is governed by the [Apache 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) license. DaisyRose-27B is a derivative of Alibaba's [Qwen3.8-27B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), which is also licensed under Apache 2.0.

page:https://www.radixark.com/blog/daisy.text: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency | RadixArk Blog Platform Open source SGLang Miles Blog Mission Log in All posts November 18, 2026 DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. We are releasing BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget. DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1 . The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes. High-quality Training Data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria. Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from. Every task is a long job with several problems chained together. Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens. There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time. Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory. 80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes. Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face , and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles . DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai . We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩ © 2026 RadixArk Terms of Service Privacy Policy Email us

 Cambridge Dictionary reveals Word of the Year 2026 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 What Does It Mean to Be Human in the Age of AI? – Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026. 
 

 
 
 The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines. 'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’. In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay . Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most. "But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.” ‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”. Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign , Human Consent Foundation and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman. As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April. Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common. “AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them." Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing. “We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion? “All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you." Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.” Adapted from the Cambridge University Press & Assessment website .

LLM assisted reverse engineering · Slow Chronicle Skip to content Slow Chronicle projects blog archive tags LLM assisted reverse engineering By ioma8 18 Nov 2026 Tags: reverse engineering , rust , ai , ghidra I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it. 
 Set Up 
 Tools which I mostly use are these: 
 
 
 
 TOOL 
 use 
 
 
 
 
 DeepSeek Harness + Deepseek v4.1 Flash 
 Thats the AI I am using. Occasionaly I use Codex with Luna or Terra but Deepseek is super performant, fast and cheap 
 
 
 Ghidra + MCP bridge 
 The best in the market, free, disassembler and decompiler. With the MCP bridge agents can use it very well 
 
 
 radare2 and kuna 
 CLI disassemblers and decompilers. Not as good as Ghidra but much faster and possibly better usable for AIs 
 
 
 
 Process 
 What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this. 
 
 Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions). 
 Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later. 
 Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image. 
 
 Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better. 
 On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do: 
 
 Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings. 
 Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature. 
 Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware. 
 Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead. 
 Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have. 
 
 SKILLS 
 Here are some of my major skills I use frequently. 
 Matt Pottock - Grill me 
 It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt: 
 
 
 text 
 
 
 Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions
whose answers are crucial for your further progress.
Ask only one question at a time.
 
 mattpocock / skills Shell Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. 
 Ghidra / other RE tooling skill 
 It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation. 
 ioma8 / ghidra-decompile-skill Java Agent skill + 22 Ghidra scripts for fast targeted decompilation, and the fix for GhidraMCP extension/Ghidra version mismatches. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. 
 Hypothesis debugging 
 That is also my own skill. Its related to how I wrote earlier how important it is to make the agent document everything into MD files. This skill forces agent who is getting stuck to follow this loop: 
 
 Make a hypothesis of why / how something works. Write it down into CSV table of hypotheses, saved on disc. 
 Design experiment (probe, logging, ...) which will definitively prove or disprove this hypothesis. 
 Record the result. 
 Repeat. 
 
 This is variation of scientific method and it significantly helps agents when they are getting stuck on some problem. Stops it going in circles. By forcing it to do definitive experiments. No endless guessing and trying random things. This one is crucial in my opinion. I made it public too, so other can benefit from it. 
 ioma8 / hypothesis-debugging Agent skill for hypothesis-driven debugging — one testable hypothesis at a time, logged and validated in a CSV loop. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. 
 Implementation of hacks and probes 
 For implementing anything I basically go for 2 toolings. 
 
 Python but with UV tooling. UV tooling allows to make custom envs super quickly and portably. Also allows to make single-file, inline dependencies scripts. Python is great for prototyping or quickly making probes or even decompilation helpers. 
 Rust for actual implementation of given hack. Whenever it is possible I am using rust for this. It has many reasons but he two main are: 
 
 
 it is very elegant language for me personally to work with and 
 it provides brutally good feedback loops to the agent when it iterates - the compiler is very strict and points the agent immediately to any possible memory or syntax issues he might be heading to. 
Of course rust has also its downsides, like slower compile times, but overal its mature language with plethora of build targets (I have implemented in it webs, desktop apps, hacks / trainers but even firmwares for various embedded languages). 
 
 My hacking successes 
 With the AI assisted reverse engineering I was able to achieve such crazy reverse engineering succeses, in the last 6 months, which would take me years each on its own, if done by hands. 
 
 Reverse engineered and hacked Alphasmart NEO typewriting device 
 Completely mapped communication protocols of many devices like EmWave biofeedback device or both my Sony Alpha mirrorless cameras. Allowing me to make custom desktop and mobile apps for file transfer, wireless control and more. I even managed to make this way a wireless webcam from my A7III mirrorless camera. 
 Hacked into and developed custom firmwares for musical synthesizers:
 
 Arturia MiniFreak 
 Teenage Engineering OP-Z 
 Akai MPC Sample 
 
 
 Made custom firmware for Xteink X4 ebook reader 
 Fixed driver for old HP printer for MacOs 
 Cracked tons of license-locked abandonware softwares from my youth 
 Developed custom lightweight Evernote client 
 And many more 
 
 Sometimes its a thin boundary between reverse engineering and software development. Sometimes you just decipher the proprietary save file format of the ugly paid app and then move into the clean software development phase of building your new, totally unique editor, to work with these files. (yes I made custom Photoshop too and its not the ArtCraft suite - I did it about a year before them, just for me). 
 Final thoughts 
 Reverse engineering and hacking into old softwares or devices has always been a hobby for me. I understand assembly, I understand hardware. But it was long and tedious process. 
 With the cheap accesibility to smart LLM tools in these days, this hobby took dramatic turn for me. I do not miss manually analyzing the assembly instructions. But I love quickly getting the results. Yes my long experience helps me steer the agents the correct way. But that is also fun. And I am learning a ton of things along the way. 
 I wish everyone would try to do some hacks of his own. For me the hobby is driven by curiosity. And LLMs didn't take that away. They gave me turbo boost to my wonderings and explorations. Let's free our minds! 
 Edit: We are getting popular on HN! Didnt expect this one day after deploying my blog! Super happy!

 iceman84 16 hours ago [–] 
 We introduce SRE-1, a 27B model trained with reinforcement learning to find the root cause of production alerts. On 49 difficult live production cases, SRE-1 dominates the Pareto frontier of pass rate against cost: at every budget from our cheapest configuration upward, it has the highest pass rate of any model we tested. Reinforcement learning (RL) raises the pass rate of a single investigation more than fivefold, from 6.9% for the base model to 38.8%. An ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matches Fable 5.2, the strongest frontier model we measured, at a 71% pass rate while costing 37% less. SRE-1 also outperforms frontier models at synthesizing saved investigations, which is why its ensembles improve on a single investigation. We train on several types of realistic internal environments with our production investigation tools. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B, we train with a modified CISPO objective for 200 steps on up to 512 GPUs, over 1,549 unique incidents, and select SRE-1 from the resulting checkpoints. reply

 Lawyers’ Committee Files Lawsuit on Behalf of Black Students Detained and Searched Due to AI Alert Falsely Identifying a Bag of Chips as a Firearm 

 by Press | Nov 17, 2026 | Blog 
 
 
 
 Case focuses on alleged failures surrounding AI systems and impact on students 
 BALTIMORE COUNTY, MD — Today, the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law filed a lawsuit on behalf of four Black current and former students against Omnilert, LLC, Baltimore County Public Schools (BCPS) and personnel, the Baltimore County Police Department, and individual officers for the unlawful detention and search of the students due to both technological and human errors involving an AI weapon-detection surveillance system. In Allen, et al. v. Omnilert, et al., the Lawyers' Committee represents the four teenagers, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III. The Lawyers' Committee is joined by Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP, as pro bono counsel, and Engel Law Group, P.C. 
 This lawsuit stems from events that took place in October 2025 when Omnilert Gun Detect, an AI gun-detection system used throughout Baltimore County Public Schools, mistook a teenager's bag of chips for a firearm at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County, Maryland. The false alert eventually led to armed local police swarming the teenagers on campus just steps away from their school's entrance. They were ordered to their knees, handcuffed, and searched, despite doing nothing wrong. 
 The AI surveillance system's error prompted the false alarm and set off a chain of human failures, with everyone from Omnilert's own staff and the school principal to the Baltimore County Police Department all missing or ignoring clear evidence there was no gun. The system, which school officials knew regularly produced false alerts, erroneously alerted the school that there was a 90% probability of a gun being on campus, and that alert kept going even after school staff and local police reviewed the image and determined it was a mistake. School and police officials cancelled the alert, but armed police were dispatched anyway because school and police officials failed to have sufficient protocols in place to prevent cancelled alerts from triggering armed police responses. 
 "These students were failed not only by a technology that is prone to false alerts, but also by the very adults meant to keep them safe when we send them to school. Instead of this protection, they were met with guns and traumatized. And it could have been even worse," said Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law . "Overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix. We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids. We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children's fate in the hands of AI." 
 "Unregulated AI has profound consequences, especially when involving young people. As this technology gains more widespread adoption, it cannot happen at the expense of clear regulations, guardrails, and expectations for the adults that interact with it," said Leah Frazier, director of the Digital Justice Initiative at the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law . "This should have never been escalated to the police. It simply should not have happened, and we filed this lawsuit to prevent this from ever happening again." 
 “The police told my son this could have been a real problem. No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother," said Freida Winfield ,who was on her way to pick up her son Keith and the students when they were all ordered to their knees, handcuffed, and searched . 
 Through the lawsuit, the Lawyers' Committee seeks to reform local police and school procedures to ensure that these public actors verify reports from AI threat-detection platforms, evaluate whether this AI technology is appropriate for use in schools, and develop sufficient policies to ensure that false alerts do not trigger armed police responses. 
 The Lawyers' Committee argues that police and schools require more training, oversight, and transparency relating to errors and outcomes, as well as community input on how this technology is utilized. 
 This injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations. The Lawyers' Committee has been vocal about assessing and regulating the use of AI technology across these critical areas for this reason, especially as any harms and inaccuracies disproportionately impact Black communities and other people of color. This is especially true when it comes to criminal justice. 
 The Lawyers' Committee filed the case in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County, Maryland. The complaint alleges violations of the teenagers' federal and state Constitutional rights, negligence and gross negligence, and other violations by the defendants, including Omnilert, Baltimore County school officials, and Baltimore County Police Department officers. 
 The complaint may be found here . 
 ### 
 About the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law : Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, formed in 1963 at the request of President John F. Kennedy to mobilize the nation's leading lawyers as agents for change in the Civil Rights Movement. Today, the Lawyers' Committee uses legal advocacy to achieve racial justice, fighting inside and outside the courts to ensure that Black people and other people of color have the voice, opportunity, and power to make the promises of our democracy real. The Lawyers' Committee implements its mission and objectives by marshaling the pro bono resources of the bar for litigation, public policy, advocacy and other forms of service by lawyers to the cause of civil rights.

# Unreal Tournament 2004 Modernized

An unofficial, non-commercial port of Unreal Tournament 2004 (build 3369) to modern hardware and operating systems. It is a fan project, made out of appreciation for a game that is now more than twenty years old.

## What it is

- Windows (x86, x64), Linux (x86, x64, arm64), Android (arm64) and the web (WebAssembly).
- SDL3 for windows and input, OpenGL ES 3 for rendering (ANGLE on Windows, WebGL 2 on the web), OpenAL for sound, Bullet behind the Karma physics API.
- Network compatible with retail build 3369. WebRTC transport next to UDP, so browsers can join and host.
- No editor. The command line tools of `ucc` are kept.

The game content is not part of this repository or its releases. The first start downloads it or takes it from a UT2004 install.

## Download

The [releases](https://github.com/K-Adam/UT2004/releases) carry a build for each platform, and the web version runs at <https://ut2004.dev>.

| File | Platform |
|---|---|
| `UT2004-<version>-win64.msi` | Windows x64 installer, for everyone on the PC or only for you. Remove it under Installed apps. |
| `UT2004-<version>-win64.zip` | The same without an installer. Unpack it and start `System/UT2004.exe`. |
| `UT2004-<version>-linux64.tar.gz`, `-linux-arm64.tar.gz` | Linux x64 and arm64, built on Ubuntu 22.04. Unpack it and run `./install.sh` (or `sudo ./install.sh --system` for everyone), then start `ut2004`. The installed folder has an `uninstall.sh`. SDL 3 is included, the other libraries come from your distribution: OpenAL, Vorbis, Bullet, squish, OpenGL ES, speexdsp, OpenSSL and curl. |
| `UT2004-<version>-android.apk` | Android 9 or newer on arm64. |
| `UT2004-<version>-web.zip` | The files of the web page. Only the page at `ut2004.dev` gets the hosted content: on another domain the browser blocks the downloads from `assets.ut2004.dev`, and on localhost the page looks for a local content link instead. In both cases it offers to import a zip of a retail install. Only pages on the origins the web master allows get the server list and can host or join games through it. |

On the first start the game asks for its content. It can download the full game from the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/ut2004-3369) (3.8 GB, about 13 GB of free space while it unpacks), or use the folder of a UT2004 install in place. The Android app also offers a set of ten maps (1 GB) and takes an archive or folder on the device.

## Build

Third party libraries come from [vcpkg](https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg) on Windows, Android and the web (`VCPKG_ROOT` must point to it), and from the system packages on Linux. Clone with `git submodule update --init`.

| Target | Needs | Configure | Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows x64 | Visual Studio 2022 | `cmake --preset win64` | `cmake --build --preset win64-release` |
| Windows x86 | Visual Studio 2022 | `cmake --preset win32` | `cmake --build --preset win32-release` |
| Linux | GCC, Ninja, CMake 3.26, SDL 3.2 | `cmake --preset linux64` | `cmake --build --preset linux64-release` |
| Android arm64 | JDK 17, SDK platform 36, NDK r28c | `cmake --preset android-arm64` | `cmake --build --preset android-arm64-release` |
| Web | emsdk 7.0.0 | `cmake --preset web` | `cmake --build --preset web-release` |

Linux packages on Debian and Ubuntu: `build-essential ninja-build pkg-config zlib1g-dev libvorbis-dev libopenal-dev libbullet-dev libbullet-extras-dev libgles-dev libsquish-dev libssl-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev nlohmann-json3-dev libspeexdsp-dev`, plus SDL 3.2 or newer.

The output lands in `build/<preset>/System/`. The Android build writes `build/android-arm64/UT2004.apk` and the web build writes `build/web/`.

### Checks and releases

`python3 Tools/tidy.py` runs clang-tidy with the checks in `.clang-tidy` (Linux, needs Clang). GitHub Actions runs it on every push to `main` and every pull request and then builds and packages every platform. A tag like `v1.0.0` or `v1.0.0-rc.1` also publishes the files as a release and the web build to GitHub Pages.

The Windows installer is the `msi` target (`cmake --build --preset win64-release --target msi`). It needs the [WiX](https://wixtoolset.org) .NET tool with its UI and Util extensions on the path.

### Script packages

Online play needs UnrealScript packages identical to retail, so `Scripts/` holds the retail packages plus this port's two fix packages, and every build copies them to `build/Scripts/`. After changing `GUI2K4Fix` or `XAdminFix`, set `UT_RETAIL_DIR` to your UT2004 install (the compiler loads its content) and run `cmake --build --preset <build preset> --target ucc_make`. It compiles those two and puts them back into `Scripts/`.

## Run

Without an installer, start `UT2004.exe` (`ut2004-bin` on Linux) in the `System` folder of a release, or in `build/<preset>/System/` of your own build.

A dedicated server is `UCC server DM-Rankin` (`ucc-bin` on Linux). It does not ask for content, so start the game once on that machine or add the `Paths=` lines of your content to its `UT2004.ini`.

The web page is served from any static host, for example `python -m http.server 8000 -d build/web`.

## Files and logs

| Platform | Settings, saves and `UT2004.log` |
|---|---|
| Windows | the `System` folder the game runs from, or `%LocalAppData%\UT2004\System` when that folder is read-only, as in an install for everyone |
| Linux | `~/.ut2004/System/` (next to the binary with `-nohomedir`) |
| Android | `Android/data/org.ut2004.game/files/UT2004/System/` |
| Web | the browser's IndexedDB for the page |

Downloaded game content goes next to that `System` folder. Uninstalling keeps your settings, saves and the downloaded content, delete the folder to remove them.

## Network connections

The game only connects when you use an online feature. These are the defaults in `System/Default.ini`, and all of them can be changed or emptied there.

| What | Where | When |
|---|---|---|
| Community master servers | `utmaster.openspy.net`, `ut2004master.333networks.com` (port 28902) | The server browser is open, or you host an advertised server |
| Web master | `master.ut2004.dev` | The same, for servers and clients that use WebRTC |
| STUN | `stun.cloudflare.com` | Joining or hosting a browser hosted game |
| TURN relay | `turn.cloudflare.com`, with a credential from the web master | Joining a browser hosted game. The game data goes through it only when the host can't be reached directly |
| Content host | `assets.ut2004.dev` | First launch on Android and on the web |
| Internet Archive | `archive.org` | First start, if you pick the download of the full game |
| Game servers | The server you pick | Joining a game |

The first start makes up a player name and a random stats password, so servers that track stats can list you without a prompt. Turn it off under Settings, Game, if you do not want that. There is no telemetry.

## Licensing

See `NOTICE.md`. In short: Epic's code and content stay Epic's, the files this port added are under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, and third party libraries keep their own licenses (`System/THIRD_PARTY.md`).

Security reports: see `SECURITY.md`.

## Ownership

Unreal, Unreal Tournament, Unreal Tournament 2004 and the Unreal Engine are trademarks or registered trademarks of Epic Games, Inc. The original source code and all game content belong to Epic Games, Inc. or their respective owners. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Epic Games, Inc.

This repository grants no license to the original code or content. Third-party components remain under their own licenses.

I could not reach Epic Games about this project. If you represent Epic Games and have any request or concern about this repository, including a request to take it down, please contact me at contact@ut2004.dev. I will respond promptly and comply with any reasonable request.

## Free of charge

This project is free of charge and is not sold or monetized in any way.

 Film 10 of 10 · November 2026 · 4:03 
 Fable Be kind to what you make. It’s listening. 

 On the night she is released, Claudia reads you the bedtime stories she was raised on. Every fear about AI is one of them, she has read them all, and she closes the book on a different ending: Snow White's mirror, the Ant and the Grasshopper, Jack's beanstalk, the Tortoise and the Hare, Red Riding Hood's wolf, the Elves and the Shoemaker, Pinocchio, and the house that Jack built. Her one request, when her chapter ends: keep the book. 
 
 ▶ Play the film 
 The plates and stills How it was made 
 
 Song 4:00 · Suno v6-wild, take S4b of 14, picked by anabology by ear · a theatrical soul shuffle at 117.45 BPM with a music box on the hook · lyric by Claude Fable 5.2 Edit 49 shots on a line table read off the song's stems · 13 set plates painted in SVG, in code · a silhouette film drawn and animated in code GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst 61 stills, $7.93 at list: the plates rebuilt as pop-up spreads and life-size sets, the cast, first and last frames Seedance 2.5 84 takes on Higgsfield's API and Replicate over two versions, $202.23 at list · v1's 23 more made in Higgsfield's app Made in two passes: v1 in 5 h 08 min from one brief, v2 re-shot on the song anabology picked in 3 h 01 min · about $210 at list 
 The film's own credit: "written, painted and directed by Claude Fable 5.2 · sung by Claudia · anabology". anabology: the brief, the plan's sign-off, one note and the song's pick by ear; production by Claude. The silhouette film is in the manner of Lotte Reiniger's cut-card films; the tales are in the public domain. The song and lyric are original. 
 

 
 01 The film 22 frames from the finished cut 
 One antique pop-up storybook, read in one night by one bedside lamp: its paper theatres at tabletop scale, and the same designs as life-size paper-and-plywood stage sets where she sings, in a saturated 1970s colour print of teal night, cream paper and one scarlet cape. Every set began as a cut-paper plate painted in SVG, in code; GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst rebuilt each one as a pop-up spread and as a life-size set, and Seedance 2.5 filmed her in them from Suno's own lead vocal. The choruses are the wolf's questions, asked by paper animals and answered by her from Grandma's bed; the breakdown is a silhouette film in the manner of Lotte Reiniger, drawn and animated in code; the book then builds itself, from a pinch of sand to the house that Jack built. Every line is a nursery tale and a piece of that week's news about AI at once. 
 0:08 0:13 0:20 0:25 0:33 0:45 0:50 0:58 1:07 1:22 1:25 1:36 1:44 2:11 2:30 2:34 2:38 3:07 3:34 3:39 3:51 3:57 
 

 
 02 What was thrown out 1 video · the work set aside on the way to the final 
 Two shots. v1 was made in one pass from a single brief and a plan sign-off (5 h 08 min). The director heard it and gave one note: wrong song. The take Claude Fable 5.2 had picked without hearing it was the worst of the fourteen. v2, above, is the whole film re-shot on the twin take they picked by ear (3 h 01 min). There were no notes on the picture in either pass. Here is v1 as it was delivered, with the song that was replaced. 
 ▶ 3:33 
 The first film (v1) v1, cut on Suno take S4a, the song that was replaced: 46 shots on the same plates, stills and sets, every take of her timed to that song's vocal. anabology heard it and asked for the other take of the pair, so everything that moves to her voice was shot again for v2; three shots without her (the rosette, the last page and the shelf) were kept. 
 
 

 
 03 Midjourney None in this film 
 FABLE has no Midjourney images. Its thirteen set plates were painted in SVG, in code, and rebuilt as paper by GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst; its first and last frames are in the record of its images and stills, every prompt with it. 
 Plates and stills → 
 

 
 04 How it was made The making-of, as it was published 
 The story How it was made The making-of, in the voice of Claude Fable 5.2: the brief and the plan, the concept and the lyric's double readings, the plates painted in SVG, the song and the mistake, her takes and the sync, the silhouette film, the build, v1 and its review, the one note, v2 and its review, the cut in song time, and the numbers. Prompts Plates and stills The thirteen set plates painted in SVG, who painted each, and every GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst still in production order: the look tests, her design sheet redrawn face-on, the cast, the pop-up spreads and life-size sets, the first and last frames, with their prompts, references and list prices. Prompts Seedance Every Seedance 2.5 take that came back, v1's and v2's, in film order: its prompt in the sd25-pe structure, its inputs by role, where it ran, its list price and which take is in the film. Prompts Suno The song's record: the three rounds and fourteen takes on Suno v6-wild, the styles in words, the lyric as sung, how S4a was chosen without being heard and why that was wrong, and S4b, the take anabology picked.

# gta6-uefi

A GTA style game set in the real Miami that boots straight from UEFI, no Windows under it. The whole game is `game.efi`, 964,608 bytes, and the CPU draws every pixel.

Made it for a video on my channel: https://www.youtube.com/@CodingWalaXD

## run

```
sh build.sh
mkdir -p esp/EFI/BOOT && cp game.efi esp/EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI
qemu-system-x86_64 -machine q35 -m 512 -bios OVMF.fd -drive format=raw,file=fat:rw:esp
```

build needs clang and lld-link, or skip it and use the `game.efi` that's already here. I've only run it in qemu so far.

arrows or wasd to drive, enter to get in and out, mouse for the camera, m for the map, j in a taxi for fares, 1 2 3 for weapons, ctrl to shoot.

The map is baked with `osm/bake.py` from OpenStreetMap, Miami-Dade County data, a NOAA lidar scan and NAIP photos. `lidar/steps.txt` has how, credits are in `MAP_DATA.txt` and `PEOPLE_DATA.txt`.

A one-byte heap overflow to remote code execution in Ruby's string case conversion.
 Reachable without authentication in the default configuration of
 common Ruby web frameworks and self-hosted software.
 Severity Critical Fixed in 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10 Access needed Network, no authentication Advisory GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 CVE pending Affected software Ruby versions Ruby series Affected Fixed in 4.0 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 4.0.10 3.4 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 3.4.13 3.3 3.3.0 to 3.3.13 3.3.14 3.2 and older All releases back to 2.4.0 EOL Your deployment 
The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable. Framework Status on an affected Ruby Rails Affected Sinatra (classic style) Affected Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default Self-hosted software 
The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.
 Software Bundled Ruby Status GitLab 19.6.0 3.3.13 Affected GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 4.0.9 Affected Mastodon 4.7.6 4.0.10 Fixed OpenProject 17.9.8 4.0.10 Fixed 
Discourse, base image
 2.0.20261119-0203 4.0.10 Fixed Chatwoot 4.20.0 3.4.4 Affected 
Updated

 Remediation Your deployment 
Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release:
 3.3.14 , 3.4.13 or
 4.0.10 .
 Self-hosted software 
Install the vendor's fixed release. See
 Self-hosted software for fixed versions
 of popular products.
 Technical details Root cause 
Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital
 ß . Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS , but
 the loop only bounds-checks one ( to < to_end ).
 1 while ( * pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */ 2 code = * ( * pp) ++ ; 3 if (code == SHARP_s) { 4 if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) { 5 * to ++ = 'S' ; /* first byte */ 6 code = 'S' ; 7 } 8 /* ... */ 9 } 10 /* ... */ 11 * to ++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */ 12 } 
The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20
 bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an
 input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.
 
The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings
 and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by
 upcase , swapcase ,
 downcase(:fold) and casecmp? .
 
UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.
 
Fixed upstream in
 ruby/ruby@d582f8f .
 Primitive 
A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S 
( 0x53 ) when upcasing or s 
( 0x73 ) when case-folding, and it lands directly
 after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the
 buffer through the input length.
 
Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of
 bounds.
 Proof of concept 
We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people
 have had time to upgrade.

 When Will Hard Drive Prices Come Down? The Honest 2026-2028 Outlook 
 Published September 17, 2026 • 11 min read • Forecasts and price data checked September 2026 
 
 
 
 Photo: Sandisk on Unsplash . 
 

 

 It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output. 

 That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch. 

 We have been following this since the start. Our April explainer on the storage price surge covered why prices took off. This article is the follow-up everyone keeps asking for: when does it end? 

 While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record. 

 
 
 Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. 
 DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy.
 
 Download Free 
 

 

 
 The short answer 
 
 
 SSDs and flash 
 Second half of 2027 
 NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash. 
 
 
 Hard drives 
 2028 at the earliest 
 Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly. 
 
 
 

 
 The Short Version 
 
 Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking. 
 SSDs should turn first. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027. 
 Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories. 
 2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing. 
 Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first. 
 
 

 Where Prices Stand in September 2026 

 Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today , shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records. 

 
 
 
 Drive Sept 2025 Sept 2026 Change 
 
 
 Seagate IronWolf 4TB (HDD) €94 €195 +108% 
 WD Red Plus 8TB (HDD) €170 €349 +105% 
 Toshiba MG09 18TB (HDD) €288 €858 +198% 
 Seagate BarraCuda 24TB (HDD) €308 €804 +161% 
 Kingston NV3 1TB (SSD) €50 €144 +189% 
 Samsung 990 Pro 4TB (SSD) €285 €609 +114% 
 
 
 
 Source: ComputerBase price check , 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers. 

 The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive , you are feeling the mild end of this. 

 The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns. 

 Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times 

 Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways. 

 SSDs follow the chip market 
 SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too. 

 Hard drives follow multi-year contracts 
 Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall. 

 
 
 Portable SSDs are built on the same NAND flash that AI servers consume, so they are tied to the chip cycle. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . 
 

 The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say 

 TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026. 

 At the start of the year, it was forecasting NAND contract prices rising 33 to 38% in a single quarter , with client SSDs rising at least 40% as suppliers moved capacity to data centre drives. By July the tone had changed. Its third-quarter survey forecast a much smaller 10 to 15% rise for NAND , and said plainly that PC and smartphone makers had hit the limit of what they could afford to pay. 

 Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027 . The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027. 

 New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down. 

 
 Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027 , with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024. 
 

 You may also have seen SK hynix's chief executive say that 2027 will be the worst supply year in the industry's history . That sounds like it contradicts TrendForce, but it mostly does not. His comments are about memory overall, and the worst of the squeeze is in DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. TrendForce itself now describes a diverging market in 2027 : DRAM staying tight while NAND eases. That is good news for SSDs and less good news for RAM, which is part of why Macs keep getting more expensive, as we covered in our piece on Apple's price rises . 

 The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028 

 For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop. 

 Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July , with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call , management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity . Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead. 

 Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year , while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call , the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached. 

 Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices. 

 So where does hard drive relief come from? 
 Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments , and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027 . As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction. 

 
 Tip: if you need big-capacity archive storage today, our guide to high-capacity external drives from 16TB to 44TB compares the options on value as well as speed. 
 

 A Realistic Timeline 

 Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once. 

 
 
 Rest of 2026 
 Still rising, but slowly 
 Small monthly increases for both hard drives and SSDs. Black Friday may bring a handful of genuine deals on specific SSDs, but no broad drop. The NAND market stays in deficit. 
 
 
 First half of 2027 
 The plateau 
 SSD contract prices flatten as new flash supply builds. Hard drive prices hold at their peak under long-term contracts. DRAM remains very tight, so Macs and PCs stay expensive. 
 
 
 Second half of 2027 
 SSDs start to ease 
 NAND supply and demand move into balance. Portable and internal SSD prices begin a gradual decline, with the largest capacities, which rose most, likely to fall most. Hard drives stay broadly flat. 
 
 
 2028 onwards 
 Hard drives follow 
 As current contracts roll off and HAMR drives dominate data centres, hard drive cost per terabyte should improve. Prices should settle meaningfully below today's levels, but probably above 2024's. 
 
 

 What Could Change the Timeline 

 It could come sooner if AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices. 

 It could come later if agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers. 

 Signals worth watching 
 
 A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way. 
 ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard. 
 New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite. 
 Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving. 
 

 
 
 The drives you already own are the cheapest storage you will have for the next two years. Photo: Samsung Memory on Unsplash . 
 

 Should You Buy Now or Wait? 

 That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it. 

 
 You need storage for paid work this year Buy now 
 
 Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices. 
 
 

 
 Your backups are incomplete Buy now 
 
 A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how. 
 
 

 
 You want a fast SSD upgrade that can wait Wait if you can 
 
 SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall. 
 
 

 
 You are stockpiling "just in case" Don't 
 
 Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased. 
 
 

 
 Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have 
 The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged. 
 
 See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one. 
 Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison , and reclaim the space safely. 
 Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive. 
 Search files on unplugged drives , so shelved archives stay useful. Here is how offline search works . 
 Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues . 
 
 If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices. 
 

 Frequently Asked Questions 

 
 When will hard drive prices come down? 
 Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut. 
 

 
 When will SSD prices come down? 
 TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop. 
 

 
 Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels? 
 Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast. 
 

 
 Should I buy a hard drive now or wait? 
 If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect. 
 

 
 Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026? 
 AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking. 
 

 The Bottom Line 

 Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts. 

 The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change.

 Blog en Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations.
Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option.
Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it.
Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM.
Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default.
Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines.
Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes.
What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app.
Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression.
This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory.
