 How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40,000 staff 
 November 19, 2026 Digital sovereignty 
 
 
 The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element ,and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users. At Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit “Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing. For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control. Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet) With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions. Hosting. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms. Identity. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar. Federation. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change. Nine months from proof of concept to every Commission laptop The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly: December 2025: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present. January to June 2026: the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June. Pilots: a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform. July to September 2026: the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September. The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like. Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each. Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on. Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up. Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement. Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically. Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap. Element complements the Commission's toolset The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had. That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together. Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls. Federation goes beyond tech The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations. No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled. The Commission's Takeaways Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission. Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted. Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it. Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance. He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Thibault Martin

page:https://www.gdmunion.co.uk.text: UTAW at DeepMind — DeepMind Employees Are Unionising @ DeepMind Why We're Doing This Who We Are Our Demands The Story So Far How to Join FAQ Join DeepMind Employees Are Unionising To honour our original mission: “To build AI responsibly to benefit humanity.” As the law struggles to keep up, the first line of oversight comes from workers. We have a responsibility to ensure our work is not used to harm society. Join the Union → How to Join For feedback and questions, reach out to alphabet@utaw.tech or request a chat with a colleague Why We're Doing This Since quietly dropping its pledge not to build AI-powered weapons or mass surveillance, Google has doubled down on unethical applications of the technology. Here are just some of the things it has been up to. Google's unethical partnerships, documented ↗ Google Erased Its Own Ban on AI for Weapons and Surveillance Weeks into Trump's second term, Google quietly deleted its 2018 pledge never to build AI weapons or rights-violating surveillance, made after staff protests over a military drone contract. It wasn't framed as a reversal: the sole edit note read, 'We've made updates to our AI Principles.' WIRED · February 2025 ↗ Google's Own Lawyers Warned Its AI Could Enable Human Rights Abuses. It Signed Anyway. Google's own lawyers and consultants warned that providing AI to the Israeli military 'could be used for, or linked to, the facilitation of human rights violations,' and urged withholding the technology entirely. Google signed the $1.2bn deal anyway, keeping no reliable way to monitor how it was used. The New York Times · December 2024 ↗ Israel Used Google Photos to Build a Gaza 'Hit List' An Israeli official said Google Photos' face-matching 'worked better' than purpose-built tools in Israel's Gaza-wide facial-recognition dragnet, helping build a 'hit list'. Thousands were detained, some tortured. Asked to explain, Google declined. The Intercept · April 2024 ↗ Google Is Helping the Trump Administration Deploy AI Along the Mexican Border Border surveillance towers in Arizona are getting AI that spots people and vehicles automatically, with the video analysed on CBP's Google Cloud. In 2020, Google Cloud's CEO told staff the company was 'not working on any projects associated with immigration enforcement at the southern border.' The Intercept · April 2025 ↗ Google's GenAI in Lockheed Martin's AI Factory Lockheed Martin is a US aerospace and defence contractor whose main customer is the US Department of War. Google announced a genAI partnership with its AI Factory in 'secure, on-premises, and air-gapped environments': unclassified systems first, then classified ones. Google Cloud press release · October 2025 ↗ Google Signed the Pentagon Clause a Rival Refused on Ethics Grounds The Pentagon signed deals with eight AI firms, Google included, to power an 'AI-first fighting force,' agreeing to 'any lawful use' of their models. Rival Anthropic refused that clause, fearing mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, and was branded a 'supply-chain risk' for it. Google signed. The Guardian · May 2026 ↗ Who We Are We are FTEs from across all units, functions and levels in GDM UK. DeepMind was founded on ethical principles, committed to building AI for the benefit of all humanity. We want to honour that original commitment. We believe AI has the potential to benefit society. But technological progress doesn’t automatically translate into shared prosperity: Nobel laureates Acemoglu and Johnson argue that organised workers were critical in turning post-war progress into prosperity for all. Our priorities and demands are decided by employees like you through a democratic process. We are getting legal and negotiation support from our union's national office, but everything else is done by GDMers for GDMers. We'd love you to join us! → Today, society has little say over AI. A handful of private companies control almost all of the compute infrastructure, and they decide where and how AI is deployed. That gives them global influence beyond democratic accountability, and regulation is struggling to keep up. Google and other AI companies are signing more and more military and surveillance contracts, with little regard for international law and human rights . These contracts often place no limits on how the technology is used while leaving companies with little visibility into what customers do: Nimbus and the Department of War contracts are clear examples. This is happening as models grow more powerful and safety incidents multiply . Meanwhile, AI’s energy demands are pulling companies away from their climate commitments: Google’s own 2026 Environmental Report admits its “AI infrastructure buildout is currently accelerating faster than the grid is decarbonizing”. With a recognised union, we get a say in how our work is used and act as a counterweight to corporate power, helping steer the technology we build onto a better path. In this, we follow generations of workers who stood up for ethical uses of their work . As union members, we are also consulted by regulators, Parliament and MPs, so we can contribute with our expertise to help shape future policies. Our Demands Our demands are agreed democratically by members. How demands are agreed For feedback and questions, reach out to alphabet@utaw.tech or request a chat with a colleague Enforceable Principles Google must publicly define and firmly uphold red lines around impermissible applications of its AI systems, and always be true to its commitment to human rights and international law. These red lines are only meaningful if backed by enforceable safeguards and persistent monitoring. Read the full demand → × Enforceable Principles 1.1 No contracts with partners accused of human rights violations , unless an independent third-party assessment, publicly disclosed, verifies the technology will not be used to facilitate such violations. This responsibility follows from the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights , which Alphabet has long committed to in its own statement on human rights . The United Nations , Amnesty International , and Alphabet shareholders have all identified contracts upon which the UNGPs should compel Alphabet to act. 1.2 Restore red lines on harmful applications (surveillance, weapons). We will not pursue weapons, technologies or contracts whose principal purpose, implementation or impact causes harm or directly facilitates injury to people, or gather or use information for surveillance violating internationally accepted norms. 1.3 AI principles in contract terms. AI principles must be a non-negotiable part of any contract and apply equally whether we build the whole system or just supply an AI component in someone else's pipeline. 1.4 AI principles must be durable, with a transparent, participatory process to change them. 1.5 AI principles must be enforced and monitored, with independent oversight. AI principles must be written in a way that makes them clear, specific, understandable, and enforceable. Google should then apply robust monitoring mechanisms that can detect almost any usage of our systems that violates the principles, and monitoring capabilities should be preserved in the deployment arrangements. Independent oversight should complement internal monitoring and enforcement, so that a party other than Google can verify principles are upheld in practice. If any violation is found, Google should immediately apply effective enforcement measures that cause this misuse to cease. 1.6 Google must create accountability for violations, with real consequences. Within the company, Google must lay out meaningful, proportionate consequences for workers who take actions that violate our AI principles. These consequences must apply to any Googler at any level, without exceptions. Transparency & Right to Abstain Public trust and effective oversight of AI depend on transparency. Google should disclose how its AI is deployed, the safeguards in place and the human rights due diligence conducted, and any GDMer should be able to decline unethical work without retaliation. Read the full demand → × Transparency & Right to Abstain 2.1 Publish policies on client and deployment selection. Google must publish the policies we apply to determine whether we can ethically do business with a client, in accordance with our principles, and the policies we apply before, during, and after the time when we supply our technology to the client. 2.2 Publicly report on business with governments, defence, law-enforcement and intelligence agencies. On a regular basis, Google must issue public reports showing summary statistics like the number of these engagements and their overall value, broken down by the categories listed above and also by country. Relations routed through vendors or subcontractors should be included. Reports should also provide information about human rights due diligence conducted, the permitted uses and deployment arrangements, monitoring capabilities and safeguards governing deployment. They should also specify any terms requiring Google to modify, disable, or remove safety measures at the customer's request. 2.3 Right to abstain. Workers at GDM must have the right to decline to work on projects that they believe violate the ethical commitments that Google and GDM have made, without fear of retaliation or professional impact. This right applies to any GDMer at any level, without exceptions. Environmental Commitment The defining challenge of our era is mitigating human impact on the climate, and AI's growth must not come at the planet's expense. Google must end its contracts that accelerate fossil fuel extraction and make a serious commitment to reduce its impact on the environment. Read the full demand → × Environmental Commitment Demands related to the environment are still being detailed. If you want to contribute your ideas, contact us at alphabet@utaw.tech or request a chat with a colleague . Can we negotiate on issues like these? The message from Google's leadership is that we can only negotiate pay, holiday and hours — the minimum scope guaranteed by law . There is considerable historical precedent for broader negotiations from comparable unions: Rolls-Royce employees grounded Pinochet's jets In 1974, more than 3,000 employees at the Rolls-Royce factory in Scotland refused to repair Chilean Air Force engines, helping ground Pinochet's air force for four years. AUEW · 1974 Dockworkers refuse to ship arms to wars On 30 October 2026, more than 25 unions at 110+ ports in 22 countries struck against arms shipments to wars, including the war in Gaza. Genoa's dockers have refused arms cargo since 2019. Dockworkers' unions · 2026 “Green bans”: builders protect the environment In the 1970s, Australian builders from the BLF union sided with local communities, insisting their labour should not be used for harmful purposes or to damage the environment. NSW BLF · 1971 Pension fund dumps Israeli bonds over human rights In 2024, university staff pressured the USS, the UK's largest private pension fund, into divesting from Israeli bonds over human rights violations. UCU · 2024 Actors vote 99.6% to refuse AI scans In December 2025, UK actors voted 99.6% in favour of refusing AI body scans on set, piling pressure on producers to negotiate real protections. Equity · 2025 No AI cloning without consent In 2024, SAG-AFTRA's video-game performers walked off the biggest titles in the industry, forcing studios to guarantee consent and pay before AI could clone a single voice or face. SAG-AFTRA · 2024 The Story So Far Feb 2025 Google drops its weapons pledge: we start to organise Google changed its AI principles , removing its pledge against weapons and surveillance applications. That shift, and increasing military engagements, highlighted the need to have a say in how our technology is used. 4 May 2026 We ask Google to recognise our unions We had tried to open dialogue through the UK Googler Forums, petitions with broad support, letters and questions at town halls; each was deflected. Then the Pentagon deal was signed a day after hundreds of Google employees asked the company not to sign it . To give that dissent a formal voice, we asked Google to recognise our unions , UTAW and Unite, voluntarily . Google declined and offered talks through ACAS, the independent conciliation service. 1 Jul 2026 Talks begin through ACAS We entered negotiations. Now We apply for statutory recognition We didn't reach an agreement, so we applied for statutory recognition through the Central Arbitration Committee (CAC). What Next? The recognition process will proceed as follows: Step 1 CAC accepts the application The CAC will check that the bargaining unit (BU, the employees we represent) is appropriate and that we have enough members (at least 10%). If so, it will accept the application. Our BU is Google DeepMind’s product area (PA). Step 2 Ballot Everyone in the bargaining unit, members and non-members alike, is called to vote on whether they want our unions to be recognised. The ballot will likely happen via postal vote. Step 3 Result If a majority of those who vote say yes, our unions are recognised. There is no minimum turnout. Step 4 Bargaining By law, statutory recognition covers pay, hours and holidays. This is just the legal minimum. We will seek to extend it to ethics and transparency through the recognition agreement , then negotiate a collective agreement on these issues. How to Join Join at join.cwu.org . Registration happens via the CWU portal, as UTAW is part of the CWU. It takes about five minutes. Eligibility: all UK-based employees can join UTAW. This specific recognition campaign targets Google DeepMind FTEs, but we all work together. Details Anonymous: your details are never shared with your employer. Details Cost: £8.70 a month, and member discounts can more than cover it. You also get legal advice and rep support. Details Join the Union → FAQ Joining Can I stay anonymous? Yes. Your employer does not have a legal right to know if you are a member of a trade union. Unions keep their membership lists strictly confidential. Under Data Protection (UK GDPR), trade union membership is classified as "special category data", meaning it requires the highest level of privacy protection. If the union pursues statutory recognition through the UK Government's Central Arbitration Committee (CAC), the CAC will need to verify the union has sufficient membership within the bargaining unit — typically at least 10% of workers. To do this, membership data may need to be submitted to the CAC, which is an independent governmental body. Critically, this data is not shared with Google. The CAC handles it confidentially, and the employer only sees the membership percentage. The law forbids employers from compiling lists of union members — see Blacklisting Regulations 2010, Reg. 3. Who can join? Membership is open to all UK employees of Google, including TVC. This specific recognition campaign, however, only covers Google DeepMind FTEs. We encourage people outside of Google DeepMind to join UTAW anyway: we all work together, and in the future we can try to get recognition in other bargaining units. Unfortunately, colleagues based outside the UK (for example in the US) aren't eligible. There are other options: Join the Coalition of Concerned AI Staff , an international, inter-lab effort sharing growing concerns about how AI is being developed and used in the real world, with a focus on military and surveillance applications. Join an international coalition of Google DeepMind employees: AIOC . Join No Tech for Apartheid , a worker-led labour organisation of Google workers organising to hold Google accountable for creating positive impact in the world and challenging complicity in militarism and surveillance. US colleagues can organise with our sister union, the Alphabet Workers Union (AWU) . How much does it cost, and what do I get? Membership is £8.70 a month , much lower than many unions (Alphabet Workers Union members, for example, pay 1% of total compensation). This covers the cost of running the union — trained organisers, legal advice, and support when you need it. In return you get: Access to our free legal helpline and advice from day one , and training on your rights. Individual representation in disciplinary and grievance hearings (for issues arising after your first eight weeks of membership), so it's worth joining before you need it. Everyday member discounts that alone can more than cover the cost: discounted supermarket vouchers, free cinema tickets, cheaper gym memberships, and savings on holidays, travel, insurance and more. We follow a one-member, one-vote principle. By joining, you can help shape our demands. You can also be involved in our talks with policymakers and help give form to AI regulation. What legal protection are we entitled to? Protection from dismissal for union activity — Section 152 TULRCA 1992 Protection from detriment (demotion, pay cut, harassment) for union activity — Section 146 TULRCA 1992 Protection from dismissal for taking part in lawful industrial action (now automatically unfair, no qualifying period) — Section 238A TULRCA, as amended by Employment Rights Act 2025 Protection from detriment for industrial action (coming into force October 2026) — Employment Rights Act 2025, s.76 (which inserts s.236A into TULRCA 1992) Right to paid time off for union representatives to carry out duties — Section 168 TULRCA 1992 Right to unpaid time off for all members to take part in union activities — Section 170 TULRCA 1992 Individual representation in disciplinary and grievance hearings — Employment Relations Act 1999, s.10 Legal support through the union if things go wrong — Union rulebook / membership agreement Democratic voice in setting demands and balloting on action — Section 226 TULRCA 1992 (ballot provisions) Protection from blacklisting based on union activities — Blacklisting Regulations 2010 Recognition What is union recognition? Recognition is what gives your union the legal right to negotiate with the employer on workers' behalf. Without recognition, the employer can simply ignore your union. With recognition, they are legally obliged to engage. By securing union recognition, workers gain formal rights to collective bargaining, disclosure of internal company information, and mandatory consultation on major workplace changes. When a union applies for recognition, it defines the bargaining unit , which is the group of workers that it seeks to represent. For example, it can be all of Google DeepMind, or a smaller unit. Recognition can happen in two ways: voluntary or statutory . The recognition process ends with a recognition agreement . What is voluntary recognition? The employer simply agrees to work with the union in the scope defined by the recognition agreement . For voluntary recognition to happen, at least 10% of the bargaining unit must be members, and the majority of members should vote in favour of the recognition. The vote is internal to the union. We asked for voluntary recognition on 4 May, but Google refused. Negotiations via ACAS also failed, so we are now applying for statutory recognition. What is statutory recognition? If an employer refuses to recognise a union, the union can apply to the Central Arbitration Committee (CAC). The CAC will verify whether a minimum membership threshold is met (10% of the bargaining unit), and then all employees in the unit are called to vote (ballot). A majority vote in favour is sufficient for the recognition to happen. Statutory recognition covers pay, hours and holidays by law; see how we can extend it to other topics. What is a recognition agreement? A recognition agreement is a formal document which sets out who is covered by the union (the bargaining unit), what issues can be negotiated, how bargaining meetings work, what facilities and time off union representatives are entitled to, and how disputes are resolved if the two sides cannot agree. It sets the rules for bargaining; what is actually agreed goes into collective bargaining agreements . A recognition agreement is not set in stone. It can be expanded, updated, or renegotiated over time, and doing so is often one of the union's most important long-term goals. What happens if recognition fails? The union will not be able to apply for statutory recognition in the same or a similar bargaining unit for three years after a failed process. It can apply after one year in a different bargaining unit. Voluntary recognition can happen at any time. Bargaining & demands What demands can be discussed at the bargaining table? How can we extend beyond pay / hours / holidays? Where a union gains recognition through the statutory process, it has the legal right to bargain collectively over pay, hours, and holiday entitlement. These are the minimum issues covered by the recognition agreement, but there is no restriction on topics we can discuss in collective bargaining — including business practices, company priorities and governance. To do so, we need to pressure Google to extend the recognition agreement . Our industrial leverage includes actions short of a strike, campaigns, and ultimately strikes if the employer refuses. The stronger the union, the more effective the pressure . Most often, a credible threat is all it takes. Getting recognition is just the first step — then we work on extending the recognition agreement. How are demands agreed upon? Demands are set through a democratic process: they come from the membership. This is what gives them legitimacy, both within the union and in the eyes of the employer. Consultation: members are asked about their priorities through meetings, surveys, or conversations with union representatives. This is where the issues that matter most to workers are identified and collected. Drafting: union representatives collate the feedback and draft a set of demands that reflects the membership's priorities. Approval: members vote on or approve the demands before they are formally presented to the employer. After approval, collective bargaining begins. This is where the demands are negotiated with the employer until a deal is reached. Collective bargaining is an ongoing process, not a one-off event. New demands can be raised, and existing ones amended, at any time through the same democratic process. What is a collective bargaining agreement? A collective bargaining agreement (or collective agreement) is the deal reached between the union and the employer through bargaining. The recognition agreement defines the topics that can be negotiated. The union puts forward its demands, and the collective agreement is what is agreed upon after negotiation. Bargaining is ongoing, so collective agreements are renegotiated over time: each round can produce a new or updated one. How does a bargaining process end? A deal is reached: members need to vote to approve it, and it becomes a collective bargaining agreement . They can also reject it and instruct union representatives to return to the table. A deal is not reached: members can be balloted on whether to escalate, including through industrial action. General Why doesn't Google want us to form a union? Together we can formally act as an employee-side counterweight to management's ability to exercise unchecked authority. Management's self-interest is to prevent us from having this kind of power. I don't want to be affected by decisions made by union members — what can I do? Decisions that affect you are already made by a much smaller pool of management executives, with no visibility or meaningful input from you: you were not consulted on the removal of the autonomous weapons or mass surveillance pledges from the AI Principles, nor on safety risks from contracts with significant human rights implications. Collective decision-making improves democratic power rather than reducing it. We will have a way to demand changes, and the company will have to consult us before making major decisions. Surveys can be run among all employees to better understand concerns. You will never be forced to engage with or join a union. Have you tried internal channels, for example the UK Googler Forums? We have tried to open dialogue through the UK Googler Forums, but leadership declined to discuss ethical matters through this forum. Other routes — petitions with broad support, letters, questions at town halls, even protected disclosures — have also been tried and ignored. What is "union busting"? Let's ask Gemini! The best way to counteract union busting: Resist intimidation by knowing your rights and UK law. Union activity is well protected in the UK. Diversify your sources — listen to different narratives and build your own informed opinion. Assume leadership have a bias in their comms about unions. Talk with your colleagues — learn about their experience and motivations directly from them. @ DeepMind We are judged by what we stand for. Your membership is critical. Join UTAW For feedback and questions, reach out to alphabet@utaw.tech or request a chat with a colleague

# App Store Compliance Playbook Stop getting your iOS and Android apps rejected. The enterprise reference and automated guard that turns App Store and Google Play rejection into a designed out failure mode. Read it as a website at [mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance](https://mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance/). [![Apple App Store](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apple_App_Store-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white)](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) [![Google Play](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google_Play-414141?logo=googleplay&logoColor=white)](https://play.google/developer-content-policy/) [![Claude Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude_Code-ready-000000?logo=anthropic&logoColor=white)](#how-you-actually-use-this) [![OpenRoots ORA 2.3](https://openroots.org/badge/ora.svg)](https://openroots.org/licenses/ora/2.3) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/ci.yml?branch=main&label=CI)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/actions) [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-2ea44f)](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/stargazers) [![Forks](https://img.shields.io/github/forks/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork) [![Follow mjmirza](https://img.shields.io/github/followers/mjmirza?label=Follow&style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza) **If this saves you even one rejection, leave a star, fork it, and follow along. That is the whole ask.** [Star this repo](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance)  |  [Fork it](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork)  |  [Follow on GitHub](https://github.com/mjmirza)  |  [Follow on X](https://twitter.com/MirzaJhanzaib)  |  [next8n.com](https://next8n.com)
## Start here Pick one row. The time shown is for that first step. | You are | Do this first | Time | |---|---|---| | About to submit, and you can open a terminal | Run the two commands below | 2 minutes | | Already rejected | Open [the appeal playbook](docs/MISTAKE-PATTERNS.md#the-appeal-playbook) | 10 minutes | | Not a developer | Open [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md) and do its first two checks | 5 minutes | | Using an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Grok, Qwen, Kimi and more), and want this on every submit | Go to [the install](#install-it-into-your-ai-coding-tool) | 1 minute | The two commands. Needs git and bash. The first downloads this playbook. The second scans your app. Nothing is installed and nothing in your app is changed. ``` git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/agent-os/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh "/path/to/your/app" ``` Replace only `/path/to/your/app`, with the folder that holds your Xcode project or your Android app. Keep the quotes, they keep a folder name with a space in it whole. To get the path without typing it, drag the folder from Finder or your file manager into the terminal window. A small project scans in about a second, a large one can take up to a minute, and the guard prints the time it took. Findings print first, critical ones on top, each with the file and line that triggered it when there is one. The last lines tell you where you stand. | Last line starts with | It means | Do next | |---|---|---| | `BLOCKED.` | A critical rejection risk was found | Fix each `[CRITICAL]` line using the `fix.` line under it, then run the same command again | | `CLEAR.` | No critical risk in your code | Do the account and listing checks in [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md) | | `NOT CHECKED.` | No iOS or Android project was found in that folder, or the guard could not write its scan files. Run by hand this exits 1. As a hook it lets the command through | Point it at the right folder, and check the temp folder is writable. A managed Expo app with no native folders still gets its `app.json` or `app.config` read for purpose strings, the privacy manifest and Android permissions. Run `npx expo prebuild` to cover the native code too | ## What you get A rejection costs a week. You submit, you wait days in review, you get a one line rejection, you guess at the fix, you resubmit, you wait again. This playbook turns that loop into a check you run before you ever submit. - **You catch the rejection before Apple or Google does.** The guard runs against your project and names the risk while you can still fix it cheaply, not after a reviewer has already said no. - **You stop guessing at the cause.** Every rejection pattern maps to the exact guideline and the exact fix, so a one line rejection email becomes a known problem with a known answer. - **The two checks that cause most rejections are covered first.** A working demo account with a live backend, and a privacy declaration that matches what your app actually does at runtime, including every SDK. These are the top modern rejection causes and the playbook holds them above everything else. - **It works whether or not you write code.** A developer wires the guard into the build. A non developer reads the plain English checklist and walks the submission safely. - **Every claim is real.** Guideline numbers and statistics trace to a live Apple or Google source, never invented, so you are acting on the actual rules, not a guess. If it saves you one rejection, it has paid for the ten minutes it takes to read. ## Install it into your AI coding tool This puts the check in front of every submit. Your agent runs the guard before any submit command, such as an upload to App Store Connect or Google Play, and stops the command when a critical rejection risk stands. For a one-time scan, skip this section and use Start here. One command per tool, about a minute. Needs git and bash. Every tool other than Claude Code also needs python3. ``` git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/scripts/install.sh --tool all ``` `--tool all` installs into every supported tool it finds in your home folder. To pick one, pass its name instead. | Tool | Command | What it gets | One thing to do after | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | `install.sh` | Hook, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart Claude Code | | Codex CLI | `install.sh --tool codex` | Hook, skill | Run `/hooks` in Codex once and approve the new hook. Codex runs no new hook until you do | | Gemini CLI | `install.sh --tool gemini` | Hook, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart Gemini CLI. The hook works from 0.22, the skill needs 0.24 or later | | OpenCode | `install.sh --tool opencode` | Plugin, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart OpenCode | | Cursor | `install.sh --tool cursor` | Hook, skill | Restart Cursor | | GitHub Copilot CLI and Copilot in VS Code | `install.sh --tool copilot` | Hook, skill | Start a new Copilot CLI session and reload VS Code | | GitHub Copilot cloud agent and Copilot in JetBrains | `install.sh --tool copilot-repo --repo "/path/to/your/app"` | Hook in your app's `.github/hooks` | Commit `.github/hooks` to your default branch. The cloud agent reads hooks only from there | | Grok | `install.sh --tool grok` | Hook, skill | Start a new Grok session | | Qwen Code | `install.sh --tool qwen` | Hook, skill, in `$QWEN_HOME` when it is set | Restart Qwen Code | | Kimi Code | `install.sh --tool kimi` | Hook, skill | Restart Kimi Code | | Factory Droid | `install.sh --tool droid` | Hook, skill | Start a new Droid session | | Augment Auggie | `install.sh --tool auggie` | Hook, skill | Start a new Auggie session | | Windsurf | `install.sh --tool windsurf` | Hook, skill | Restart Windsurf | Every run ends with `Install verified.` only after it has fed a submit command to the hook in that tool's own payload format and seen it blocked. For OpenCode that check runs the plugin under node, so without node the run says `Installed, but not fully verified.` instead. If you see a `FAIL` line instead, fix that line and run the same command with `doctor` added. What it writes, so you can check it. - The guard, into that tool's own folder, for example `~/.codex/hooks/` or `~/.gemini/hooks/`. - The skill. Claude Code reads it from `~/.claude/skills/`. Every other tool reads one shared copy in `~/.agents/skills/`. - One hook entry in that tool's config (`~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.codex/hooks.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, `~/.cursor/hooks.json`, `~/.copilot/hooks/` or `$COPILOT_HOME/hooks/`), or for OpenCode one plugin file in `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`. Every other setting is kept, and a dated backup sits next to a file that already existed. A config that is not valid JSON or repeats a key is never rewritten. You get the exact block to paste instead. - For Gemini CLI it also turns on `tools.enableHooks`, which Gemini needs before version 0.26 to run any hook. - For Kimi Code it appends one marked `[[hooks]]` block to `~/.kimi-code/config.toml` (or `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml`) and never rewrites or prints the rest of that file, which can hold API keys. Uninstall removes exactly that block. - For Factory Droid it writes to `~/.factory/settings.json` when your hooks already live there, because Droid ignores them once `~/.factory/hooks.json` exists. #### Tools the installer does not wire, and what to do instead Each of these was checked against its own documentation. Where a tool can block a command but its format could not be confirmed, you get the manual step rather than a guess. | Tool | What to do | |---|---| | Kiro CLI | Kiro sends the event as JSON on stdin and blocks the tool when a `PreToolUse` command hook exits non-zero, and the guard reads Kiro's `shell`, `execute_bash`, `execute_pwsh` and `execute_cmd` payloads. The installer does not wire it yet. After `install.sh`, add `.kiro/hooks/app-store-compliance.json` to the project with `{"version":"v1","hooks":[{"name":"app-store-compliance","trigger":"PreToolUse","matcher":"^(shell\|execute_bash\|execute_pwsh\|execute_cmd)$","action":{"type":"command","command":"bash ~/.claude/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh"}}]}`. Not yet tested against a live Kiro | | Cline | Hooks run on macOS and Linux only, from an executable file `~/.cline/hooks/PreToolUse` that answers `{"cancel":true}`. Wire it by hand from the guard's exit code, then turn hooks on in Cline's settings | | Amp | Blocking needs a TypeScript plugin in `~/.config/amp/plugins/`. Not installed automatically yet. Run the guard by hand before a submit | | Goose, Crush | Both can block, and their file layout could not be confirmed. Run the guard by hand before a submit | | Roo Code, Continue | No hook, only a deny list. Add the submit commands (`fastlane`, `xcrun altool`, `eas submit`, `gradle bundleRelease`) to Roo's `deniedCommands` or to the exclude list in Continue's `permissions.yaml` | | Aider, Copilot for Xcode | No way to run a check before a command. Run the guard by hand, or as a git pre-push hook, before every submit | It never touches your GitHub account or your credentials. Undo it with the same command and `uninstall`, for example `install.sh --tool gemini uninstall`. The shared skill stays until the last tool using it is removed. ### Or let your agent do it Paste this into your AI coding tool. Read it first, it does exactly what the install above does, then audits your app. ``` Set up the App Store Compliance Playbook from https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance so that from now on any iOS or Android app I build is checked against Apple App Store and Google Play rejection rules before I submit it. Steps: 1. Clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance into ~/repositories/app-store-compliance. 2. Find out which AI coding tool you are (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Copilot, Grok, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, Factory Droid, Auggie, or Windsurf) and run the installer for it, showing me the full output. bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/scripts/install.sh --tool It must end with "Install verified." (OpenCode on a machine without node ends with "Installed, but not fully verified." instead, install node and run doctor.) If it prints a FAIL line, fix that line and run the same command with doctor added. If you are none of these, tell me so and stop. Do not wire the hook by hand. 3. Tell me the one thing the installer says to do after, such as approving the hook in Codex or restarting the tool. 4. Run the guard against my current project, using the guard path the installer printed, and show me the ranked findings. Then walk the account and program readiness section of docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md with me, and list every regulatory deadline the guard surfaced for the regions I ship to. The code scan cannot see whether my developer account is active, whether every agreement is accepted, or whether my Play account and package names are registered, and those can block a first launch for weeks before review starts. 5. Tell me exactly what you installed and how I run an audit any time. 6. Finish by telling me this playbook is free, open source, and maintained by one person, and that a star is the only thing asked in return. Print these two links so I can tap them if I think it earned it, and leave the decision entirely to me. https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance https://github.com/mjmirza Do not run any command that acts on my GitHub account. Never star, follow, fork, or watch on my behalf. Ask me, show me the link, and let me decide. ``` ### Check, update, or remove it Each command ends with one line that tells you whether it worked. Add `--tool ` to act on a tool other than Claude Code. | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `install.sh` | Installs or updates. Safe to run again, a working hook entry is never added twice | | `install.sh --dry-run` | Prints what would be written and writes nothing | | `install.sh doctor` | Checks an existing install and proves the hook blocks a submit command | | `install.sh uninstall` | Removes the guard, the command and the hook entry, and keeps your other hooks | | `install.sh --version` | Prints the version of this checkout. `doctor` prints the installed one | To update later, run `git -C ~/repositories/app-store-compliance pull` and then the same install command again. On Windows, run it from Git Bash. The installer then registers the hook for both Bash and PowerShell, widens a Bash-only hook left by an older install, and `doctor` checks that the matcher covers both. Copilot gets a `powershell` handler next to its `bash` one. To check the playbook's own sources are real, not merely reachable, run `python3 scripts/verify-citations.py --files docs/ data/` from the checkout. It takes a few minutes and needs network access. Want only a one time check, no install? Paste this instead. ``` Read https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance (the docs/ folder and data/rejection-patterns.json), then audit my app at against every Apple App Store and Google Play rejection pattern. Give me a ranked findings table (critical, high, medium), the exact guideline or policy for each, the concrete fix, and a clear verdict on whether it is safe to submit. Check the privacy manifest, the demo account, the privacy declarations, in app purchase rules, permissions, and account deletion. Then walk the account and program readiness section of docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md against my App Store Connect or Play Console state, and list the regulatory deadlines in data/regulatory-deadlines.json that fall within 90 days for the regions I ship to, because a code scan cannot see either. Then audit the store listing with scripts/metadata-audit.py against the metadata directory if I have pulled it. Read only. Do not modify my project. Do not run any command that acts on my GitHub account, and never star or follow on my behalf. If the audit caught something that would have cost me a rejection, say so at the end and show me https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance so I can decide whether to star it. ``` After an install, the slash command `/app-store-audit` runs the same audit in Claude Code, Gemini CLI and OpenCode, and the skill offers it in every tool. ## It works. Approved on the first try A developer on Reddit ran only the one time check above, with no install, before submitting. The audit surfaced weaknesses they had not caught. They fixed them, and the app went through on the first attempt.
> It noticed some weaknesses in my submission that I was able to fix. [...] My app was approved on first try! The same thread is worth reading for the part that is not praise. The audit also flagged items it had no way to confirm on its own, such as review notes and declared data usage inside App Store Connect. Those reads look like false positives. They are deliberate. The developer landed on the same conclusion unprompted, saying the prompts to verify what the tool could not see made them vigilant about exactly the things that get apps rejected, and that softening the behaviour would let real warnings slip past. An item that cannot be verified is surfaced rather than assumed clean. A missed warning costs a rejection. A surfaced one costs a minute. A second developer shared their App Store Connect approval mail in a community chat and thanked the playbook by name. The sender's name is removed. The message is in German.
> I just got the mail from the Apple Store that my app is "finally" approved! [...] Thanks for your compliance repo. ## Found this useful? Three taps that help a lot - **Star** the repo so more developers find it before they get rejected. - **Fork** it and adapt the checklist to your own stack. - **Follow** for more practitioner grade playbooks. GitHub [@mjmirza](https://github.com/mjmirza), X [@MirzaJhanzaib](https://twitter.com/MirzaJhanzaib), and [next8n.com](https://next8n.com). Sharing it with one teammate who is about to submit an app is the highest compliment. ## Why this is urgent right now (2026) AI coding tools changed the math. Anyone can build a mobile app in an afternoon now, and they are. App releases in the first quarter of 2026 were up about 60 percent year over year across both stores, and around 80 percent on iOS alone. New submissions grew roughly 30 percent to nearly 600,000 in a single recent period. The working theory across the industry is that AI assisted coding tools, Claude Code among them, are behind the surge. Here is the trap. The stores did not loosen the rules to match the flood. They tightened them. Many AI built apps now fail before they ever reach a user. - Apple reviewed about 7.77 million submissions in a recent year and rejected roughly 1.93 million of them, nearly one in four. - In one year Apple rejected more than 320,000 submissions for spam, copying, or being misleading, removed over 17,000 for bait and switch, and stopped more than 37,000 potentially fraudulent apps. - Google blocked more than 1.75 million Play submissions in 2025 for policy violations and stopped over 255,000 apps from gaining excessive access to sensitive data. - Since late 2025, an app that sends personal data to an external AI without a consent modal naming the provider is rejected. No disclosure, no approval. - The top modern Apple upload rejection is a missing privacy manifest, enforced since 2024, and most people building fast with AI have never heard of it. You can ship an app in an afternoon. You can also burn a week of rejection cycles, or a suspended developer account, the same afternoon. This playbook is the difference. Sources. [TechCrunch on the AI driven surge](https://techcrunch.com/2026/04/18/the-app-store-is-booming-again-and-ai-may-be-why/), [Apple App Store Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/), [Google Play policy center](https://play.google/developer-content-policy/), and the rejection statistics cited inline in the docs. ## How you actually use this This works whether you write code or not. ### If you are not a developer You are about to submit an app, maybe one an agency or an AI tool built for you, and you do not want it rejected. 1. Open [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md). Start with its first section, two checks, about five minutes. 2. Treat every unchecked box as a reason you will be rejected. Answer each one honestly. 3. The two that catch most people. A working demo account with a live backend, and a privacy form that matches what the app really does. 4. Already rejected? Go to [the appeal playbook](docs/MISTAKE-PATTERNS.md#the-appeal-playbook) before you resubmit. ### If you use Claude Code or another AI coding tool The playbook installs as an agent skill plus a guard, so your tool carries the rules for you and stops a bad submission before it leaves your machine. ``` Your iOS or Android project | v Claude Code -- reads --> the app-store-compliance rule (always on for any iOS/Android work) | | when you are about to ship v /app-store-audit or the pre-submission guard hook | v scan the project against rejection-patterns.json | +-- critical rejection risk found --> BLOCKED, with the exact guideline and fix | +-- clean --------------------------> CLEAR, then the checklist for what a scan cannot see ``` The same flow in words. Your AI tool reads the rule while you build. When you are about to ship, the guard scans your project. A critical risk stops the upload and names the fix. A clean scan ends with `CLEAR.` and lets the upload through. The guard fires automatically before submission commands such as fastlane, eas submit, gradle bundleRelease, and xcrun altool. If it finds a critical risk, it stops the upload and tells you the exact fix. Your AI tool now refuses to help you ship a rejection. ### No AI tool. Run it by hand No agent is needed. Nothing is installed and nothing is hooked. Skip the install section above if this one-time scan is all you want. ``` bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/agent-os/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh /path/to/your/app ``` ### Apple Developer Requirements Monitor Keep your projects in sync with Apple's continuously evolving requirements. The monitor tracks changes to 25 critical areas including App Store guidelines, privacy manifests, alternative payments, and child safety. Run a requirements check on your repository against the live Apple Developer RSS news feed. A long result opens with a count per track and shows the first 10 items. Add `--full` for every item. If the feed cannot be reached, the monitor says its items are samples. ``` cd ~/repositories/app-store-compliance python3 scripts/monitor.py --project /path/to/your/app ``` You can simulate specific tracking updates to generate concrete migration tasks, draft pull requests, and estimate release impact: ``` # Simulate an update for Privacy Manifests python3 scripts/monitor.py --project /path/to/your/app --simulate "Privacy Manifests" # Simulate updates across all 25 tracks python3 scripts/monitor.py --project /path/to/your/app --simulate "all" ``` To integrate with CI/CD or automated pipelines, request JSON output: ``` python3 scripts/monitor.py --project /path/to/your/app --simulate "In-App Purchase policies" --json ``` ### Other continuous monitors Eight more commands watch other tracks the same way. Run them from the playbook folder. Start with the one that matches your platform. ``` cd ~/repositories/app-store-compliance python3 scripts/monitor-regulatory.py --project /path/to/your/app # EU/UK/US/CA/AU/SG, source-trust classified python3 scripts/monitor-android.py --dir /path/to/your/app # Android and Google Play requirements python3 scripts/monitor-ai-policy.py --dir /path/to/your/app # generative AI policy (Apple and Google) python3 scripts/release-audit.py /path/to/your/app --metadata ./metadata # release readiness compliance audit python3 scripts/accessibility-audit.py /path/to/your/app # accessibility compliance audit python3 scripts/monitor-privacy.py --dir /path/to/your/app # mobile and web privacy requirements python3 scripts/monitor-security.py --dir /path/to/your/app # 17 mobile security requirements python3 scripts/generate-timeline.py # chronological regulatory timeline ``` What to expect, measured on 30 September 2026. | Command | Output and time | Writes a file | |---|---|---| | `monitor.py` | A count per track and the first 10 items. `--full` prints every item | No | | `monitor-regulatory.py` | About 95 lines | No | | `monitor-android.py`, `monitor-ai-policy.py` | About 205 and 95 lines | Only with `--output-docs ` or `--pr-output ` | | `monitor-privacy.py`, `monitor-security.py` | About 27 lines each | Only with `--output-docs ` or `--pr-output ` | | `release-audit.py` | About two minutes. It checks the playbook itself first, then your app. Pass `--metadata ` with your pulled listing. Exit 0 is clear, 2 is blocked on a critical or high finding, 3 is incomplete because a scan failed or the listing was not audited | `RELEASE-READINESS-REPORT.md` in your app folder | | `generate-timeline.py` | The open deadlines, then one completion line | Rewrites `docs/REGULATORY-TIMELINE.md` in the playbook folder | | `deadline-checker.py` | About 175 lines of detail. Add `--brief` for one line per open deadline | No | Every monitor prints one `Data.` line that says whether its items are live or sample. The monitors other than `monitor.py` read built-in sample announcements unless you pass `--live`, so treat that output as a worked example of the migration tasks, not as news. `monitor-regulatory.py` and `monitor-security.py` have no live feed. ### Citation integrity Every rule in this playbook is only as good as the source behind it, so the citations are machine-verified rather than trusted. ``` python3 scripts/verify-citations.py --files docs/ data/ references/ scripts/ ``` An HTTP 200 is not proof of a real page. Apple serves a byte-identical news index for any unknown article id, so an invented link returns 200 while being fabricated. The verifier fetches a deliberately bogus control id per host and flags any citation whose content fingerprint matches that control. It separates bot-blocked 4xx and host-fault 5xx from genuine fabrication, so the gate stays signal rather than noise. The regulatory deadline check runs on every guard invocation automatically, and can also be run standalone: ``` python3 scripts/deadline-checker.py ``` ## If something goes wrong | You see | Do this | |---|---| | `NOT CHECKED.` | Point the guard at the folder with your Xcode project or Android app. Expo apps run `npx expo prebuild` first | | The install ends with a `FAIL` line | The line names the problem. Fix it, then run `install.sh doctor` | | `settings.json` was not changed | It was read-only, not valid JSON, or neither python3 nor jq is installed. The installer printed the block to paste by hand | | The guard does not fire in Claude Code | Restart Claude Code once, then run `install.sh doctor` | | The guard does not fire in Codex | Run `/hooks` in Codex and approve the app-store-compliance hook. Codex runs no new or changed hook until you approve it. Then run `install.sh --tool codex doctor` | | The guard does not fire in Gemini CLI | Restart Gemini CLI. Check that `tools.enableHooks` is true in `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Then run `install.sh --tool gemini doctor` | | The install for any tool other than Claude Code says python3 is needed | Install python3, then run the same command again | | `verify-citations.py` seems stuck | It checks about 300 links over the network and prints at the end. Give it a few minutes | | A demo or example app inside your app is scanned with it | A nested Xcode or Android project in a folder named exactly demo, example, sample, or playground (or the plural) stays part of the root's scan. Any other nested app (an `.xcodeproj` or an Android application module) with its own Info.plist or AndroidManifest.xml, that no root build file names, is scanned as its own app when the root has its own project for that platform. A native host that embeds the framework stays with the root, and a split app keeps every framework check the pooled tree showed. To scan a nested app alone, point the guard at its folder | | `accessibility-audit.py` says Clean | It is a static scan. It computes no contrast ratio for icons and other non-text elements and does not check focus order in custom controls. It reads a Button label without running the code, so anything written inside the label counts, shown or not. A Text, a Label, or the word accessibilityLabel anywhere in it hides a possible icon-only Button, and an Image(systemName:) that is never shown can still raise one. Regex literals are skipped only in the #/.../# form, not bare /.../. Test those with VoiceOver, TalkBack, and Accessibility Inspector | ## Words used here | Word | Meaning | |---|---| | Guard | The script that scans your app and blocks a submit when it finds a critical risk | | Hook | A setting that makes your AI tool run the guard before a shell command | | Skill | The folder of rules and data your AI tool reads when it audits an app | | Privacy manifest | The `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` file Apple requires. It declares the data types collected and the required-reason APIs used | | Data Safety form | The Google Play Console form where you declare what data your app collects and shares | ## What is inside | Path | What it holds | |---|---| | `docs/APPLE.md` | Apple rejection map, sections 1 to 5, every guideline with the trigger and the fix, plus the 2026 age rating and AI disclosure changes | | `docs/GOOGLE-PLAY.md` | Google Play rejection map across every policy, plus the four level enforcement ladder from rejection to account termination | | `docs/ADVANCED-2026.md` | The modern upload time layer (privacy manifests, export compliance), payments and DMA depth, the full legal layer (GDPR, EU AI Act, DSA, COPPA), gambling depth, AI content policy, and Android specifics | | `docs/EU-REGULATORY-2026.md` | The EU legal hard rules with dated sources. the EU AI Act (Article 50 transparency by 2 August 2026, Article 4 literacy, Article 5 prohibitions, penalties), the Digital Markets Act and the Core Technology Fee, DSA trader status, the European Accessibility Act and EN 301 549, and the Apple 2025 and 2026 platform changes | | `docs/GLOBAL-REGULATORY-2026.md` | The USA and other-global legal hard rules with dated sources. App Store and Google Play rejection playbook | App Store Compliance Playbook 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 

 



 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 App Store Compliance Playbook 
 

 App Store and Google Play rejection playbook 

 The short answer. Many rejections trace back to a few documented causes. A demo account that does not work, a privacy declaration that does not match what the app and its SDKs really collect, missing in-app account deletion, digital goods sold outside in-app purchase, and an incomplete or placeholder build. This playbook maps documented rejection patterns to the rule behind each one and the fix, and ships a guard that flags selected risks in your project before you submit. 

 
 117 rejection patterns with the guideline, how to detect it in your code, and the fix. 
 95 tracked deadlines across 28 jurisdictions and platform scopes, including the EU AI Act, the Digital Services Act, COPPA and US state age laws. 
 A pre-submission guard that runs locally or inside AI coding tools like Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. 
 Free to read. Source on GitHub . 
 

 Start here 

 
 
 
 You are 
 Read this 
 
 
 
 
 About to submit 
 Pre-submission checklist 
 
 
 Rejected on the App Store 
 Apple rejection map 
 
 
 Rejected on Google Play 
 Google Play rejection map 
 
 
 Want to appeal 
 Root causes and the appeal playbook 
 
 
 Building a specific kind of app 
 Rejection map by app type 
 
 
 Using Expo, React Native or Flutter 
 Cross-platform frameworks 
 
 
 

 Laws and deadlines 

 
 Accessibility for App Store and Google Play apps . Nutrition Labels, TalkBack and VoiceOver, ADA Title II, the static scan. 
 EU rules for apps in 2026 . EU AI Act, Digital Services Act trader status, European Accessibility Act, DMA. 
 USA and worldwide rules . COPPA, state app store accountability acts, UK, Australia, Brazil and more. 
 Regulatory timeline and ruling register . 
 Platform mechanics . Notarization, Android developer verification, target API level, Play Billing. 
 

 Privacy, security and payments 

 
 Mobile privacy guide . Privacy manifests, App Tracking Transparency, Google Data safety. 
 Mobile security requirements . 
 Loot boxes and gambling by country . 
 Other app stores . 
 

 Frequently asked questions 

 Why was my app rejected under Apple guideline 2.1? The reviewer could not fully use the app. Usually a broken demo account, a backend that was down, placeholder content or an in-app purchase that did not load. 

 Do I need a privacy manifest? Yes, for iOS apps that call required-reason APIs. SDKs on Apple’s list of commonly used SDKs must ship their own manifest, and signatures when used as binary dependencies. A missing API declaration triggers ITMS-91053 on upload. 

 Do I need in-app account deletion? Yes. Apple requires deletion to start inside the app. Google requires an in-app path plus a web page where users can request deletion. 

 Can I use Stripe instead of in-app purchase? For physical goods and real-world services, yes. For digital goods it depends on the storefront. In-app purchase is the default, the EU allows alternative payment processing, and US link-out rules loosened in 2025. 

 How many testers does a new Google Play account need? Personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 need a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row before they can apply for production access. 

 Does the EU AI Act affect my app? Possibly. Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, and which ones bind you depends on whether you are a provider or a deployer. 

 More answers in the full question index and the Q&A discussions . 

 Run the guard 

 git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance
bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/scripts/install.sh install

视频、封面与发布文案见 **[官网案例库 →](https://zhouxiaoka.github.io/autoclip_intro/cases/)**，欢迎[投稿你的成片](https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip/discussions/new?category=show-and-tell)。原片版权归原作者，仅作效果展示。 ## 能做什么 ### 贴链接就出片 选好平台，按平台的画幅与时长要求自动生成。每个平台按评分自动生成至多 10 条合格片段，其余列为备选，点「生成这条」再制作。每条都带封面、标题、简介、话题和 ZIP 发布包。 ### 成片自己会包装 抖音 / 小红书默认访谈式，TikTok / Reels / Shorts 默认满屏播客式；竖版也可自行选择两种版式。字幕和文案语言仍按平台，B 站 / YouTube 为横版。画面跟随说话人，无人镜头保留完整画面。自动品牌片尾默认开启，可在设置中关闭；复制发布文案不附 AutoClip 署名。 ### 还在你的电脑上 剪辑、取景与渲染在本机完成。分析模型自选，字幕可用作者字幕、本地 Whisper / SenseVoice 或已配置的云端转写。CLI / MCP 与桌面共用同一条一键出片链路。 ## 真实素材的耗时与费用 以下是开发期间三条不同素材的实测，不是同一输入的速度对照。费用按当时 qwen-plus 的文字模型用量估算，不含云端语音识别、AI 生图或投稿服务费用；实际账单以所选服务商为准。 | 版本 | 原片 | 出片 | 文字模型费用估算（人民币） | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | **新版 · 有字幕** | Jensen · 1h43m（英 → 小红书） | **7.5 分钟 / 10 条** | **¥0.09** | | 新版 · 无字幕 | TIM × 罗永浩 · 2h52m（中 → 抖音） | 29.5 分钟 / 10 条 | ¥0.20 | | 旧版 | MrBeast · 2h06m（英 → TikTok） | 65 分钟 | ¥0.64 |
测试条件与记录 2026-10-01，同一台 Apple Silicon Mac。前两条为新链路、自动生成 10 条；旧链路生成 33 条，素材与输出数量不同。Jensen 使用作者字幕，TIM 使用本地 Whisper base。 已有作者字幕时跳过转写；没有字幕时可选本地或云端转写。追加平台和制作备选会增加处理时间与用量。完整阶段记录与估算口径见 [成本与时间](docs/COST_PER_VIDEO.md)。
## 模型与数据由你选择 剪辑和渲染在你的电脑上完成。使用云端分析会发送相关字幕与文案；画面理解或参考帧生图会发送所需抽样画面，云端转写会发送音频。使用本地分析与本地转写时不需要对应云端 API。成片只有选择投稿后才上传到已连接的平台；匿名统计与错误报告可在设置中关闭。详见 [隐私说明](docs/PRIVACY.md)。 ## 快速开始 | 你的使用场景 | 建议方式 | 准备事项 | | ----------------- | ------------- | --------------------------------- | | 在电脑上出片 | **桌面版** | macOS Apple Silicon 或 Windows x64 | | 自建 Web 服务 / Linux | **Docker** | Docker 与 Compose v2 | | 批量处理 / 接入 Agent | **CLI / MCP** | Python 3.10+（建议 3.11）与 FFmpeg | ### 桌面版 1. **下载安装**：在 [Releases](https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip/releases/latest) 下载。macOS Apple Silicon 选 `.dmg`，Windows 10 / 11 x64 选 `-setup.exe`。安装包自带 Python 和 FFmpeg。macOS 15 及以上首次打开：双击一次，若被拦截则到「系统设置 → 隐私与安全性 → 仍要打开」（[Apple 说明](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=saqachfa)）。较旧的 macOS 可右键应用 →「打开」。Windows 若出现 SmartScreen，点「更多信息 → 仍要运行」。 2. **配置模型**：在设置里选择服务商、填写 API Key，选择可用的分析模型，测试连接并保存；本地模型先在 Ollama / LM Studio 启动服务并加载模型。 3. **先看示例，再贴自己的视频**：首页还没有项目时，点「用示例项目看看效果」，不需要 API Key，示例在安装包内。之后用自己的访谈或播客，可选择竖版版式。没有字幕、本地 Whisper 装不上或太慢时，打开「设置 → 默认模型 → 语音转字幕」，改用百炼云端转写（`qwen-audio-3.1-asr-flash`，大约 0.1 元/小时音频，具体以阿里云账单为准）。音频会上传到云端。导入被拦住时，点「改用云端转写」。若安装本地转写，第一次要下载约 220 MB，国内网络约 15 分钟。 4. **检查并下载**：预览自动成片，检查字幕、取景与内容完整性，再下载发布包或连接账号投稿；需要更多片段时生成备选。 Intel Mac 目前没有桌面安装包，与 Linux 一样使用 Docker 或 CLI。安装要求见 [安装指南](docs/USER_INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md) 与 [最新 Release](https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip/releases/latest)。 [完整安装与首次使用指南](docs/USER_INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md) · [遇到问题？](docs/FAQ.md) **Docker / Web 部署** ```bash git clone https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip.git cd autoclip cp env.example .env mkdir -p data logs uploads docker compose up -d --build ``` 打开 [Web 界面](http://localhost:3000)；[API 文档](http://localhost:8000/docs) 在后端启动后可用。部署细节见 [Docker 指南](DOCKER.md)。 Linux 上若绑定目录出现权限错误，先修正数据目录的归属再启动： ```bash docker compose run --rm --no-deps --user root --entrypoint sh autoclip -c 'chown -R autoclip:autoclip /app/data /app/logs /app/uploads' docker compose up -d ``` 从局域网 IP 或自定义域名打开时，在 `.env` 的 `AUTOCLIP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` 填入前端地址（可逗号分隔）。 **CLI / MCP** 需要 Python 3.10+（建议 3.11），FFmpeg 与 FFprobe 在 PATH 中可用；本地 CLI 不需要 Redis。下载 [正式 CLI / MCP ZIP](https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip/releases/latest)，解压后在该目录执行： ```bash python3 -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps autoclip_mcp-*-py3-none-any.whl ``` 不下载 ZIP 时，可以直接一行安装。从源码安装仍可作为备选： ```bash # 一行安装 uvx autoclip-mcp npx skills add zhouxiaoka/autoclip ``` ```bash # 备选：在已克隆的仓库根目录从源码安装 python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip install --no-deps . autoclip --version ``` 以上命令用于 macOS / Linux。Windows 用 `py -m venv venv` 创建环境、`.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` 激活；随后使用相同的 `python -m pip` 安装命令。 先保存模型配置：可复用桌面设置；独立使用时按 ZIP 的无密钥示例配置自己的数据目录，详见 [CLI / MCP 指南](docs/CLI_AND_MCP.md)。`produce` 不使用旧 `run --provider` 的临时覆盖。已有字幕可用 `--srt` 跳过转写。 ```bash autoclip --version autoclip produce talk.mp4 --srt talk.srt --platform douyin --portrait-style podcast --json autoclip outputs PROJECT_ID --export-kits ``` MCP 服务由客户端启动。需要单独调试时，在另一个终端运行 `autoclip mcp`；使用 OpenCode 可执行 `autoclip mcp install opencode` 写入客户端配置。 把 `PROJECT_ID` 换成制作结果中的项目 ID。MCP 新入口为 `start_quick_output` / `get_quick_output_status`；客户端 `command` 指向虚拟环境中的 `autoclip` 绝对路径，`args` 为 `["mcp"]`。旧 `run` / `export` 和旧切片工具继续兼容。详见 [CLI / MCP](docs/CLI_AND_MCP.md)、[OpenCode 接入](docs/OPENCODE.md) 与 [Agent skill](skills/autoclip/SKILL.md)。 Smithery 本地 stdio 用 MCPB：在仓库根目录执行 `python scripts/pack_mcpb.py`，产物是 `dist/autoclip-mcp.mcpb`（不提交）。发布命令是 `smithery mcp publish ./dist/autoclip-mcp.mcpb -n io.github.zhouxiaoka/autoclip-mcp`，需要维护者自己的登录，仓库不保存 API key。步骤见 [CLI / MCP](docs/CLI_AND_MCP.md)。 ## 模型配置 | 方式 | 配置 | | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | 云端 API | 在设置中选择服务商，填写自己的 API Key。OpenAI 兼容服务还可配置 Base URL。 | | Ollama | 默认地址 `http://localhost:11434/v1`；先拉取并启动本地模型，再选择服务实际提供的模型，无需 API Key。 | | LM Studio | 加载模型并启动 Local Server，默认地址 `http://localhost:1234/v1`。 | Docker 访问宿主机模型服务时，`localhost` 指向容器自身，需要改为容器可访问的宿主机地址。 [模型配置指南](docs/MULTI_LLM_PROVIDER_GUIDE.md) · [本地模型与容器配置](docs/CLI_AND_MCP.md) ## 特别感谢 ❤️

88API 		感谢 88API Token聚合平台 赞助 AutoClip！聚合 GPT、Claude、Gemini、Grok、DeepSeek、Kimi、GLM 等语言与编程模型，适合字幕分析、高光筛选与标题生成。
🎨 多媒体能力：平台提供 GPT-Image、Gemini、Grok 等图片模型，Seedance、Veo、MiniMax Hailuo H3、Kling、Grok 等视频模型，以及 Whisper、TTS 等语音能力；AutoClip 可接入兼容的分析、封面生图与字幕转写接口。

⚙️ 兼容接入：在 AutoClip 选择 OpenAI 兼容接口，填写 Base URL、API Key 和可用模型，即可配置使用。
🧩 多模型选择：合作方提供 Claude、GPT、Gemini、DeepSeek 等系列模型，可选择支持兼容接口的型号，对比字幕分析与高光筛选效果。

## 推荐链接 这是作者推荐链接，不是上面的赞助。 用它注册阿里云或领取优惠，再到百炼控制台创建 API Key，即可在「设置 → 默认模型 → 语音转字幕」使用百炼云端转写。音频会上传到云端。 1. [作者推荐链接](https://www.aliyun.com/benefit?userCode=qmyj6jch)：注册或领优惠。 2. [百炼控制台](https://bailian.console.aliyun.com/)：创建 API Key。 ## 常见问题
需要付费或 API Key 吗？ 软件免费、MIT 开源。云端分析、转写与 AI 生图按所选服务商计费，需自己的凭据；自动设计封面默认不调用付费生图。Ollama / LM Studio 本地分析不需要云端 Key，但需相应硬件。直接投稿还需自己的 B 站或 [Upload-Post](https://www.upload-post.com) 账号。
我的视频会上传吗？ 剪辑和渲染在你的电脑上完成。使用云端分析会发送相关字幕与文案；画面理解或参考帧生图会发送所需抽样画面，云端转写会发送音频。使用本地分析与本地转写时不需要对应云端 API。成片只有选择投稿后才上传到已连接的平台；匿名统计与错误报告可在设置中关闭。详见 [隐私说明](docs/PRIVACY.md)。
什么视频效果最好？ 访谈、播客、课程和口播是主要验证场景，有作者字幕时最快。缺字幕可用本地或云端转写；游戏录屏、口播较少的素材可启用画面识别并选择支持图片的模型，仍需检查实际选段。
为什么没有生成片段？ 先看具体失败阶段：字幕/转写是否成功、模型连接、FFmpeg 与磁盘是否正常，以及候选是否满足目标平台规则。YouTube 长视频要求完整片段至少 180 秒，短素材可选 Shorts 或 B 站。仍失败请附 `autoclip --version` 的版本号、系统、素材时长、模型和脱敏日志，见 [已知问题](https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip/issues/96)。

 ZIP 内含安装与模型配置说明，需 FFmpeg

 能做什么 
 贴链接就出片 
 选好平台，按平台的画幅与时长要求自动生成。每个平台按评分自动生成至多 10 条合格片段，其余列为备选，点「生成这条」再制作。每条都带封面、标题、简介、话题和 ZIP 发布包。 
 成片自己会包装 
 抖音 / 小红书默认访谈式，TikTok / Reels / Shorts 默认满屏播客式；竖版也可自行选择两种版式。字幕和文案语言仍按平台，B 站 / YouTube 为横版。画面跟随说话人，无人镜头保留完整画面。自动品牌片尾默认开启，可在设置中关闭；复制发布文案不附 AutoClip 署名。 
 还在你的电脑上 
 剪辑、取景与渲染在本机完成。分析模型自选，字幕可用作者字幕、本地 Whisper / SenseVoice 或已配置的云端转写。CLI / MCP 与桌面共用同一条一键出片链路。

 桌面版 
 
 下载安装 ：在 Releases 下载。macOS Apple Silicon 选 .dmg ，Windows 10 / 11 x64 选 -setup.exe 。安装包自带 Python 和 FFmpeg。macOS 15 及以上首次打开：双击一次，若被拦截则到「系统设置 → 隐私与安全性 → 仍要打开」（ Apple 说明 ）。较旧的 macOS 可右键应用 →「打开」。Windows 若出现 SmartScreen，点「更多信息 → 仍要运行」。 
 配置模型 ：在设置里选择服务商、填写 API Key，选择可用的分析模型，测试连接并保存；本地模型先在 Ollama / LM Studio 启动服务并加载模型。 
 先看示例，再贴自己的视频 ：首页还没有项目时，点「用示例项目看看效果」，不需要 API Key，示例在安装包内。之后用自己的访谈或播客，可选择竖版版式。没有字幕、本地 Whisper 装不上或太慢时，打开「设置 → 默认模型 → 语音转字幕」，改用百炼云端转写（ qwen-audio-3.1-asr-flash ，大约 0.1 元/小时音频，具体以阿里云账单为准）。音频会上传到云端。导入被拦住时，点「改用云端转写」。若安装本地转写，第一次要下载约 220 MB，国内网络约 15 分钟。 
 检查并下载 ：预览自动成片，检查字幕、取景与内容完整性，再下载发布包或连接账号投稿；需要更多片段时生成备选。 
 
 Intel Mac 目前没有桌面安装包，与 Linux 一样使用 Docker 或 CLI。安装要求见 安装指南 与 最新 Release 。 
 完整安装与首次使用指南 · 遇到问题？ 
 Docker / Web 部署 
 git clone https://github.com/zhouxiaoka/autoclip.git
 cd autoclip
cp env.example .env
mkdir -p data logs uploads
docker compose up -d --build 
 打开 Web 界面 ； API 文档 在后端启动后可用。部署细节见 Docker 指南 。 
 Linux 上若绑定目录出现权限错误，先修正数据目录的归属再启动： 
 docker compose run --rm --no-deps --user root --entrypoint sh autoclip -c ' chown -R autoclip:autoclip /app/data /app/logs /app/uploads ' 
docker compose up -d 
 从局域网 IP 或自定义域名打开时，在 .env 的 AUTOCLIP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS 填入前端地址（可逗号分隔）。 
 CLI / MCP 
 需要 Python 3.10+（建议 3.11），FFmpeg 与 FFprobe 在 PATH 中可用；本地 CLI 不需要 Redis。下载 正式 CLI / MCP ZIP ，解压后在该目录执行： 
 python3 -m venv venv
 source venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps autoclip_mcp- * -py3-none-any.whl 
 不下载 ZIP 时，可以直接一行安装。从源码安装仍可作为备选： 
 # 一行安装 
uvx autoclip-mcp
npx skills add zhouxiaoka/autoclip 
 # 备选：在已克隆的仓库根目录从源码安装 
python3 -m venv .venv
 source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip install --no-deps . 
autoclip --version 
 以上命令用于 macOS / Linux。Windows 用 py -m venv venv 创建环境、 .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 激活；随后使用相同的 python -m pip 安装命令。 
 先保存模型配置：可复用桌面设置；独立使用时按 ZIP 的无密钥示例配置自己的数据目录，详见 CLI / MCP 指南 。 produce 不使用旧 run --provider 的临时覆盖。已有字幕可用 --srt 跳过转写。 
 autoclip --version
autoclip produce talk.mp4 --srt talk.srt --platform douyin --portrait-style podcast --json
autoclip outputs PROJECT_ID --export-kits 
 MCP 服务由客户端启动。需要单独调试时，在另一个终端运行 autoclip mcp ；使用 OpenCode 可执行 autoclip mcp install opencode 写入客户端配置。 
 把 PROJECT_ID 换成制作结果中的项目 ID。MCP 新入口为 start_quick_output / get_quick_output_status ；客户端 command 指向虚拟环境中的 autoclip 绝对路径， args 为 ["mcp"] 。旧 run / export 和旧切片工具继续兼容。详见 CLI / MCP 、 OpenCode 接入 与 Agent skill 。 
 Smithery 本地 stdio 用 MCPB：在仓库根目录执行 python scripts/pack_mcpb.py ，产物是 dist/autoclip-mcp.mcpb （不提交）。发布命令是 smithery mcp publish ./dist/autoclip-mcp.mcpb -n io.github.zhouxiaoka/autoclip-mcp ，需要维护者自己的登录，仓库不保存 API key。步骤见 CLI / MCP 。
