# springrep

[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/springrep.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/springrep)
[![docs.rs](https://docs.rs/springrep/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/springrep)
[![MIT licensed](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep/blob/main/LICENSE)

An exact boundary-representation (B-rep) geometry kernel, in safe Rust with no dependencies.

springrep builds solids from exact analytic and swept surfaces. Every operation returns a solid
that passes the validity checker, or an error.

- **Build:** extrude, revolve and sweep planar profiles, along a path or a helix.
- **Combine:** union, intersection and difference.
- **Finish:** chamfers and fillets, shells and drafts.
- **Measure:** area, volume, mass properties, bounding boxes, closest distances and ray crossings,
  from the exact geometry.
- **Exchange:** read and write STEP AP214, and make watertight triangle meshes for display.
- **History:** every face carries the names of the operations that made it, so a later operation
  selects faces and edges by name.

## Example

A plate with a filleted bore through it:

```rust
use springrep::{
    blend::fillet,
    boolean::difference,
    math::{Frame, Vec2, Vec3},
    measure,
    profile::Profile,
    step,
    sweep::extrude,
};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let base = Frame::new(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Z, Vec3::X)?;
    let below = Frame::new(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, -1.0), Vec3::Z, Vec3::X)?;

    let plate = extrude(&Profile::rect(Vec2::ZERO, 60.0, 40.0), &base, 8.0, "plate")?;
    let bore = extrude(&Profile::circle(Vec2::ZERO, 12.0), &below, 10.0, "bore")?;

    let part = difference(&plate, &bore)?;
    let part = fillet(&part, &[("plate.end", "bore.side")], 1.5, "round")?;

    println!("volume {:.3} mm³", measure::volume(&part));
    println!("area   {:.3} mm²", measure::area(&part));
    let text = step::write(&part, "bracket")?;
    println!("{} faces, {} bytes of STEP", part.face_count(), text.len());
    Ok(())
}
```

More examples are in [`examples/`](https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep/tree/main/examples).
Run one with `cargo run --example bracket`.

## Installation

```toml
[dependencies]
springrep = "1"
```

## Documentation

- API reference: <https://docs.rs/springrep>
- Website: <https://springcraft-ai.github.io/springrep/>
- [Design](https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep/blob/main/doc/design.md): the
  representation, the tolerance policy, the validity rules, the history rules and the module map.

## Contributing

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md)
before you open an issue or a pull request.

## Licence

springrep is under the MIT licence: see
[LICENSE](https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep/blob/main/LICENSE).

Open-source B-rep CAD kernel in Rust | springrep 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 spring rep 
 
 API docs 
 
 github 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 spring rep 
 Exact CAD geometry in pure Rust. 
 MIT open source license 
 A boundary-representation (B-rep) kernel. Booleans, fillets, sweeps and STEP on exact geometry, accurate to 1e-7 mm, with every result validated. 
 
 brep-conformance leaderboard 
 kernel license pass at 1e-7 mm speed 
 
 see the benchmark ↓ 
 
 
 github 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 Exact to 1e-7 mm Surfaces are analytic or NURBS, not meshes, so volume, area, and mass properties are computed from the real shape. 
 Valid or a clear error Every result is checked for validity, and if it fails you get an error instead of a broken solid, so nothing downstream gets built on a bad shape. 
 Fast and safe It has the fastest median case time on brep-conformance, with public results anyone can check. It's pure Rust with no dependencies and no unsafe code, and it compiles to WebAssembly. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 Get started 01 
 
 
 
 
 01 add the crate 
 
 $ 
 
 copy 
 
 
 
 02 run it 
 
 $ cargo run 
 volume 18276.001643 mm³ 
 area 6452.128187 mm² 
 wrote bracket.step, 8 faces 
 
 
 
 or 
 copy prompt for AI agent 
 
 Set up springrep, an exact B-rep CAD kernel in Rust, and run its first example.

1. If this folder is not a Cargo project, run `cargo new springrep-start` and work in that folder.
2. Run `cargo add springrep`.
3. Write the program below exactly as given. In a new project it replaces src/main.rs. If the
 project already has its own src/main.rs, save it as examples/bracket.rs instead.
4. Run it with `cargo run`, or `cargo run --example bracket` if you saved it as an example. It
 must print:
 volume 18276.001643 mm³
 area 6452.128187 mm²
 wrote bracket.step, 8 faces
 If it prints anything else, stop and tell me what it printed. Don't change the part to make
 the numbers match.
5. Run `cargo doc -p springrep` and read the module docs before writing any new geometry. Then
 ask me what I want to build.

```rust
 use springrep::{
 blend:: fillet ,
 boolean:: difference ,
 math::{Frame, Vec2, Vec3},
 measure,
 profile::Profile,
 step,
 sweep:: extrude ,
};

 fn main() -> Result <(), Box < dyn std::error::Error>> {
 let base = Frame::new(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Z, Vec3::X)?;
 let below = Frame::new(Vec3::new( 0.0 , 0.0 , - 1.0 ), Vec3::Z, Vec3::X)?;

 let plate = extrude (&Profile::rect(Vec2::ZERO, 60.0 , 40.0 ), &base, 8.0 , "plate" )?;
 let bore = extrude (&Profile::circle(Vec2::ZERO, 12.0 ), &below, 10.0 , "bore" )?;

 let part = difference (&plate, &bore)?;
 let part = fillet (&part, &[( "plate.end" , "bore.side" )], 1.5 , "round" )?;

 println!( "volume {:.6} mm³" , measure::volume (&part));
 println!( "area {:.6} mm²" , measure::area (&part));
 std::fs::write( "bracket.step" , step::write (&part, "bracket" )?)?;
 println!( "wrote bracket.step, {} faces" , part.face_count());
 Ok (())
}
```

Things to know:
- Every operation returns a Result. Propagate errors with ?; never unwrap a geometry result.
- Faces are named after the feature that made them: plate.end is the top of an extrusion named
 plate, bore.side is the wall of one named bore. Fillets and chamfers pick an edge by the names
 of the two faces either side of it.
- Run springrep::check::check on each new solid and treat any issue it reports as a bug.
- Units are millimetres.

};

}

Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests ( springcraft-ai.github.io ) 31 points by atomarch 15 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 7 comments Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses. The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right. The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome. kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep 
conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/ help

 [Submitted on 31 Jul 2026] 
 Title: PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction 
 Authors: Pirzada Suhail , Nagasai Saketh Naidu , Atanu R Sinha , Amit Sethi View a PDF of the paper titled PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction, by Pirzada Suhail and 3 other authors 
 View PDF 
 HTML (experimental) 



 
 Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text by auto-regressively sampling the next token. This inherently leads to a many-to-many mapping between prompts and responses, complicating the task of inferring prompts from observed outputs. Prior work on LLM inversion frames prompt recovery as a semantic reconstruction task. They rely on fine-tuning pretrained sequence-to-sequence models on large external datasets--and requiring access to model weights or logits--to generate semantically plausible prompts. In contrast, we present a functional approach to inverting a given LLM in a black-box setting, without auxiliary aids. We train an explicit inverse language model entirely from scratch on data synthetically generated from the target LLM itself. Analogous to forward next-token prediction, our inverse model is trained using previous-token prediction, establishing a generative link between the forward and inverse processes that enables faithful prompt reconstruction. Moreover, it naturally supports diverse prompt reconstructions through sampling, whereby all such prompts induce similar responses under the forward, target LLM. Our approach generalises across datasets and exhibits transferability in reconstructing prompts from responses generated by different LLMs. Further, across the set of token based evaluation metrics for prompt and response reconstructions, our approach outperforms prior work.

page:https://www.anthropic.com/research/.text: Claude Fable 5.2 solves two open problems in the physics of black holes \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude 01 Introduction Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes 01 Introduction 02 A note about Claude’s methods 03 The Hawking-Page transition 04 The modular bootstrap 05 Conclusion Published Nov 17, 2026 Team Science Topics Discovery Agents Reasoning Beneficial Deployments See more... Related articles Science Nov 4, 2026 Investigating vault particles with Claude View more Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies. To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension. Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is “written” on its surface. The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time. Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop. In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment. Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer. If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out. The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories? This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin. Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question. Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve . Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper. This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search. Conclusion These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research. Read the black hole phase transition paper here , and the modular bootstrap paper here . The value has an electrostatic origin: as a function of a complexified dimension, c − 1 log ⁡ ∣ g ∣ c^{-1}\log\lvert g\rvert c − 1 lo g ∣ g ∣ of a functional g g g is a two-dimensional potential with positive charges at the zeros of g g g . Positivity forces g g g to fall as fast as the Cardy density of states grows, and the maximum principle bounds the potential by an explicit harmonic function, which fixes Λ V \Lambda_V Λ V ​ . The field of this potential is the spectral curve of a mean-field theory of the optimal functionals, and its charge density is the distribution that the zeros of any functionals attaining Λ V \Lambda_V Λ V ​ must follow.  Apple Inc and Secretary of State for the Home Department and (1) Privacy International (2) Liberty (3) Ian Hosein (4) Ben Wizner vs Secretary of State for the Home Department 
 
 
 
 IPT/26/191/CH and IPT/25/83-86/CH 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 19 November 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Download supporting full judgment documentation 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Neutral Citation Number: [2026] UKIPTrib 9 
 Case Nos: IPT/26/191/CH and IPT/25/83-86/CH 
 IN THE INVESTIGATORY POWERS TRIBUNAL 
 Date: 19 November 2026 
 Before: 
 LADY CARMICHAEL (PRESIDENT} 
MR JUSTICE CHAMBERLAIN 
and 
MR JUSTICE JOHNSON 
 Between: 
 IPT/26/191/CH 
 Apple Inc 
 Claimant 
 – and- 
 Secretary of State for the Home Department 
 Respondent 
 And Between: 
 IPT /25/83-86/CH 
 (1) Privacy International 
(2) Liberty 
(3) Ian Hosein 
(4) Ben Wizner 
 Claimants 
 -and- 
 Secretary of State for the Home Department 
 Respondent 
 — 
 Daniel Beard KC, Julian Milford KC, Gayatri Sarathy and Raphael Hogarth (instructed by Fieldfisher) for the Claimant in case IPT/26/191/CH 
 Ben Jaffey KC, Celia Rooney and Abe Chauhan (instructed by Leigh Day) for the Claimants in case IPT /25/83-86/CH 
 Neil Sheldon KC, Christopher Knight KC, Karl Laird and Hugo Murphy (instructed by Government Legal Department) for the Respondent 
 Jason Beer KC and Paul Skinner (instructed by the Tribunal) as Counsel to the Tribunal 
 Hearing date: 17 September 2026 
— 
 Judgment 
 Lady Carmichael, Mr Justice Chamberlain and Mr Justice Johnson: 
 
 This judgment concerns two separate claims and complaints. We adopt the shorthand used by counsel, and refer to the claimants in the two claims as “Apple” and “the NGOs”. We refer to the claims and complaints, compendiously, as “the claims”. 
 The claims raise issues as to the Secretary of State’s powers to give a “relevant operator” a “technical capability notice” under section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. The respondent says that it would be damaging to national security if she is required publicly to confirm or deny whether a technical capability notice has been given to Apple. The claimants disagree and say that the open justice principle requires that this central feature of the case is not kept secret. They say it is already clear from what is in the public domain that a technical capability notice has been given to Apple, and that it could not conceivably damage national security for that fact to be confirmed in these proceedings. In the event that Apple has been given a technical capability notice, there is then a further issue as to whether its content should be publicly revealed in these proceedings. 
 We heard submissions from Daniel Beard KC for Apple, Ben Jaffey KC for the NGOs, Neil Sheldon KC for the respondent and Jason Beer KC as counsel to the Tribunal. 
 The hearing was divided into three components. The OPEN component was heard in public, with all parties represented. There was then a PRIVATE component, with the NGOs excluded and with Mr Beer advancing submissions that supported their interests. A CLOSED hearing also took place, with the NGOs and Apple excluded and with Mr Beer advancing submissions supporting their interests. 
 We are handing down separate PRIVATE and CLOSED judgments at the same time as this judgment. The substance of our decision and reasoning is set out in this judgment. The PRIVATE and CLOSED judgments contain additional details that cannot be published without damaging the public interest. The Tribunal is therefore prevented from publishing those judgments by rule 7 of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal Rules 2018. 
 
 The facts 
 Apple ‘s first claim 
 
 In early 2025 Apple brought a claim against the respondent. At the time, the respondent said the existence of the claim must be kept secret and any hearing should not be published in the daily case list. The Tribunal disagreed. It listed a hearing and the court listing was published on the Tribunal’s website. The listing did not reveal the parties’ identities, so as not to pre-judge the respondent’s arguments that they should be kept secret. After a hearing, which also had OPEN, PRIVATE and CLOSED components, the Tribunal rejected the respondent’s contention that the identity of the parties should be kept secret. It also rejected the respondent’s contention that the subject matter of the claim should be kept secret. It was therefore publicly revealed that the claim had been brought by Apple against the Secretary of State for the Home Department and that it concerned the power to give a relevant operator a technical capability notice. The Tribunal’s reasons are set out in OPEN, PRIVATE and CLOSED judgments dated 7 April 2025. Shortly thereafter, the NGOs commenced their claim. The NGO claim was listed for a substantive hearing in December 2026. 
 Apple’s claim was subsequently dismissed because of a change of circumstances. In July 2026 Apple commenced this second claim. 
 A case management hearing was listed, in part to determine whether a trial could still take place in December 2026 and what further directions were necessary. The parties agree that a substantive hearing in December 2026 is impractical. They indicate they are likely to be able to agree case management directions with a view to a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. The principal issue between the parties which the Tribunal is asked to resolve is whether it would damage the public interest to reveal if the respondent has given a technical capability notice to Apple, and, if so its content. The resolution of that issue is likely to impact on the extent to which the substantive hearing can take place in OPEN. It will also affect the extent to which evidence can be exchanged in OPEN as opposed to PRIVATE or CLOSED. Media reporting, public comment and correspondence with the Tribunal 
 There has been extensive media reporting to the effect that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice requiring it to be able to maintain access to its users’ data in decrypted form, so that such data is available to be passed to intelligence agencies. That reporting, and other public comment, is summarised in the Tribunal’s OPEN April 2025 judgment at paragraphs 14-19. The reporting includes a report in The Times that the Home Office issued an order under the 2016 Act to require Apple to provide access to encrypted material, and that this had been “confirmed by Home Office sources”. The public statements include statements made by Tulsi Gabbard, who was then US Director of National Intelligence, and statements attributed to the President of the USA. 
 There have been further public statements and media reporting since the April 2025 hearing. 
 On 20 July 2025, The Financial Times published an article which said that the newspaper had been told by “two senior British officials” that the Government was “seeking a way out of a clash with the Trump administration over the UK’s demand that Apple provide it with access to secure customer data”. It quoted an official in “the UK’s technology department” as saying “This is something that the vice-president is very annoyed about and which needs to be resolved … The Home Office is basically going to have to back down.” 
 On 19 August 2025, Ms Gabbard published a post on X that was viewed more than three million times: 
 
 “Over the past few months, I’ve been working closely with our partners in the UK, alongside @POTUS and @VP, to ensure Americans’ private data remains private and our Constitutional rights and civil liberties are protected. 
 As a result, the UK has agreed to drop its mandate for Apple to provide a “back door” that would have enabled access to the protected encrypted data of American citizens and encroached on our civil liberties.” 
 
 On the same day, The Financial Times published an article under the headline”UK has ‘agreed to drop’ demand for access to Apple user data, says US” and the sub-headline “Move protects Americans’ civil liberties, Trump’s director of national intelligence Tulsi  Gabbard tells FT.” 
 On 1 October 2025, The Financial Times published an article under the headline “UK makes new attempt to access Apple cloud data” and the sub-headline “Order issued in September comes after Trump administration said London had backed down in fight over encryption”. The article quoted the Home Office as stating that it did not comment on operational matters and would not confirm or deny the existence of any technical capability notice. However, the article also stated: ”two senior British government figures said the US administration was no longer leaning on the UK government to rescind the order.” 
 Shortly before the hearing, the Tribunal received a letter from US Senator Ron Wyden and US Congressman Warren Davidson. The letter was also published by The Guardian newspaper. The letter asked the Tribunal to permit greater transparency into the “the challenge reportedly filed by Apple concerning a surveillance directive from the UK government under the Investigatory Powers Act.” The letter said that Apple had been authorised by the UK Government to brief certain members of the US executive and legislature about the issue:”Apple recently informed Congress that it is challenging the UK government’s authority to issue surveillance directives. Apple sought permission from the UK government to discuss this issue in more detail with both the executive and legislative branches of the US government. Apple further informed Congress that the UK government granted Apple permission to brief the Attorney General, the Vice President, and their staff, while explicitly prohibiting the company from discussing the issue in further detail with the US Congress.” 
 
 The respondent’s evidence 
 
 The respondent relies on a witness statement of Lucy Montgomery-Pott that was served for the hearing in April 2025. Ms Montgomery-Pott is the Head of the Investigatory Powers Unit which is part of the Homeland Security Group within the Home Office. The statement was only served in PRIVATE. Ms Montgomery-Pott explains the damage to national security that she says would arise if “the fact, substance or parties to these proceedings be made public.” Ms Montgomery-Pott said that there had been an investigation into the reference in The Times article to Home Office sources confirming that Apple had been ordered to provide access to encrypted material. She said that “no Government source has been identified”, but provided no detail of the investigation undertaken and no copy of any investigation report. She did not identify who had been investigated, or what investigative steps had been taken (for example whether electronic devices had been examined). She did not say whether Ministers or senior officials (including special advisers) had been asked if authority had been given to brief The Times or, if they had been asked, what they said. 
 The respondent also relies on an OPEN and a PRIVATE witness statement of Andrew Scurry, the Director of Technology, Data and Innovation in the Homeland Security Group of 11 September 2026. Mr Scurry says that he agrees with and adopts the views set out by Ms Montgomery-Pott in her statement. He says that, although there has been significant media reporting and public commentary concerning “matters alleged to relate to Apple and a TCN”, there is an important distinction between such reporting and confirmation by the Government. He says that, if the Government confirmed the existence of a technical capability notice and/or its technical details, that would damage national security. It is therefore necessary for the Government to maintain its approach of neither confirming nor denying whether a technical capability notice has been issued. He says that “the NCND principle is only effective when it is maintained consistently.” He claims that “Ministers and Home Office officials have consistently neither confirmed nor denied the existence, contents, scope or operational effect of any individual TCN.” If that sentence were true, then the statements in The Times and The Financial Times to the contrary effect would be false 
 Mr Scurry adopts the account of Ms Montgomery-Pott that, followingpublication of the article in The Times, an investigation was conducted, butwithout giving any further detail. In respect of the subsequent articles in TheFinancial Times, he says: “Both of these Financial Times articles were subjectto a leak investigation by Government Security Group.” Again, no further detailis given of what this investigation involved, nor indeed of what (if anything) itrevealed. 
 The respondent’s evidence does not include any assessment that damage hadbeen caused to national security as a result of the Tribunal’s publication, in April2025, of a public case list that revealed the existence of a claim, or its order thatrevealed that the claim was brought by Apple and that it concerned therespondent’s powers to give a relevant operator a technical capability notice. 
 
 Legal framework 
 
 The applicable legal framework is set out in the Tribunal’s April judgments. We repeat part of that account here. 
 
 Open justice 
 
 Open justice is a fundamental common law constitutional principle which applies to all courts and tribunals exercising the state’s judicial power: Dring v Cape Intermediate Holdings Limited [2020] AC 629 per Lady Hale at [41]. It applies to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal: Various claimants v Security Service [2022] UKIP Trib 3, [2023] 2 All ER 849 per Singh LJ (President) at [71]. However, the Tribunal operates in a different procedural and legislative context compared to other courts and tribunals. That difference impacts on the application of the open justice principle: Various claimants at [75]-[76]. 
 
 The Tribunal’s rules 
 
 Rule 7(1) of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal Rules 2018 states:”The Tribunal must carry out their functions in such a way as to secure that information is not disclosed to an extent, or in a manner, that is contrary to the public interest or prejudicial to national security, the prevention or detection of serious crime, the economic well-being of the United Kingdom or the continued discharge of the functions of any of the intelligence services.” 
 
 Approach to claimed risks to national security 
 
 The executive is entitled to take a precautionary approach when assessing risks to national security. Courts and tribunals must accord particular weight to such assessments made by the executive. Those assessments should usually be accepted, unless they are shown to be irrational or otherwise vitiated by a public law error: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Rehman [2001] UKHL 47, [2003] 1 AC 153 per Lord Hoffinann at [50] and [62], Lord Slynn at [17] and [27] and Lord Steyn at [42]; R (Lord Carlile of Berriew QC) v Secretary of  State for the Home Department [2014] UKSC 60, [2014] AC 945 per Lord Sumption at [22]-[33]; R (Begum) v Special Immigration Appeals Commission  [2021] UKSC 7 [2021] AC 765 per Lord Reed at [53]-[62], [70] and [109];  Various claimants v Security Service [2022] UKIP Trib 3, [2023] 2 All ER 849  per Singh LJ (President) at [47]. 
 In Attorney General v BBC; R (Beth) v Investigatory Powers Tribunal [2025] EWHC 1669 (KB), the Divisional Court (Lady Carr CJ, Dame Victoria Sharp PKBD and Chamberlain J) said, at [19]: 
“The justification for the respect owed to [ national security assessments by the executive branch of government] is in significant part based on institutional matters including the expertise and experience of the personnel involved and the wide range of sources of information available to them. However, this respect is warranted only if, and to the extent that, the courts can have confidence without reservation in the processes by which such assessments are prepared and presented.” 
 
 Neither confirm nor deny policy 
 
 To protect the secrecy of sensitive intelligence, the Government adopts a policy of neither confirm nor deny: NCND. It is in furtherance of this policy that the Government has publicly  either confirmed nor denied whether Apple has been given a technical capability notice. 
 NCND is an important Government policy for the protection of national security: In re Scappaticci ‘s application for judicial review [2003] NIQB 56 per  Lord Carswell CJ at [ 15]. Its efficacy depends on it being maintained generally:Restriction order ruling in the Dawn Sturgess Inquiry per Lord Hughes at [15]. But it is not an absolute or blanket rule of law: “It is not simply a matter of a governmental party to litigation hoisting the NCND flag and the court automatically saluting it”: Mohamed v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2014] EWCA Civ 559, [2014] 1 WLR 4240 per Maurice Kay LJ at [20]. 
 The Tribunal’s decision making is governed by rule 7 of the 2018 Rules. If a departure from NCND in a particular case would involve damage to national security then rule 7 requires that the Tribunal carries out its functions in a manner that would enable the Government to maintain NCND in that case. If, conversely, a departure from NCND would not involve damage to national security then rule 7 does not prevent the Tribunal from conducting an OPEN hearing which would have the effect of disclosing information to the public that the Government regards as being subject to the NCND policy. 
 
 
 In its PRIVATE April 2025 judgment (which can, in part, now be put into OPEN), the Tribunal explained why it was appropriate to publish the fact and subject matter of these proceedings and the names of the parties, notwithstanding the Government’s wish to maintain NCND:”53. Further, the respondent continues to retain a degree of choice and control over the maintenance of NCND. In legal proceedings, it occasionally happens that the continuation of the proceedings requires a departure from NCND (for example the revelation of the identity of a human source in order to protect the fair trial rights of a defendant in criminal  proceedings where a public interest immunity application is refused). In such cases, the authorities can decide whether to depart from NCND or whether, instead, to withdraw or  compromise the underlying proceedings. [ … ]54. Further, although NCND can only be effective if it is generally maintained, it is not a blanket rule and its utility is not defeated by occasional and exceptional departures from its application. There are a number of examples of departures from the NCND policy. The so-called Wilson doctrine (under which the Government indicated that it did not intercept the communications of Parliamentarians and that if that position changed Parliament would be informed at a suitable point) involves a departure from NCND in both of its aspects. In the inquest into the death of Diana, Princess of Wales, the Secret Intelligence Service denied that the Princess of Wales had been a subject of intelligence interest. The Foreign Secretary in  2012, in response to a question as to whether Nigel Heywood was a source for the Secret Intelligence Service, responded that he had not been employed by the British  Government in any capacity. In 2012 the Secret Intelligence Service gave evidence as to the nature of Gareth Williams’ employment by the intelligence agencies at the time of his death: Undercover Policing Inquiry, ruling on legal principles and approach, 3 May 2016 per Sir Christopher Pitchford at [128].55. [ … ]56. [ … ]57. It follows that … the application must be dismissed …
 58. Although not necessary (or, arguably, relevant) to our decision, there are further reasons why it is desirable for the bare details of the case to be public. It is likely to raise legal issues of some considerable importance, [ … ] It is undesirable, and injurious to the public development of legal principle, for such issues to be resolved entirely in secret. Sometimes, that has to happen, where the public revelation of a legal issue in a particular context would tend to reveal underlying facts and where the revelation of those underlying facts would be damaging to national security. For the reasons we have given, that is not the case here.” 
 
 
 
 
 There is a further factor that is relevant to the issue that now arises. The utility of NCND in an individual case depends on its being maintained consistently in that case. If the Government itself has not been consistent in maintaining NCND in respect of a particular matter, the court is unlikely to give weight to an assertion that a departure from NCND would be damaging to national security. It follows that there is an obligation on a party seeking to apply NCND to ensure that the court is aware of any arguable departure from NCND. In BBC and Beth the Divisional Court said, at paragraphs 27-28:”27 … .it is important that a party seeking to adopt a NCND stance in relation to a fact relevant to legal proceedings ensures that the court is candidly informed (if necessary in CLOSED pursuant to a public interest immunity application or a closed material procedure) about:(a) the existence and terms of any relevant policy relating to the use of NCND and/or to the circumstances in which it may be departed from; and(b) the circumstances of any departure from NCND in the particular case or other related cases and the precise terms of the departure (including whether the departure was authorised, whether the information was conveyed in confidence and the precise terms of any departure).28. If it is unclear whether there has been such a departure, any material which evidences or suggests that there has been must always be candidly disclosed to the court (if necessary in CLOSED pursuant to a public interest immunity application or closed material procedure). This is an incident of the duty owed by any party engaged in court proceedings to ensure that the court is able to carry out its functions on a properly informed basis …. “ 
 
 Submissions 
 
 Ben Jaffey KC, for the NGOs, submits that the Secretary of State’s continued reliance on NCND as to the existence of a technical capability notice, and its terms, is no longer tenable in the light of the extensive public reporting and official statements. He says that the sequence of events, which include the dismissal of Apple’s first claim, and then the bringing of a subsequent claim, mirrors the public reporting that Apple had been issued with a technical capability notice, that this had been withdrawn following pressure from the US government, and that a new notice had then been issued. He says that it follows as a matter of irresistible inference that it is now in the public domain that the Secretary of State has given Apple a technical capability notice. It could not conceivably damage national security for that fact to be acknowledged in these proceedings. He says that the Tribunal should determine the “NCND issue” now, because the respondent’s reliance on NCND materially impairs open justice and the claimants’ ability to make submissions, obtain disclosure and rely on expert evidence. 
 
 
 Daniel Beard KC, for Apple, was constrained in what he could say in OPEN pending the Tribunal’s resolution of this issue. He submitted that Apple should have permission to refer openly to “certain key facts” in these proceedings, including whether the respondent has, in fact, given Apple a technical capability notice. He says that open justice, fairness and the extensive public reporting that has now taken place justify greater transparency and would not damage national security. He says that Apple would otherwise be unfairly prevented from publicly advancing facts it knows to be true. 
 
 
 Neil Sheldon KC, for the respondent, submits that NCND should continue to be maintained because its effectiveness as a policy to protect national security depends on its consistent application. Official confirmation or denial of the existence of a technical capability notice in this case would create a damaging precedent for future national security cases. He argues that there is a critical distinction between media speculation and formal confirmation or denial by Government. The Tribunal should give substantial weight to the Home Office assessment that public disclosure of the true position would damage national security, and that the balance falls decisively in favour of protecting national security. 
 Jason Beer KC, as counsel to the Tribunal, did not advance substantive submissions in OPEN. In the PRIVATE part of the hearing, he supported the submissions that were advanced in OPEN by the NGOs and contended that the PRIVATE (and CLOSED) evidence advanced by the respondent did not establish that it would be damaging to national security to reveal whether a technical capability notice had been given to Apple. He pointed out that the respondent’s documents which explain the true position are marked “OFFICIAL SENSITIVE” rather than “SECRET” or “TOP SECRET”, which he said was inconsistent with the respondent’s contention that their disclosure would be damaging to national security. 
 
 Would it be damaging to national security to reveal whether the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice? 
 
 The submissions were, understandably, advanced by reference to the NCND policy. However, as Mr Beard noted, the underlying issue for the Tribunal is what is required to secure open justice so far as consistent with rule 7 of the Tribunal’s rules. That in turn requires the Tribunal to decide if it would be damaging to national security to reveal whether the  respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice. If so, then any part of the substantive hearing which would tend to reveal that fact cannot be heard in public. 
 
 
 The Tribunal has already decided that it would not be damaging to national security to reveal the fact of these proceedings, the parties to the proceedings and the fact that it  concerns the respondent’s powers to give a technical capability notice to a relevant operator. There was extensive media coverage both before and after that decision to the effect that a technical capability notice had been given. That coverage was consistent with public statements made by the US Director of Intelligence and with statements attributed to the President of the USA. It was also consistent with what, if the media coverage is taken at face value, were private media briefings provided by Government officials. There is no evidence that any of this is assessed to have damaged national security. 
 
 
 Further, the evidence shows that the Government has not consistently applied NCND in this context. First, two different reputable newspapers have reported that Government officials departed from NCND and positively confirmed the existence of a technical capability notice. Journalists protect their sources and sometimes describe them in terms that are not entirely precise ( and on occasion not entirely accurate). Some care therefore needs to be taken before assuming the truth of the content of a newspaper article. However, it is difficult to see any source protection reason why The Times and The Financial Times should have described their sources as Government officials if they were not either a member of the Government or a civil servant or special adviser. Notwithstanding what is asserted at paragraph 15 of Mr Scurry’s statement, Mr Sheldon did not submit that we should find the reporting to be untruthful or materially misleading. 
 The assertion that investigations did not reveal a Government source has little or no evidential value in the absence of any further detail about what the investigations involved: see, by analogy, Attorney General v BBC [2022] EWHC 380 (QB)per Chamberlain J at [30]-[31]. 
 
 
 Moreover, we infer that it is extremely unlikely that multiple Government sources would have briefed the media in the absence of authorisation for such briefing. Otherwise, the  sources would have exposed themselves to the jeopardy of disciplinary and criminal proceedings for no evident personal gain. Conversely, there is nothing inherently unlikely about a scenario in which Government formally maintains NCND in the face of media inquiries (to seek to preserve the integrity of its NCND policy and its litigation stance) whilst at the same time informally departing from NCND by providing briefings to journalists (to provide a narrative that might have political or diplomatic benefit). 
 
 
 Importantly, it was open to the respondent to file detailed evidence on this issue. She has chosen not to do so. We were told that it is not usual practice for a Government Security Group investigation to be disclosed, even to the sponsoring department. That is nothing to the point. There is no suggestion that there is any legal impediment to the disclosure to the Tribunal (in CLOSED if necessary) of the relevant investigation reports. In any event, it was open to the respondent to file direct evidence from Ministers or senior officials that the media briefings were unauthorised. Again, she has chosen not to do so. In all the circumstances, we infer that the briefings that are reported by The Times and The Financial Times did take place, and that they were authorised by Government Ministers or senior department officials or special advisers. This amounts to a significant departure from NCND. 
 
 
 There are, additionally, the briefings of members of the US executive and legislature. The fact that the UK Government has confidentially briefed a foreign intelligence liaison partner will not generally undermine its NCND stance. This is because, ordinarily, intelligence partners respect confidences. Here, however, it was abundantly clear by April 2025 that the most senior US officials and politicians were not prepared to keep secret what they regarded as an egregious breach of the First Amendment rights of US citizens. In that context, the respondent’s decision to authorise Apple to conduct further briefings of members of the US executive, without any apparent assurance of confidentiality, amounted to a further clear departure from NCND. 
 
 
 The cumulative effect of these departures from NCND is that anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability  notice on Apple. We use the word “knows” advisedly. We accept that in some contexts there may be a real difference between strongly suspecting something on the basis of credible reporting and knowing it on the basis of specific confirmation by a Government source. In this context, where ( as we find) authorised confirmations have been given to reputable newspapers and to foreign officials and legislators who do not regard themselves as bound by any duty of confidence on the subject, it is in our view a distinction without a difference. We have also borne carefully in mind that any assessment of the national security impact of confirming a particular fact must take account of the range of capability of malign actors. Some, including some adversary states, will be sophisticated. Others, such as those who may be contemplating lower level terrorist or criminal activity, may be much less well-informed. We have no doubt that confirmation of the fact at issue here would supply those in the first category with no information whatsoever that they do not already have. We are also satisfied that anyone in the second category who is remotely interested in discovering whether a technical capability notice had been served on Apple could already find the answer to that question with ease. We were told, for example, that an affirmative answer, backed by reference to the press reporting we have discussed, can be found by simply typing the question into Google’s chatbot. On the facts of this case, the suggestion that official confirmation would add materially to the stock of information available to a unsophisticated malign actor seems to us to be fanciful. 
 
 
 All that being the case, we do not give any significant weight to the respondent’s assessment that it would be damaging to national security publicly to depart from NCND, in these proceedings, on the question of whether she has given Apple a technical capability notice. We have carefully considered the evidence that is relied on by the respondent in support of that assertion, including the evidence served in CLOSED. Given that which is already in the public domain, and the extensive (but unacknowledged) departures from NCND that have already taken place, none of that evidence provides convincing support for the respondent’s assertion. We consider the assessment contained in that evidence to be flawed in the public law sense because it fails to take into account or properly grapple with a critical material consideration: the extensive-and on our findings authorised-departures from NCND. 
 
 
 Accordingly, we agree with the NGOs and with Apple that the respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the  case, that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice. It follows that any part of the substantive hearing in these proceedings which involves such confirmation can  properly take place in OPEN unless there is some separate basis for requiring secrecy to prevent damage to national security or the broader public interest. 
 
 Practical impact of allowing the existence of a technical capability notice to be disclosed during the OPEN proceedings 
 
 The practical consequence of recognising that it is not damaging to the public interest to disclose the existence of a technical capability notice is that much of the substantive hearing in these claims can take place in OPEN. 
 Apple has five grounds of challenge. The first two concern whether the respondent has power to issue warrants for targeted interception of communications outside the United Kingdom, and whether the statutory power can be used to regulate the security or privacy services offered by a technology company to its customers. These are questions of statutory interpretation that do not depend on evidence. They can be determined entirely in OPEN. The third ground concerns the consultation process. It is likely that the substance of that ground can also largely be determined in OPEN. 
 The fourth ground concerns whether the technical capability notice amounts to a disproportionate interference with qualified rights under the European Convention on Human Rights. That will require an assessment of whether four tests are satisfied: Bank Mel/at v Her Majesty’s Treasury (No 2) [2013] UKSC 39; [2014] AC 700 per Lord Reed at [74]. Those tests are (1) whether the objective of the measure is sufficiently important to justify the limitation of a protected right, (2) whether the measure is rationally connected to the objective, (3) whether a less intrusive measure could have been used without unacceptably compromising the achievement of the objective, and (4) whether, balancing the severity of the  measure’s effects on the rights of the persons to whom it applies against the importance of the objective, the former outweighs the latter. It is likely that the first three of those tests can largely be determined in OPEN. We do not prejudge where the precise dividing line should fall between that which can be published without damaging the public interest. On any view, however, it is likely that the determination of the fourth test may involve the consideration of evidence that would be damaging to the public interest. 
 
 
 The fifth ground concerns whether Apple has been treated differently from other technology companies. Again, it is likely that will involve consideration of evidence that cannot be disclosed in OPEN. 
 
 
 It follows that revelation of the fact that there is a technical capability notice allows much (but not all) of the substance of these claims to be determined following public hearings conducted in OPEN. 
 
 Disclosure of the detail of the technical capability notice 
 
 The disclosure of the detail of the technical capability notice is another matter. Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content. All parties recognise that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now. That is because the key issue for the Tribunal is the extent to which the open justice principle requires public disclosure, so far as that can be secured without damaging national security. The resolution of that issue requires a close analysis of what relevant evidence and arguments the parties will seek to deploy at the substantive hearing. We have already observed that it may be possible to determine the first two grounds of claim entirely in OPEN. If so, it may not be necessary to confront the question of whether disclosure of some details that are not relevant to those grounds would be damaging to national security. It is also likely that parts of the remaining grounds will, in any event, have to be considered in PRIVATE and CLOSED. It will only be after the parties have exchanged their evidence and written arguments that it will be possible to draw dividing lines as to what evidence is truly relevant to each issue, what is truly damaging to national security, and where the OPEN/PRIVATE/CLOSED boundaries should lie. There is also the possibility that some parts of the hearing could be litigated on the basis of assumed facts, or on the basis of highly generalised gists of the actual facts. Again, that cannot sensibly be determined now. 
 
 Outcome 
 
 We reject the respondent’s contention that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the fact that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice. The extent, if at all, to which some of the detail of the technical capability notice may be disclosed without damaging national security or the public interest is better addressed separately, after disclosure of evidence and when the precise issues to be determined at the hearing are clear.

 Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest. I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people. Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up). reply happyopossum 1 hour ago | parent | next [–]
