 Ben Lorica. So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications. 
 I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons? 
 Pete Warden. I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces. 
 You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard. 
 Ben Lorica. Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause. 
 Pete Warden. Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you. 
 We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive. 
 I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward. 
 Ben Lorica. By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right? 
 Pete Warden. Yeah, absolutely. 
 And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well. 
 When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider. 
 If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax. 
 So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for. 
 Ben Lorica. So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong. 
 What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind? 
 Pete Warden. One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search. 
 Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.” 
 Ben Lorica. Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.” 
 Pete Warden. What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes. 
 They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one. 
 And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening. 
 Ben Lorica. Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me. 
 Pete Warden. No, I can see. 
 Ben Lorica. No, no, but in general, right? In general. 
 Pete Warden. Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned. 
 I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing. 
 So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally. 
 And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically. 
 With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy. 
 Ben Lorica. So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area. 
 In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right? 
 So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs. 
 For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models? 
 Pete Warden. There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model. 
 Ben Lorica. “Machines of Loving Grace.” 
 Pete Warden. Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies. 
 Ben Lorica. Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right? 
 Pete Warden. Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them. 
 Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task. 
 So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech. 
 Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information. 
 You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff. 
 Ben Lorica. Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata? 
 Pete Warden. You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output. 
 But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training. 
 If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing. 
 If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately. 
 But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points. 
 So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies. 
 Ben Lorica. Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal. 
 And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video. 
 So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech? 
 Pete Warden. They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma. 
 The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech. 
 So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it. 
 So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models. 
 Ben Lorica. By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right? 
 Pete Warden. I mean, right now, only… 
 Ben Lorica. For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on. 
 Pete Warden. One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM. 
 Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always… 
 Ben Lorica. And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right? 
 So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception? 
 Pete Warden. Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things. 
 With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system. 
 And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment. 
 I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI… 
 Ben Lorica. But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech. 
 You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right? 
 Pete Warden. Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model. 
 I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses. 
 I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems. 
 You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript. 
 And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies. 
 Ben Lorica. Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right? 
 So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that. 
 So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general? 
 Pete Warden. Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions. 
 Ben Lorica. But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on. 
 Pete Warden. Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X. 
 And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it. 
 I often say, “AI wants to be local.” 
 If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity. 
 So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense. 
 So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes. 
 If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day. 
 So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops. 
 And I can keep going on and on. 
 Ben Lorica. Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right? 
 As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model? 
 Pete Warden. And why not do fine-tuning on your own model? 
 Ben Lorica. Yeah, I mean, with that data. 
 Pete Warden. Yeah, exactly. 
 Ben Lorica. And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else. 
 No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right? 
 Pete Warden. Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight. 
 Ben Lorica. Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right? 
 Pete Warden. Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside. 
 Ben Lorica. So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right? 
 Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware? 
 Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general? 
 Pete Warden. So watch Apple. 
 And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years. 
 But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators. 
 I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU. 
 Ben Lorica. So you just run everything on a CPU? 
 Pete Warden. Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator. 
 Ben Lorica. Oh, okay. That’s not a… 
 Pete Warden. GPU. 
 Ben Lorica. I see. I see. So CPU… 
 Pete Warden. Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the… 
 Ben Lorica. The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right? 
 Pete Warden. And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training. 
 I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping. 
 They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware. 
 Ben Lorica. One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash. 
 Pete Warden. Absolutely. 
 Ben Lorica. Right. So what’s your take? 
 Pete Warden. So that’s another example. 
 I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side. 
 I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.” 
 So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually. 
 So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM. 
 I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like. 
 Ben Lorica. Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai.

OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem - Media over QUIC Demo Blog Docs GitHub Discord moq.pro → October 27, 2026 · kixelated OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem 
 On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News . 
 thx 
 A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant.
You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didn’t. 
 Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over.
deus vult 
 Hot Take Alert 
 Let’s say you’re a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product. 
Let’s say you’re making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash. 
Let’s say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France? 
 If your AI ever replies with: 
 
 I’m sorry, you broke up, can you repeat that? 
 
 You fucked up .
You picked WebRTC for voice AI. 
 The Danger that Lurks Beneath 
 You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPT™. You click on the microphone and grunt: 
 
 What is le capital of France? 
 
 OH NO , hypothetical sudden packet loss .
A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable.
All too common I’m afraid. 
 WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices.
It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time .
Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old. 
 WebRTC gives up on late audio ▶ spoken / understood received, not yet understood lost forever What is le France? 
 This kind of sucks for a voice AI product .
You walk out of wifi range, hit a cellular dead zone, or starlink terminal switches satellites.
Oops, your tokens are wasted , or worse, AI tries to guess what you said . 
 WebRTC can usually detect packet loss and retransmit.
But retransmissions are disabled by default for audio.
And even when enabled, the audio jitter buffer won’t wait for them. 
 But why not? 
Isn’t this networking 101?
Just send that shit again? 
 It’s because of us . 
 The Speed of You 
 We flesh bags consume/produce audio in “real-time”, aka a human clock rate .
Our neurons can only fire so fast. 
 For a real-time conferencing product like Google Meet, latency needs to be near zero.
Any delay is super fucking annoying, which is why WebRTC does everything in its power to minimize it. 
 Blocking on retransmissions will cause delays.
It’s the fatal flaw with TCP and why WebRTC is UDP based in the first place.
And worse yet, retransmissions will cause a rapid burst of audio on recovery. 
 This is a bad user experience .
Humans do not want to wait, then process a burst of audio at 10x speed.
WebRTC instead primarily* relies on human retransmissions . 
 You: What is le … France? 
 Me: 🔇 
 You: I said, what is le capital of France? 
 * Before a WebRTC warrior flames me on LinkedIn, read the fix it fix it fix it section. 
 Are we doomed to mediocrity? 
 Clock That Solder Boy 
 Of course not.
 Wake up old man , it’s not 2020 any longer.
The internet is no longer for our flabby lips. 
 Our robot overlords produce/consume audio based on a silicon clock rate .
We shoved electricity into a rock and now it can read a library in minutes.
What a time to be alive. 
 Voice agents can hear and speak audio faster than real-time. 
Listening at 20x the speed? No problem. 
Speaking at 20x the speed? No problem. 
 Humans stuck at real-time. 
We speak too slowly, so speech-to-text has to wait for us. 
We hear too slowly, so text-to-speech has to wait for us. 
 WebRTC is designed for humans, not voice AI agents.
These poor robots are being held back by our mediocrity. 
 I Require Context 
 When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird . 
 Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can.
However, LLMs are blocked on context . 
 i require context 
 Here’s a dumb example of context growing over time: 
 
 1s : What 
 2s : What is 
 3s : What is le 
 4s : What is le capital 
 5s : What is le capital of 
 6s : What is le capital of France? 
 
 If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck.
 France is le gatekeeper , and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite.
In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet . 
 Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken?
WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty.
The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU ) noticing a thing. 
 So that’s what Mr. MoQ does.
No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio. 
 MoQ retransmits for up to 5s ▶ spoken / understood received, not yet understood waiting for retransmit get stuffed mr kraken 
 It’s not expensive either: audio is tiny .
1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets.
We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact. 
 And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time! 
 The model no longer has to guess.
It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either.
 This is a pure user experience win . 
 Not Just Mics 
 Guess what?
WebRTC doesn’t just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS. 
 cars suck too, I’m an equal opportunity hater 
 Fun Fact : WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives , not when it is supposed to be rendered .
Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal.
Sure, it’ll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio. 
 This is a huge problem for voice AI .
TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp.
But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTC… the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet . 
 And if there’s any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada. 
 WebRTC sends at human speed, gives up on late audio ▶ sent / played generated / buffered lost forever When the kraken attacken, there’s no coming backen. 
 If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet.
A stamp of sorts. 
 Random Access Memory 
 Welcome back to the future Marty .
We faster than real-time now. 
 RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive.
And being able to store stuff locally.
You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers. 
 We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM.
Absurd, I know. 
 MoQ sends everything ASAP, the player buffers ▶ sent / played generated / buffered waiting for retransmit I’m fast as fuck boye 
 It’s how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity.
MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI.
Your sick baking recipe won’t be subject to surprise congestion. 
 And don’t you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB.
You’re not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick. 
 Disclaimer : this behavior is not IETF standardized.
It’s something only my moq.dev clients (and thus Pipecat) support.
Be my guest if you want to argue with Cisco and get it into the official standards. 
 Enter the Antagonist 
 Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC ? 
 WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio.
It’s available in every browser via libwebrtc , a C++ monolith maintained by Google.
It’s so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else. 
 The problem is that WebRTC is the Google Meet client .
It is designed specifically for Google’s conferencing product, not their voice AI product (they use WebSocket), and certainly not your product. 
 quite the anti-competitive ruse tbh .
Google can ship product updates without consulting the other browser vendors.
No other conferencing app can do this on the web. 
 Fun Fact : This is why every other conferencing app recommends a native client.
Otherwise, they can only reach parity with Google Meet at best .
Native apps can do whatever they want over UDP instead. 
 Fix It Fix It Fix It 
 So that’s why your hyper deluxe ChatGPT™ voice AI model, after billions invested, has the audacity to ask:
 can you repeat that? 
 I could dump on WebRTC for days, but I want to be positive for a change.
 Here’s how to fix it. 
 First off, I need to acknowledge what WebRTC does have: 
 
 NetEQ is amazing. It changes audio playback speed based on jitter. But not packet loss. 
 Audio retransmissions can now be enabled via SDP munging ( disgusting ). But the NetEQ jitter buffer won’t wait for them. 
 The playout-delay RTP extension is perfect for voice AI. But it’s video only. 
 
 To fix WebRTC, we need to petition Google to: 
 
 Implement playout-delay for audio. 
 Allow the jitter buffer to grow, both in the past and into the future (for TTS). 
 Render audio based on timestamps not vibes. 
 IDK some RTP extension to bump the track generation (for interruptions). 
 
 And of course, petition the wider WebRTC ecosystem to do the same. 
 Gatekept 
 The main problem with WebRTC will remain: Google is the gatekeeper . 
 Your Claude friend can’t just fork libwebrtc and fix these issues.
Google is required for web support, at least until Theo spends $420k to rewrite Chromium in Rust. 
 I think it’s amazing that playout-delay was merged 10 years ago and audio still doesn’t have it.
Higher latency/quality playback has never been a priority for WebRTC, since Google Meet is the only product that matters . 
 Fun Fact : This is why I ended up creating MoQ.
We tried using WebRTC at Twitch but the real-time-or-else made for a poor user experience.
I am but a humble software engineer, and despite trying, we failed to petition Google. 
 But OpenAI has enough sway to fix WebRTC.
One long-deserved improvement is WARP (not that WARP ), which was hot on the heels of my last blog post.
Keep at it Justin, or join the Dark Side with me . 
 Enter The Protagonist 
 In my humble and handsome opinion, it’s time to invest in a better transport .
Take a few of the M’s from the B’s and T’s; nobody will notice. 
 A voice agent should never ask the user to retransmit a prompt. 
A voice agent should instead ask the transport to retransmit a prompt. 
 Spoiler alert : Media over QUIC is that better transport btw. 
 Pipecat now supports MoQ !
A huge thank you to Vanessa and Claude Code for putting in the work and putting up with my constant “improvements”. 
 Here’s a crude demo with my credit card deets attached.
please don’t milk me dry. 
 
 Note that I’ve only spent like a day of work prompting on this.
It took me significantly longer to write this damn blog post.
Don’t judge too harshly pls. 
 And yes, it sometimes says “can you repeat that?” which is hilariously ironic .
The first/last hop is MoQ, but I don’t control the rest of the pipeline.
If Deepgram, OpenAI, or Cartesia drop ur packets then there’s nothing I can do about it. 
 Interruptions 
 We’re not done yet.
I wanted to shill the MoQ in the middle of the blog and use the rest… 
 at least it’s not the owl 
 Sometimes the AI is monologuing and you need to tell it to STFU .
It’s pretty easy to do with WebRTC because of the sleep before sending each packet.
But with MoQ, we need some signal to tell the player to abandon the playout buffer . 
 Here’s the naive approach without a signal: 
 MoQ (naive) one track, so the reply waits behind the buffered answer ▶ sent / played generated / buffered I definitely did not do this on my first implementation. 
 My solution for this is deviously clever.
 So clever . 
 For MoQ, we’ve prioritized the ability to add/remove tracks dynamically.
Most media protocols have fixed tracks and it’s a pain in the butt : HLS, DASH, RTMP, WebRTC, etc.
You can’t add 1080p, or switch codecs, after a broadcast is live. 
 My super clever idea is to reuse this functionality for interruptions.
Just make a new audio track (and remove the old one) as the STFU Signal™ . 
 MoQ a new track replaces the old one, and its buffer is discarded ▶ sent / played generated / buffered discarded home of le crepes 
 This works on a generic MoQ player .
We automatically switch tracks, using timestamps to keep synchronization. 
 ez 
 Butt-to-Butt 
 
 Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. You didn’t mention speech-to-speech ? 
 
 Look, Dunning-Kruger is the only reason the previous blog post exists .
I didn’t know speech-to-speech existed until the comment section.
What can I say but ur welcome . 
 DISCLAIMER : I still haven’t done any research on the state of voice AI.
I give you full permission to tweet @kixelated ur stupid . 
 The idea behind speech-to-speech is to cut out the text middleman.
The disjoint STT -> LLM -> TTS pipelines get smashed together , reducing latency while preserving verbal context.
OpenAI is the pioneer in this space and they deserve mad props . 
 So this vindicates WebRTC right?
The speech-to-speech latency can be low enough to justify dropping packets? 
 Not so fast literary strawman.
 There’s a fundamental trade-off between latency and quality . 
 Latency Budgets 
 The more time you have to work on something, the better the result. 
Good things take time, like Fable changing a single line in README.md because I’m too poor to pay 3.5x for ultrafast. 
 Networks are the same.
 The more time you have to transmit something, the better the quality. 
It’s why retransmits exist in the first place. 
 Unless you’re doing broadcast TV, which still uses MPEG-TS and still results in glitchy messes.
Seriously wtf guys, TV is no longer over the air, and we don’t need 188 byte packets any longer. 
 Anyway, the amount of time a user is willing to wait for something is a product decision .
Put on your big boye pants, it’s time to be a PM.
Do users want something fast and lossy, or slow and reliable? 
 Why not both ? 
 That’s the idea behind speech-to-speech.
Do a low-latency STS pass for easy prompts and to generate filler noise. 
 
 Human: What is le capital of France? 
 
 
 ChatGPT: One second, let me look that up. 
 
 Boom, even that useless “I’m thinking” response makes the human feel good chemicals.
But more importantly for us anti-PMs, it buys us enough time to start a slower pass. 
 I don’t work at a frontier lab so this is all speculation , but I imagine STT->LLM->TTS is still used for these slower passes.
A STS model with Astra/Fable quality is absolutely ideal… but probably not worth the investment. 
 Either way, doesn’t matter if it’s STS or STT->LLM->TTS.
The only thing that matters is the latency budget . 
 MoQ do Both 
 One of the core problems we’re trying to fix with MoQ is the whole “one transport per latency” issue in the industry.
It’s face-palmingly common to use different protocols based on the latency budget. 
 For example, an all-hands presentation where the speakers use Zoom, while everybody else watches via HLS and can’t participate. 
 Fuck that noise, MoQ supports multiple latency targets with a single connection.
In the case of voice AI: 
 
 real-time latency for rapid replies (STS). 
 loss-less quality for slow replies (STT->LLM->TTS). 
 
 How? 
Every MoQ subscription includes how long the subscriber is willing to wait . 
 Your real-time model can have a maximum latency of 500ms while your more accurate model might have a maximum latency of 5s.
Both get coalesced into a single upstream subscription which can fanout. 
 MoQ one upstream, two subscribers with different latency budgets ▶ spoken / understood received, not yet understood waiting for retransmit lost forever it’s all about the size of the jitter buffer baybee 
 And note that this is the maximum latency .
The latency is 0 except during terrible network conditions, and eventually we give up.
This is the core difference between MoQ and TCP/WebSocket for Voice AI. 
 Your transport latency should be aligned with your product latency budget. 
 It’s Simple: Predict the Future 
 One more strawman to beat into the dirt. 
 
 Hey stupid, your blog post is wrong. WebRTC doesn’t care about packet loss because it uses FEC . 
 
 M8 go read my previous blog posts: never use datagrams and forward error correction .
This is like my dumber one hot take. 
 WebRTC (and Opus) include Forward Error Correction to help mask packet loss.
The idea is to stuff a crappier, lower bitrate copy of the previous audio frame into the next packet. 
 But only a single last packet .
It can’t even handle two lost packets in a row, let alone a full network blip. 
 This is fine for WebRTC because it doesn’t give a shit about audio older than 30ms.
But it’s not fine for voice AI or really anything on the internet.
 Packet loss due to congestion is bursty, not random. 
 A common “fix” is to spread these copies over time, so you can handle X lost packets in a row.
See Opus 1.5 .
All of this extra data has a real cost, and if you don’t know what you’re doing (and you don’t), then you will aggravate bufferbloat . 
 In my humble (and attractive) opinion, FEC is best for huge RTTs, like transmitting to le moon.
In <current year> , we instead use CDNs to shrink the lossy first/last mile which makes retransmissions OP .
Why send more bytes spread over 400ms, instead of retransmitting in 40ms? 
 But if a WebRTC warrior insists, QUIC libraries can retransmit stream data as many times as they want.
Basically RED but based on byte offsets, not packets, and fully transparent to the receiver.
That’s a free idea btw. 
 More Free Ideas 
 I should end the blog post here but seriously, I’m 3 weeks in and need this shit forwarded internally.
Take a screenshot of it on your internal Slack. 
 Hey, OpenAI. 
I’m sorry for flaming you for representing state-of-the-art for voice AI.
We may have gotten off on the wrong foot. 
 Hey, Anthropic. 
I’m sorry that I called you the orange butthole company.
We may have gotten off on the wrong foot. 
 I’ll make it up to both of you.
Here’s some free ideas you could prototype with your unlimited Fable/Astro 7 tokens.
Just give me Co-Authored-By credit on the git commits.
Or Scion, I don’t care. 
 Please I need more green squares on my Github. 
 
 You can spot the exact moment I started token maxxing. 
 Decouple Compute 
 I know you have obscene amounts of capital, but getting GPUs next to every single user in the world is hard.
But getting cheap DELL servers next to every single user in the world is easy. 
 
 Run moq-relay within CDN edges. 
 Run models where GPUs are available. 
 
 Like I said earlier, this is basically the premise of CDNs .
A huge number of edge nodes close to users minimizes the congested first/last mile .
Over-provision the backbone so you can get the traffic to the GPUs without congestion . 
 You can independently scale network and compute. 
 Which I hope you guys already do, and are big enough to justify a custom Voice AI protocol instead of using a standardized MoQ implementation. 
 For everybody else, MoQ is generic enough to serve more than just Voice AI .
Think of MoQ like a live HTTP.
It’s an IETF standard after all , the same body that does that HTTP thing. 
 In fact, my first big customer is using moq.pro to mass fanout JSON blobs.
Literally a generic pub/sub protocol masquerading as an A/V protocol. 
 Prioritize Context 
 I’m a transport and ideas guy, not an AI scientist.
Don’t flame me if this is obvious and/or impossible. 
 The core problem with WebRTC+AI is that there’s a disconnect between the model and the transport.
This blog focused on aligning latency… but what about aligning context? 
 After all, not all tokens have the same weight .
If we knew the relative importance of each token, we could use that to make informed networking decisions. 
 high priority : what capital france 
 low priority : is le 
 zero priority : <silence> 
 To implement this via MoQ, you would split the audio track into separate tracks that are encoded independently.
The high priority track would get first dibs on available bandwidth, and the subscriber would wait longer for it. 
 But TBH the hard part is actually giving a shit.
Audio bitrates are so low that you rarely get a chance to prioritize anyway, and it’s not worth the hassle of doing a client-side tokenizer.
Maybe it could matter for video tho. 
 Back-fill that Boye 
 The other problem with dropping audio after 30ms is that it’s a one-way door. 
 Bold prediction : The next Claudism will be one-way door after it’s been trained on this post. 
 Once a network transport decides to drop data over the network, it can’t be used for other things.
Now, I don’t know if frontier labs store raw audio… but maybe they should. 
 Eventually the AI model has to stop waiting and guess based on incomplete data.
Did it do a good job or bad job?
 How can we know? 
 Well… maybe don’t actually drop the audio; keep that shit in RAM.
Audio is tiny after all.
We can set max-latency to 10 minutes and it will be transmitted eventually at the lowest priority .
We backfill that boye only when the network has fully recovered. 
 Why backfill via MoQ?
Why not save it as a file and train on it later? 
 Vroom vroom , the GPU is warm. Ask the model if it did a good job guessing what the user said X seconds ago while the context is cached.
Use it as training data.
IDK I’m not a scientist. 
 FIN

You get a discount while I’m spiritually unemployed and easy to impress.

 I've had some experience with audio on the web, back in the day I built a weird collab music streaming system in the browser and presented at NIME. Back then AudioWorklets were new and I didn't understand WebRTC. The initial design used Raspberry Pis and IceCast. However, the setup was not only difficult to me but beyond the abilities of my target audience. I was more familiar with web dev and figured why can't something similar work for the browser, truly naive. After lots of learning through trial and error and understanding how these types of streaming worked, I ended up with something in hindsight worked pretty simply and was beautifully naive. It took audio input, fed it into a wasm opus encoder, output audio in "segments" of audio, and uploaded via typical HTTP. No WebSockets or WebRTC or QUIC (I don't even think I used HTTP2). The only reason it wasn't just a full encoded recording was because I wanted to make it continuous and streamed. I basically learned this via HLS, but also didn't understand HLS nor was it easy to encode and stream data (in my mental model) from the browser to the server. On the server and streaming to the client, it just collected the segments and told clients when they were ready, via polling, similar to HLS. The client would download, wasm decode, and add the audio to a buffer. The thing is that because of the nature of the project it didn't really have much to do with one continuous stream, but it did take sequences of the segments from multiple user's uploads and combine them for the different audio channels.  Chrome AI Features Wasting Much Bandwidth 
	
 
 
 ♦ Posted by Jeff Starr in Tech 
 
 
 Updated November 19, 2026 
 • Leave a comment 
 
 
 
	
 🔎 Finally solved the mystery . At some point this year (around a few months ago), my bandwidth/data usage went thru the roof. Figured out it was Chrome’s recent AI features. Then got immediate bandwidth-relief after disabling all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Here is a screenshot of the settings: 
 
 Find the Chrome AI settings under "AI innovations" 
 I simply disabled everything on that settings page, and the needless bandwidth leakage stopped immediately . 
 Don’t take my word for it. Fire up your favorite activity/network monitor. Watch the network activity while Chrome’s AI features are enabled, which they are by default . Note the continual bandwidth/data spend coming from Chrome, which if you care to monitor long-term adds up to hundreds of GBs per month (depending on setup, usage, etc.). 
 After watching the meter spin for a while, go into the Chrome settings and disable all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Then return to the network monitor and watch it virtually flatline. Problem solved . 
 Commentary 
 Chrome should have left the AI resource hogs disabled by default. Someone do the math on how much energy and bandwidth is absolutely wasted by all the people (such as myself) who never even touch the AI stuff . 
 Before I disabled the AI settings, Chrome was chewing up literally hundreds of GB s per month. Now multiply that by the number of Chrome users who aren’t using “AI whatever neat”, and you’re talking real numbers. Real waste . For something that serves absolutely no purpose, that’s a ridiculous spend. 
 That’s all for now, I’m off to try some new browsers. There are quite a few great Chrome-alternatives these days.

Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you ( foolscap.works ) 99 points by atugard 7 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 80 comments People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here. It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work. The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it. I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome. Thanks,
David help

# An Open-Source, Visual-First Canvas for Code Craft websites, prototypes, and designs with AI on a canvas built for creative work. See your real app running live, shape it visually, and let your own agent write the code. An open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44, Webflow, etc. ## Why Onlook - 🎨 **Built for design.** Onlook is the open-source developer tool for designers. You see your real app running live on a canvas, explore ideas side by side, and shape the interface visually instead of from a terminal. Design apps, websites, posters, graphics, and more with your local fonts and assets. - 🤖 **Bring your own agent.** We don't ship our own model. Connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account you already have, and that agent does the work inside your project. Plug in more tools through MCP connectors to bring all of the context you need to your creative workflow. Work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages. - 📁 **Works on your real repo.** Onlook opens any Git repository on your machine and runs your own dev server, so what you design is your actual product, not a mockup that someone has to rebuild later. - 🖥️ **A desktop app, local-first.** Onlook runs on your computer. Your code stays on your computer, and the source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys, or `.env` file. - 📤 **Share what you make.** Export artifacts as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG, or PDF to hand off, review, or post. - 🧡 **Open source.** Apache 2.0. Read it, fork it, and customize it yourself (we'd love to hear how you customize it!) ## What you can do with Onlook - [x] Design on your real codebase - [x] Live app on an infinite canvas - [x] Mobile, tablet, and desktop frames side by side - [x] Safe worktree copy, so your folder is never touched - [x] Parallel projects as tabs - [x] Design with your own agent - [x] Bring your own Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex plan - [x] Ask about any element on the canvas - [x] Agent arranges the canvas for you (variations, states, flows) - [x] Reference images on the canvas - [x] Sketch and share - [x] Artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside your repo - [x] Export to HTML, PDF, PNG, and JPEG - [x] Ship it - [x] Import a GitHub repo - [x] Start entirely new codebases from scratch - [x] One-press pull requests, from checks to merge ## Getting Started 🖥️ [Download the Desktop App](https://www.onlook.com/install) (Recommended) – The fastest way to get started with Onlook. * macOS (Apple Silicon · Intel x64) → [Download](https://www.onlook.com/install) * Windows – Coming soon. Join the [Windows waitlist here](https://www.onlook.com/waitlist?os=windows) and be emailed when we have updates. * Linux – No Linux artifact is published and we're still gauging demand for Linux. Join the [Linux waitlist here](https://www.onlook.com/waitlist?os=linux) and be emailed when we have updates. 🧑‍💻 Build from source – [SOURCE_BUILD.md](SOURCE_BUILD.md) covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. No Onlook account or cloud keys needed. ## How it works 1. **Open a project.** Point Onlook at any Git repository on your computer, or import one. Your code stays where it is. 2. **Onlook runs your app.** It starts your own dev server locally, the same way you would from a terminal. 3. **See it live on a canvas.** Your running app appears in frames on an open canvas, so you can look at pages, sizes, and ideas side by side. 4. **Design with your agent.** Describe what you want in chat. Onlook hands the request to the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account you connected, and that agent edits the real files in your repo. 5. **Watch it update.** Changes show up on the canvas as your dev server reloads, and Git keeps track of everything that changed. 6. **Share the result.** Export artifacts as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG, or PDF. Because Onlook runs your project with its own tooling, it works with all web frameworks or languages your dev server already supports. ## An example workflow 1. Start a new empty project by clicking the "New Draft" button in the upper left corner of the projects page. 2. Use the input box in the lower right corner of the screen to write what you'd like to be designed in Onlook. 3. Answer clarifying questions from the agent, and wait for it to build 4. Click to select individual frames for context in follow-up prompts, or double-click on a specific element to use the inline chat and guide the AI to edit that specific element. 5. Prompt more ideas on one or multiple designs until you're ready to share your work with a colleague. 6. Select the frame you'd like to share, and ask the agent to convert it into an Artifact for exporting. 7. Export the artifact as HTML/CSS or as a PNG using the export button in the upper right corner of the frame. 8. Paste the exported artifact in Slack, email, or any messaging tool. ## Our Tech Stack | Layer | Stack | |---|---| | Desktop | [Electron](https://www.electronjs.org/) · [React 19](https://react.dev/) · [Astryx](https://astryx.atmeta.com/) (Design system)· [React Flow](https://reactflow.dev/) · [Zustand](https://zustand.docs.pmnd.rs/) · [CodeMirror](https://codemirror.net/) | | Your project | [Git](https://git-scm.com/) for working directly on your repo · [node-pty](https://github.com/microsoft/node-pty) for running your dev server and shells | | Tooling | [Bun](https://bun.sh/) · [Turborepo](https://turbo.build/) · usage analytics (see [Usage data](#usage-data)) | | Export | HTML · PNG & JPEG ([Electron capturePage](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/web-contents#contentscapturepagerect-opts)) · PDF ([Electron printToPDF](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/web-contents#contentsprinttopdfoptions)) & [pdf-lib](https://pdf-lib.js.org/) | ## Contributing If you have a suggestion that would make this better, please fork the repo and create a pull request. You can also browse [open issues](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook/issues). See the [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for instructions and code of conduct. To report a security issue, follow [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue. #### Contributors ## Contact - Contact us: [Discord](https://discord.gg/hERDfFZCsH) - [Email](mailto:contact@onlook.com) - Updates: [Twitter](https://twitter.com/onlookdev) - [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/onlook/) - [YouTube](https://youtube.com/@onlookdev) - [Substack](https://onlook.substack.com/) - Project: [https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook) - Website: [https://onlook.com](https://onlook.com/?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=github) ## Looking for the previous version of Onlook? - **Onlook v1 (web):** the browser-based version lives on the [`v1` branch](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook/tree/v1) of this repository. - **Onlook Desktop (Electron, original):** the first desktop version is at [onlook-dev/desktop](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop). ## Usage data Onlook collects product usage analytics to help us improve the app. In the official download they are on by default; a build from source asks first. You can turn them off in Settings, or set `STUDIO_TELEMETRY=0` to run or build without them. See the [privacy policy](https://www.onlook.com/privacy-policy) for details. ## License Onlook's source code is distributed under the Apache 2.0 License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details. The license covers source code, not every asset in this repository. Onlook's icons come from [Central Icons](https://iconists.co/central) by Iconists. They are licensed to Onlook for its own product, and that license does not extend to forks. Onlook's brand marks, DMG art, and sounds aren't covered either. # The open-source Cursor for Designers Seamlessly integrate with any website or web app running on React + TailwindCSS, and make live edits directly in the browser DOM. Customize your design, control your codebase, and push your changes without compromise. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c8782d1e-fedc-46f3-8735-c3a762d4db16 ![Onlook-GitHub-Example](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/642de37a-72cc-4056-8eb7-8eb42714cdc4) ### Built With - [![React][React.js]][React-url] - [![Electron][Electron.js]][Electron-url] - [![Tailwind][TailwindCSS]][Tailwind-url] - [![Vite][Vite.js]][Vite-url] ## Stay up-to-date Onlook officially launched our first version of Onlook on July 08, 2024 and we've shipped a ton since then. Watch releases of this repository to be notified of future updates, and you can follow along with us on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/onlook-dev) or [Substack](https://onlook.substack.com/) where we write a weekly newsletter. ## Getting Started ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/18b6ad5a-1d5a-4396-af8c-8b85936acf39) ### Installation 1. Visit [onlook.com](https://onlook.com/) to download the app. 2. Run locally following [this guide](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop/wiki/Building-from-source) ### Usage Onlook will run on any React project, bring your own React project or create one using Onlook Use the chat to create or edit a project you're working on. At any time, you can always right-click an element to open up the exact location of the element in code. Just be sure to choose your preferred IDE in the upper-right Corner of the screen. ## Roadmap ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f64b51df-03be-44d1-ae35-82e6dc960d06) See how we're tracking towards major [milestones](<[url](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop/milestones)>), and read the [wiki](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop/wiki/Roadmap) for details on each version of Onlook. Here's a rough overview of some of the major features we're looking at: - [x] Browser - [x] Editor - [x] Write-to-code - [X] AI chat - [ ] Variables - [ ] Components - [ ] Hosting Also check the [open issues](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop/issues) for a full list of proposed features (and known issues). ## Contributing ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ecc94303-df23-46ae-87dc-66b040396e0b) If you have a suggestion that would make this better, please fork the repo and create a pull request. You can also [open issues](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop/issues). See the [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for instructions and code of conduct. #### Contributors ## Contact ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/60684b68-1925-4550-8efd-51a1509fc953) - Team: [Discord](https://discord.gg/hERDfFZCsH) - [Twitter](https://twitter.com/onlookdev) - [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/onlook-dev/) - [Email](mailto:contact@onlook.com) - Project: [https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop](https://github.com/onlook-dev/desktop) - Website: [https://onlook.com](https://onlook.com) ## Acknowledgments Projects we're inspired by: - [Visbug](https://github.com/GoogleChromeLabs/ProjectVisBug) - [Responsively](https://github.com/responsively-org/responsively-app) - [Supabase](https://github.com/supabase/supabase) - [ShadCN](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui) - [hymhub/css-to-tailwind](https://github.com/hymhub/css-to-tailwind) ## License Distributed under the Apache 2.0 License. Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers ( github.com/onlook-dev ) 57 points by D_R_Farrell 4 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 57 comments Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code! The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day! help

One thing that is a bit different about how Onlook is built versus other design tools is that we are local first. But it's a challenge we're definitely able to solve with some tuning and UX. reply Bnjoroge 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 Awesome! Definitely a much needed tool. How does it compare to paper/pen? I've been preferring the former, since pen has its own format and I prefer not to use it. nit: it was pretty hard to find pricing info. I had to scroll down to the footer to see it. Would recommend adding it to the navbar reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 The key difference for Onlook is that we work on the real running application. Paper and Pen are excellent tools for working on abstractions of what you'd like to ship, but still are constrained in a way that favors the editor experience, not the building experience. This is totally ok in our opinion – you want to choose the right tool for the job – we just think the job for designers is trending towards being right up against the real medium of code and how it gets represented when it ships. Your point on the proprietary format is a good one. There are so many ways to build a design tool, and it felt like agents give us an opportunity to make an entirely new way to craft designs that doesn't require a strict format. Why can't we just select the thing we want to change and do it, regardless of what it is? reply ringstar 1 hour ago | prev | next [–] 
 i use claude design for a lot of design work but it always struggles with keeping new components and designs in style with existing components and designs so i have to spend a lot of time telling it to constantly "use the same design system". how do you guys solve this? reply thebrubaker 39 minutes ago | parent | next [–] 
 I personally rely on my claude setup and it's memory feature, and that's what plugs right into onlook. I don't end up repeating myself because those lessons learned across sessions persist. That and having a good base design reference to work from. Also the agent in onlook is very visually aware and capable, it's constantly verifying work and sees exactly what you see, so I've rarely seen it diverge from the existing components or screens you have up. give it a try and see if it feels more aligned than you get in something like claude design. reply D_R_Farrell 29 minutes ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 that's pretty frustrating and there are a lot of ways we keep designs aligned with your real product When you work in Onlook you work on top of the real codebase, so whether you're starting a project to make a real edit on the running app, or you're just starting a project to make prototypes or sketches off of the foundational codebase, you are pointing the agent to the real code. Think of Onlook more along the lines of working on top of code and apps rather than just flat HTML/CSS (like what Claude design does). It gives you more power because if you wanted to, you can actually reference a specific part of your repo and build with real React components. If you set up your codebase to have a design system, you can start every ideation exercise as a new project in Onlook from that repo. reply adinagoerres 1 hour ago | prev | next [–] 
 this is very cool. how can I make use of it as someone who doesn't code but uses claude/ codex for everyday things? I do a lot of design work in claude or grok. reply krisodd 1 hour ago | parent | next [–] 
 When you start onlook you can select claude as your agent, then you can import the projects you're working on to continue the work in onlook! reply thiagoperes 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 Very very cool. Seems like there's a huge opportunity here. Cursor got stuck after the acquisition. And especially if paired with open models, I'd definitely use this to avoid using my limits on cc/codex reply D_R_Farrell 3 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 I do think that there is a great opportunity to bring in open models into this interface. We've also heard from a lot of designers how Cursor has fallen short when it comes to helping them get their design work done. There are a lot of features that Cursor offers that we still need to meet parity on, but We do see an opportunity to build an excellent tool for creatives to work in code on an infinite canvas that aligns better to the divergent process of design vs. the convergent process of engineering. reply thebrubaker 2 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 we have MCP prepped as another connection, that should let you drive onlook from your open model / harness too. What open models are you using (and what client are you driving them from?) reply forsalebypwner 7 minutes ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I basically only use DeepSeek via their API and Pi as my coding harness. Was surprised to see there isn't any support for other LLMs, looks like a very cool app otherwise. reply threecheese 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 "World's best, top-most agent recommended #1 Developer tool for Designers and Visual Engineers to design with Real Code." Did you agent also recommend this copy??? Fire it! :) reply D_R_Farrell 3 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 hahahaha we borrowed it from TLDraw! https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw We also think it's a pretty hilarious idea... maximum agent-discovery. reply farukparhat 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 I think this makes sense,
I have customers that still use figma, how does this differ from some of Figma's new capabilities? reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 Figma is of course the UI/UX design industry leader that we're all familiar with, but the flaw in their primary vector editing tool has been its disconnect from code. They are adding-on code-related features, but those features will always be secondary to their ultra-powerful editor as the foundation of their business. Onlook will always be code-native and caters to the ways designers will need to work with code specifically, not vectors. That means being local-first, but also flexible for the challenges and diversity of code that will have to continue to be maintained in the future. Onlook will feel a bit light to start when compared to Figma 1:1 on every feature, but the foundation enables us to focus on the future of designers coding and generating assets with AI, not drawing vectors. reply thebrubaker 1 hour ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 also your cc / codex is the driver, so if you have Figma's MCP connected you'll see that in Onlook, and you can treat them as complimentary reply artur_makly 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 Congrats on the launch. How does it differ from tools 
like pen.dev? reply D_R_Farrell 3 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 Pen.dev chose to go the route of a specific file format for design in favor of building an editor around that, which is a more constrained approach in our opinion. Meaning that the work you do in the canvas is always a "copy" or "mock" of what is actually being implemented. For Onlook our goal is to make everything you do truly 1:1 with no translation layer in between what you see and what will ship. It's a small nuance but makes a big difference in the design process. They certainly have an impressive product that is quite performant from what I remember. reply esafak 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Do you mean you render the code for perfect fidelity instead of having the LLM translate it to JSON? reply D_R_Farrell 51 minutes ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Yes exactly. What you're looking at in Onlook is essentially a canvas of browser windows, so what you see is exactly what you're going to get. reply crve 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 Is this cc api only? This is exactly the workflow I've been imagining, so eager to try it out. reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 We detect your cc subscription automatically, so you get your subsidized intelligence right out of the box :) The onboarding is super fast in Onlook you may be surprised how quickly you can go from starting to designing (which you'll see as a claim on our install page: https://www.onlook.com/install ) reply thebrubaker 1 hour ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 yup! we work with your existing cc setup / subscription, so if you're already logged in you're good to go. same claude you use every day, and onlook is just the canvas you build on top of reply RyanShook 2 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 What's the business model? reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 We're free for now but have collaboration + cloud features planned, and there's a lot of additional paid services that we'll bundle like image generation, vector generation, even font generation (which I'm super stoked for) and that will require some spend on our side that we'll charge for in a general subscription. Also, as is popular with working on major codebases these days, we see a lot of interest in VMs and/or sandboxes, and there's an opportunity to do that in the canvas, but specialized for the ideas that people cook up quickly in Onlook. reply rgbrgb 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 cool, congrats on launch. the designers in my life are all loving claude code rn. > Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription this was first thing i looked for in the readme and didn't see it. recommend putting it in there :) reply thebrubaker 1 hour ago | parent | next [–] 
 hah I agree, I think this should be higher up. under the hood we're built on the agent SDK and codex's app server, so the agent you drive is what you're already using every day, and onlook just brings the canvas / tools / workflows that help them be most effective in that space. the agent relationship is between you and anthropic / openai, agents and code are local, and the chat is basically a rendering layer for you to not have to jump between multiple apps. reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 thanks! we mentioned it on this line – but we can make it more prominent thanks for the suggestion > Bring your own agent. We don't ship our own model. Connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account you already have, and that agent does the work inside your project. Plug in more tools through MCP connectors to bring all of the context you need to your creative workflow. Work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages. reply truetraveller 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Isn't it illegal (TOS) to use subs outside of Claude/ChatGPT proper? reply D_R_Farrell 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 We work like other IDEs do by using the same subscription that is on-device reply written-beyond 1 hour ago | prev | next [–] 
 I was a pre-YC acceptance user for onlook. You're V1 desktop release, interesting to see you're still on this. I hate UI in this LLM world, this could just improve it a little bit. Congratulations! and I hope the YC experience was worth it. reply D_R_Farrell 54 minutes ago | parent | next [–] 
 oh no waaaayy!! haha stoked!! Yes, it was a bit of a journey – we had our original v1 release, then we went to the web, then built an infinite canvas that worked on top of Storybook, and realized that the v1 users were still using the old product. The YC experience was truly unlike anything I've ever done. You meet incredibly kind, intelligent, and ambitious people and the YC community has been so generous with support and feedback. I was surprised to see that YC also does a lot for open-source startups too, with dedicated open-source events and many YC companies offer deals to support OSS. If you're considering applying to YC, my tips are: 1) do it even if you don't think you're ready. The track record of your applications all feeds into getting you an interview, even if you feel like you're wandering around and experimenting. 2) don't use an LLM to draft your application. They really really value reading your raw thinking. In any event, thanks for trying v1 – would be keen to hear how you like v2! reply instagary 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] 
 Nice demo video and love that’s open source! reply D_R_Farrell 3 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 Appreciate it! Took a lot of takes but Screenstudio made it much less painful to edit the final take. reply maxdo 3 hours ago | prev [–] 
 what's the main benefit of using this over cc design? reply D_R_Farrell 3 hours ago | parent [–] 
 CC design is a great product for sketching out ideas but works more like a canvas of artifacts that a dedicated dev environment for working on running apps and codebases. There are also some odd UX decisions they've made with that product in favor of competing for a general design tool but constrained by how they render designs in code. I get the sense that the mega-bundling of Design into Artifacts is an added step for creatives who want to just dive into a tool made for explicitly design work. Do you use cc design a lot? What do you like about it? reply

 Onlook 
 
 The developer tool for Designers 
 
 Onlook is a free, local-first editor where designers craft exceptional experiences in code
 
 
 → Download today 
 
 
 👨‍💻👩‍💻👨‍💻
 We're hiring engineers and designers in SF! 
 👩‍💻👨‍💻👩‍💻
