 Software companies are trying to kill home computing If you use a computer or any other device which runs software on it, here's something which you might want to know: Software companies are not your friends, and in fact, they are trying to kill personal and home computing. The reason for this is simple: Software companies, like any other business, are out to make money, but what's good for computer users is not good for software companies, and the reason for this is that software companies are not selling a physical product. Hardware companies are different. Hardware companies usually want to make good products, because they can get repeat sales. Hardware wears out, breaks, or simply gets replaced, and so in the hardware business, mostly the same laws of business and economics apply as in any other home-appliance business such as selling refrigerators, ovens, and washing machines. I say "mostly" because computer hardware is still experiencing some minor amount of technological development, particularly in the field of GPUs, but in contrast to the 1980s and 1990s, this development is no longer proceeding so rapidly that it's likely to fuel an upgrade cycle (a person today is not likely to buy a new computer because their old computer is obsolete, for the simple reason that computer hardware no longer advances quickly enough for a still-operating computer to become obsolete within its working lifetime), but people who want to have the absolute latest technology may still buy new hardware for that reason alone; this is a fairly small niche of hardcore technology enthusiasts, but such consumers may provide considerable revenue to companies like Nvidia, which specialize in bleeding-edge hardware. Most other hardware companies, however, are selling commodity hardware in an established market which is not likely to experience much growth or other change, and thus the business model works on the same principle as companies selling refrigerators: You're selling durable goods to people who are making a one-time purchase, but if your products are good, then you'll develop a reputation for quality, and so other people in the situation of making a one-time purchase will also buy your products. There are some hardware companies which take the opposite approach, namely the thinking that if you sell fragile products which break quickly, then you can get more business because people will buy replacements more quickly, but the same principle applies here as in other businesses selling physical products, like the car business: If you develop a reputation for selling cheap junk which breaks quickly, then you'll lose a lot of business long-term, so most hardware companies (at least those with widespread name-brand recognition) want to protect the value of their brand and sell good products which work well and last a long time. Business comes not from customers re-buying stuff to replace cheap junk which breaks quickly, but quite the opposite: From customers who need to replace hardware which worked well for long enough that they feel it's worth buying another product from the same brand. Hardware companies are selling a real, physical good which can't be copied but which can wear out with time, and so just as with companies who sell refrigerators and cars, this provides some steady level of business. The same is not true for software companies. The problem with software is that if you make a really good product, it will only get bought once. Software doesn't wear out; it has no moving parts, and so one software program which does its task very well can keep functioning forever, in the way that a math formula never stops working. Of course, unlike hardware, software can also be copied, and software piracy is a serious problem as well, but even when customers buy a software product legitimately, the problem remains that if the software works well, it will only be bought once, and people may use it indefinitely without paying any money to the software company after that. In the 1980s and 1990s, personal computing was still in its infancy, and no one had yet figured out what kinds of software people and businesses would or could use in their everyday work, so software companies could still make a living by being creative and introducing new features or even whole new types of programs. Today, however, patterns of software usage are long established: We know what kinds of programs people use and want to use, what kinds of features they use and don't use, and so there is not much room left for creativity or innovation, not much possibility remaining for creating new programs for people since all the software which the world needs has not only already been created, but in fact released as open-source software, given away for free on the Internet. In other words, there is no need for any new software. How can a software business stay in business in an environment where there is no need for their products? How can any business stay in business when the market for their product has dried up? In most cases, such a situation would signal the end of the industry: Typewriter companies hardly exist anymore, because computers with laser printers can produce printed pages faster and more easily than a person working with a typewriter. The typewriter market didn't evolve; it disappeared entirely. Okay, this isn't strictly true; typewriters are still used in remote locations without electricity or in other situations where operating a computer is impractical, but this is such a niche usage that you probably haven't seen anyone productively using a typewriter in decades. The point still stands: When the need for a particular product disappears, the market for that product disappears, too. For the vast majority of users today, just as with typewriters, the need for new software disappeared decades ago, because all the software people need has already been written. So for software companies to remain billion-dollar businesses, they can't make their living selling things which people actually use or need. They need to make a living some other way. In recent years, that "other way" has often focused on turning software into a service rather than a product: The phrase "software as a service" has become ubiquitous, and in fact, the tag "as a service" has become such a cliché that whole new industries have sprouted around the idea of selling something "as a service"; there's even a Wikipedia article which lists several such variants, including data-oriented products such as "database as a service", "IT as a service", "desktop as a service", and even "DDoS as a service" (the article lists several illegal cybercrime services which are being sold on a per-use basis), but also several things which are physical products, such as "transportation as a service" (which, in its most basic form, is just a new term for taxi rides and car rentals), "energy storage as a service" (which sounds like just a new term for paying the electric company, but is a bit more complicated than that because it focuses on having an on-site energy storage system, which can be a set of batteries or something larger and more complex than that), and even "lighting as a service" for people who don't want to own their own lighting fixtures. The idea of loaning out physical products as a service is not a new one, and historically has made sense for customers when it would be cheaper to rent something than to buy something. Perhaps the most common and familiar form of this business model is the car-rental business: If you're travelling somewhere on a short-term trip, it's obviously easier and cheaper to rent a car there for the duration of your stay rather than to buy a car there. Other more niche businesses have long-standing traditions, such as tuxedo rental: Most people rarely wear tuxedos except for special occasions such as weddings, and since tuxedos are expensive, it's cheaper to rent a tuxedo for the day than to buy one. Utilities as a service have also long been standard for most homeowners, because for most people, it's not feasible to have an electric plant and a water-treatment plant at home; it's easier and cheaper to have some company produce electricity and water and pay to have these sent to people's homes through wires and pipes. (There are people who generate their own electricity and draw their own water at home, but these people tend to be a minority in most industrialized countries.) So it makes sense for people to rent very expensive things which they'll only use short-term, but companies are increasingly interested in trying to get people to pay regular payments for common products that used to be single-purchase items. Imagine if you bought a t-shirt but had to pay a service fee every month for the ability to wear that t-shirt, or the same business model applied to things like furniture or kitchenware. (Furniture rental exists as a business as well, but usually not for people who are planning to live long-term in the same house with the same furniture over a period of years.) Businesses like this idea because it obviously means a constant, long-term flow of money: Instead of selling people a product once and then never making any more money from them after that because they already bought the product, businesses are realizing that they can rent everything to people but retain ownership of what they're offering, thus forcing users to pay a monthly service fee for the privilege of using those products. The increasing adoption of this business model was the inspiration for the now-famous and widely-repeated quote that in the future, "You'll own nothing, and you'll be happy". Businesses will sell the idea that it's inconvenient to own something yourself because ownership means responsibility: If the product breaks or if there's some other problem with it, then you're responsible for fixing or maintaining it, whereas if you rent something, you can just let the owner fix any problems. Convenience and a lack of personal responsibility for fixing any problems are big selling points for the set of "as a service" industries. But there is no industry which is more famous for its transition to the "as a service" model than the software industry, and the reasons for this are fairly clear: Software is relatively cheap to buy, and again, once you've bought it, you could theoretically keep using it forever. There are people who are still using software programs which were developed literally decades ago, simply because these programs still work fine for their purpose, and there is no need to keep buying new software if it can just be copied. Even if you buy a new computer, you can just install the software onto the new computer and keep using it, and in fact, such usage is typically legal, because software-piracy laws usually only apply if you make a copy of the installation disk(s), but if you install the software from the original disks on your own computer(s), then this is legal, because once you bought the software, you are legally the owner of that copy of the software, and may use it for your own usage however you wish. This is why software companies want to get rid of the concept of users owning their own copies of the software; under the "software as a service" model, instead of owning your own copy of the software, the software company retains ownership of the product, and they're just renting it to you on a provisional lease. Why didn't software as a service exist in the past? There were a few reasons for this; one reason, as I've mentioned, is that in the 1980s and 1990s, software was still evolving, and since new versions of software typically sold themselves on the basis of new features which were useful enough that people would actually be willing to pay for a new version of the software, you could make a software business just on the basis of selling new features. But the biggest reason why software as a service didn't and couldn't exist in the past is because the Internet was not widespread back then: In the 1980s and 1990s, most people were not yet connected to the Internet, and so there was no way for computers to connect to the licensing servers which would verify the presence of a current and paid-for software license on the computer. Today, most computers are connected to the Internet, and it is this Internet connectivity which has enabled the software-as-a-service business. This does raise the valid question of how people are supposed to install software on computers which don't have an Internet connection, but as people without an Internet connection are a minority today, the stance of software companies has generally been that people without Internet connections are not a market worth considering. Essentially the thinking is: If you're not on the Internet, then tough luck, getting software for your computer is your own problem. The idea is generally that everything is on the Internet now, and the idea of storing data locally on your own computer is an obsolete idea which software companies would very much like to get rid of. Even game companies have long been trying to get rid of physical copies of games and only sell games as downloadable products through online game stores like Steam. The news recently broke that the upcoming and highly-anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) will not include a physical disc in the game packaging, meaning that the physical game package will be a plastic shell with nothing more than a slip of paper inside it. Games, however, have some slight technical justification for this practice: Games are ridiculously large now. The latest games from major game developers are literally about 100 gigabytes in size now, and back when games were shipped on DVDs, this would mean shipping a box with more than 20 DVDs in it, since original DVDs held just under 5 gigabytes of data. But technology has moved on, and current triple-layer Ultra HD Blu-ray discs can in fact hold about 100 gigabytes of data, which means that even current-generation games could be shipped on a single disc. Still, it has become almost a standard, expected process among gamers buying the latest game that they will "install" the game which they just bought from a disc, but then have to wait hours downloading 40 to 80 gigabytes of "updates" before they can actually play the game. Essentially the disc contains a launcher and some basic game data, but the full game's content is only stored online and can only be downloaded through a long process that can take hours. Most games from major game studios also require product activation before they can be played: Most games bought through Steam require Steam to be running and logged in before the game will start, and each major game publisher has their own online store which does something similar. Of course, this functionality is often couched in marketing terms; for example, Rockstar Games, the developer and publisher of the Grand Theft Auto series, operates the "Rockstar Games Social Club", which is actually their DRM system to ensure that only people with a valid game license can play their games, but which is branded as an online "social club" which allows gamers to connect with other gamers. People who play video games have long gotten used to these practices, but the situation specifically with GTA 6 was interesting, because the backlash against the idea of buying a game with no disc in the package led Rockstar to release a statement saying that they will consider releasing a physical game disc later. I don't know why people were so outraged about not having a physical disc when it is, as I said, already a long-standard practice to ship only a fraction of the game on its physical disc and download the rest of the game's content from the Internet after the game has been "installed", but gamers are sometimes quite possessive of their games and want to feel like they own a physical product instead of just a license to download some bits from the Internet. Businesses are typically more willing to tolerate software as a service, because they have the money to pay regular monthly fees, and also because their software is often more expensive than personal software anyway, but home-computer users are resistant to this idea, because they see no reason why they should have to pay a regular fee to use a program: A typical piece of home-computer software usually costs less than $100, which means that even if you pay a monthly service fee of only $10 to use software, within less than year, the service fees for renting software become more expensive than just buying the software outright. A single license for Windows 11 Home costs $139, and a license for Windows 11 Pro costs $199, so even if you want to use the more expensive Windows 11 Pro, the monthly subscription fee had better be less than $16.50, or else renting the software on a subscription basis will get more expensive than just outright buying it after a year. This business model of renting out software makes very little sense for home users unless someone just wants to use a program once for a very specific one-time purpose; renting games in this way has been a long-running practice since people often just play a game once for a few days and then never play it again, but for operating systems and any kind of productivity software, renting out software is a non-starter for the home market, and software companies know this: They know that there is no business in trying to sell software to the home-computer market. That market dried up years ago. So the solution which software companies came up with is to get rid of home computing altogether. Software companies are trying to kill home computing, and their reason is simple: They know that they have nothing to gain from home computing. When you have a home computer, all your software runs locally on a machine which you own, and you can choose which software runs on it. Today, most of the software which home-computer users need is available for free, so software companies won't even make money on the initial software sale, but even if you do buy a software program, it's a one-time purchase: Once you've bought the software, you can keep using it forever. That's not a sustainable business model; a business needs to stay in business, which means it needs a steady flow of income. And so software companies have largely given up on the idea of selling software in favor of the idea of selling services, something for which you have to pay a monthly usage fee, rather than something you just buy once. But how do you get people to pay a monthly service fee for software when people can just get a software program once and install it on all their computers forever? The solution is to eliminate the concept of the "personal computer" or "home computer" altogether, which is exactly what software companies are trying to do. And to be fair, hardware companies are complicit in this process. The hardware and software industries have long existed in co-dependence on each other, because each industry knows that their products are useless without the other, and so they have generally been willing to work together and accommodate each other's needs. If the software industry dies, there will be no reason for people to buy computer hardware since there will be nothing to run on it, and so computer-hardware vendors are willing to make changes that support the survival of the software industry. You might intuitively think that hardware companies are exempt from this process since hardware companies are selling physical products, and thus people will keep buying it just based on its function, even if it doesn't do anything new: If people need more RAM, they'll buy more RAM. It doesn't need to do something which no RAM has ever done before; it just needs to work, and as long as it works well, people will buy it. However, hardware companies are quietly making changes which support the needs (or demands) of the software industry. One of the biggest recent changes in the computer-hardware industry was the need for a TPM (Trusted Platform Module) 2.0 chip; this requirement was introduced with Windows 11, and since most computers still run Windows, hardware vendors understood that their computers would need to contain a TPM 2.0 chip going forward, so they simply started introducing this as a standard component of all their computers. Computer hardware vendors have also allowed storage capacities to stagnate: Standard sizes for computers' storage drives have hovered around one terabyte or even less for over a decade, reflecting a shift toward people no longer storing data on their own devices, but rather storing all their data in the "cloud", meaning online in some company's remote server. But although hardware companies tend to quietly accommodate the wants and needs of the software industry, it is the software companies that most urgently want to erase the memory of personal computing, and although it isn't my intention to pick on one company in particular, it is pretty well inevitable that any such discussion will center around Microsoft, as Microsoft is the company which still defines the personal-computing experience for most home-computer users. The only company which really competes with Microsoft in this realm is Apple, but Apple is a special case, because Apple is not a software company. Apple is a hardware company. Yes, of course they make an operating system for their products (actually a couple of operating systems: macOS for desktops and iOS for phones (or, technically, even more than that, since they also make variants like watchOS for smartwatches and tvOS for their TV device)), but Apple is a big business only because they sell physical hardware, and as such, they have no need to kill home computing since the sale of consumer hardware continues to make Apple the largest manufacturing company in the world by revenue. Apple is destroying home computing by making devices which are closed (the operating system hinders the installation of "unapproved" software, and it also hinders users from directly accessing the computer hardware, in addition to the hardware itself being physically designed in such a way that it's difficult to access or replace parts for), but Apple is not trying to kill the home-computing market in the way that Microsoft and other big software companies are. And yeah, it's not just Microsoft. Google is doing the same thing: Google's ChromeOS, which does not yet have much usage share but still regularly pops up in discussions just because it's from Google (which absolutely dominates the operating-system usage share on mobile phones with Android), represents a similar idea: ChromeOS seeks to eliminate the concept of a personal-computer operating system altogether, focusing everything around the web browser. Essentially ChromeOS is an "operating system" in which the sole program is a web browser, and everything which the user does happens online, within that browser. ChromeOS completely eliminates the concept of a home computer and turns the "computer" into nothing more than a screen which pulls its content from the Internet. To be fair, this has changed somewhat since ChromeOS was first released; more recent versions of ChromeOS have added the ability to install local programs and run these on the computer itself rather than in a browser, but Google's focus is clearly on getting people into the cloud and eliminating the concept of locally-run, home-based computing. How far they'll get with that remains to be seen, since as of this writing, ChromeOS still has less than 10% overall usage share, but Android also started off with a very small set of users (remember the T-Mobile G1, also known as the HTC Dream? I used one when it came out, and it was slow, clunky, and nearly useless) before becoming what it is today, and people are increasingly seeing Google as picking up the personal-computing market from Microsoft, which seems eager to abandon it, but as Microsoft is still by far the leading provider of home-computer operating systems as of this writing, I'll continue to focus on Microsoft for now. I wasn't always against Microsoft. Through the 1980s and 1990s, I actually enjoyed and enthusiastically used Microsoft's products. That was a time when Microsoft actually made functional, usable products with useful, helpful features that people could utilize. Some people disliked Microsoft because they thought that Microsoft products were inferior; they said that MS-DOS wasn't as good as competitors like PC DOS, DR-DOS, or 4DOS, and when Windows first came out, it certainly wasn't as good as the Mac OS which ran even on the very first Macintosh computers, but Windows became better, to the point where Windows 3.0 and 3.1 were pretty decent, and even though there were still complaints that Windows 3.1 wasn't as good as IBM's OS/2, I was satisfied with Windows 3.1 and never had any serious complaints about it. That was a time when Microsoft understood that home computing was still a very new and rapidly growing market. I often repeat that quote from Bill Gates where he claimed, at that time, that Microsoft's vision was "A computer on every desk and in every home. We've never wavered from that vision." Microsoft was making home computing more accessible to the world, and even if their products might have not been the very best in the industry, they were good enough. People don't hate the Volkswagen Beetle just because it isn't a Porsche 911; it does what it needs to do well enough, it's accessible for a lot of people, and you can even have some fun with it, so it's a pretty okay product for regular people. But things started to change around the time that Windows XP was released. That was the first version of Windows to contain Microsoft Product Activation: You couldn't just install Windows XP and use it, you had to register its license online for the system to work correctly. If you didn't have a product key which was registered with some central Microsoft server online, Windows XP would stop working after 30 days. Now you couldn't just buy Windows once and install it on all your computers; you had to buy a separate Windows license for every computer you had. This addressed a legal gray area which had long been an issue in the home-computing industry: It was generally accepted that businesses would and should buy a separate software license for each of their computers (if a business had thousands of employees, they would need to buy thousands of licenses, one for each computer), but there had long been an implicit sort of understanding that if you had two computers at home, you could and would install the same copy of the same software program on both computers. Even if this was technically against the legal terms of the software license (which it often wasn't), there was no way to prevent people from doing this, and few people ever even really thought about it, because it was simply accepted that this was a given in the home-computing industry. Today, things are different. The consumer-software market has long since settled down: There are no real new programs which users want, or features from those programs. Today, people already have a working operating system, so when Microsoft (or any other company) introduces a new operating system, it needs to do something which other operating systems don't do, or else people won't buy it. This is essentially an impossible proposition since all the things which people do with their computers have already been put into operating systems long ago; many people consider Windows XP, which was released in 2001, to be "feature complete" since it already did all the things which people use their computers for. In fact, you could arguably go back even further in time and make similar claims for Windows 95 or Windows 98, but if we allow that Windows XP basically does everything that regular people need in an operating system, this means that Windows has already been feature-complete for 25 years. In that time, Microsoft has been desperately trying, and failing, to give people new reasons to buy the latest version of Windows. Microsoft knows that this is a losing battle; Microsoft knows that people no longer have reasons to upgrade Windows since what they had 25 years ago worked well enough. Microsoft knows that for the majority of computer users, Windows is nothing more than a program menu. Windows may have a lot of features that you could put into a list, but for the majority of people who have a computer, Windows is nothing more than a desktop and a "Start" menu with a few icons which people click on to run their applications. That's the limit of people's interaction with Windows, and Microsoft's efforts to add new features to Windows are only resulting in a product that's less usable for those people. How can you make money in a market like that? You really can't, because those users don't need a product that would cost money; they just need the simplest of menus from which to run their applications. Microsoft has known this for decades, and so to survive in a market like today's home-computing market, Microsoft (and other software companies) need a different strategy. But what kind of "different strategy" could a software company, a company which makes and sells software, adopt other than selling software? Again, going back to what I said before about typewriters, this situation would normally simply mean the end of the industry altogether. But Microsoft and other big software companies aren't just big software companies; they are among the largest and most powerful companies of any industry in the entire world. And they aren't going down without a fight. Since they can no longer sell useful or usable products, their strategy has become to kill home computing altogether. I have written in the past that there has been a long-running trend to transform home computing by making it more like business computing: To take computer features which are more suitable for business environments and incorporate them into home-computer software, despite the fact that these features do not benefit home-computer users. And to be fair, this trend is not only prevalent among software companies; even anti-corporate software developers have apparently unconsciously adopted this mentality. There's a video which made the rounds on YouTube about Terrence Andrew Davis, better known simply as Terry Davis, comparing his operating system TempleOS to Linux. Davis was a controversial character, both because of his views on computer software and because of his social and political statements. It is generally understood that he suffered from schizophrenia and probably some other mental disturbances as well, and he was often reviled for his openly racist views and his tendency to go on at length about conspiracy theories; videos still widely circulate of him going on long, incoherent rants saturated with his perpetual use of the word "nigger" and variations thereof, including the adjective "niggerlicious", which he apparently coined to mean simply "bad". Despite his lifelong struggles with mental health which culminated in his death in a 2018 accident which may have been accidental or may have been intentional suicide, Davis was often respected for his talents in developing software, with commentators noting that when he got off the topic of politics and began talking about computer software, he often became someone who could speak lucidly and knowledgeably about the topic of software development. Specifically with regard to Linux, Davis criticized Linux for incorporating features which made sense in a corporate computing environment, but had no place in a person's home. Among the most significant of these is the concept of a file system with built-in file permissions. Davis explicitly states that "File permissions do not belong in a consumer product," and I've always agreed with him: Your personal computer is your personal computer . You are the only person using it. What is the purpose in having a permissions list attached to every single file when there is literally only one person who accesses every file? A file system with user and group permissions for every file makes sense in a business or other shared environment where there are several people using the computer system, but operating-system companies like Microsoft made the bad decision to take file permissions, which are a concept from the business world, and put them into a personal operating system. Mysteriously, macOS and Linux do the same thing, even in personal-computing contexts. By the same token, Davis stated that he did not like the use of "public" and "private" spaces in software code: What's the point? Everything is running on your computer, so why act like something needs to be walled off from something else? In his talk on Linux, Davis also denigrated the practice of virtual memory using a hard disk. Davis concludes that this practice is inherited from mainframe computing when a single computer with a few megabytes of memory may have had several users using it at once. When a computer has a very limited amount of memory, maybe it makes sense to do disk swapping, but today's computers usually have multiple gigabytes of memory. If your program can't fit into that space, the solution isn't to start swapping stuff to the disk and using it as memory, the solution is to get a programmer who can write a program that doesn't occupy literally about one million times as much memory as it should need. Again, Davis concluded explicitly: "Virtual memory doesn't belong on a modern computer." And then there's the whole topic of "scaling": Being able to expand your computer to something several times its current size if a future need for such growth arises. This is a concept from business. Applying it to a personal computer used by a single person to run their personal software at home makes no sense. Davis ignored all of these concepts in his operating system TempleOS, because he intended it to be used on one computer by one person in a personal capacity, not by business users in a corporate environment. The result is that an operating system like TempleOS is uniquely usable for one person on one computer to perform personal tasks. This isn't to say that TempleOS is the best or most useful operating system out there; its user interface is clearly aimed at developers and isn't very usable for regular users who just want an operating system which acts as a shell from which to launch applications, but the point is that the technical concepts which Davis addressed represent a mentality which wants to make a usable software product for home users, and these concepts are directly opposed to the direction which big software companies have taken with their operating systems. And again, the problem isn't just big software companies: Even Linux, which is supposedly a personal operating system for people who reject corporate values, is based on UNIX, and as such, it inherently contains the previously-mentioned corporate concepts, from file-system permissions to using disk swapping as a substitute for RAM, which have been inherited from corporate computing environments and have no place in a personal operating system. It's clear that Microsoft doesn't care about any of this. Microsoft is no longer focused on the consumer market: Its target market is no longer people who use personal computers at home. For many years now, Microsoft's main revenue stream has been business-oriented products (Windows Server, Office 365, and Azure). Windows for personal computers is more of a legacy product which Microsoft would like to get rid of. They are no longer focused on making Windows usable or putting helpful features into it; Windows has become Microsoft's own advertising platform where they try to sell you useless apps and AI features which nobody cares about. But it has long been an established idea in business that while the B2B (business-to-business) market appeals because your customers there have much bigger budgets, it's hard to ignore the B2C (business-to-consumer) market because that market is so much larger: When you sell personal software to the world, your target market is billions of users, and it's hard to ignore those numbers even if the market seems dead. And so Microsoft and other companies which are still in a position to sell software to home users must find a way to kill home computing. And the general way that they are doing that, and have been doing that for several years, is by fighting to bring everyone into the "cloud". From the aforementioned list of "as a service" offerings, I mentioned the concept of "desktop as a service". This is one of the biggest Holy Grails of the software industry, because it would eliminate the whole concept of a personal computer and transform it into a program running in the cloud: Instead of owning your own computer running in your own home with its own storage and processing capacity, you'd just have a screen which is remotely connected to some server in a distant "cloud" datacenter, and all your data and programs would be stored there. Anything you see on the screen would be sent from the remote server, and anything you do on that screen would be sent back to that remote server. You'd have no control over what software is installed on the computer; all of that would be administered by the company who owns the virtual desktop. This is the perfect solution for the software industry, because it minimizes how much hardware you'd have (you would have only a screen and a simple input device); everything else would be software, offered as a remote service rather than something which runs in your own home, and this means, of course, that they can charge you a recurring service fee for all of it. Now, obviously many people will resist such a loss of control and ownership over their own computers, and indeed, many are resisting it right now. How can software companies convince people to give up ownership of their own computers? The answer is simple: They'll make owning a computer so bothersome and intolerable that it will be easier to get rid of it. Perhaps you've heard of the recent law which was passed in the European Union which requires all new cars sold in the European Union to have a camera mounted in such a way that it constantly monitors the driver. A similar law has already been passed in the United States (specifically, it's section 24220 of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, titled "Advanced Impaired Driving Technology"), with the only question being when and how the law will be implemented; several news outlets indicate that the new requirements are set to come into force in 2027. Why would anyone do this? Why would anyone pass a law which requires a camera to monitor the driver at all times? The reason given is that this is to monitor drivers for distractions: Because too many people are paying attention to their mobile phones while driving, this will ensure that drivers are paying attention to the road and prove whether drivers were paying attention in case of an accident. But "texting while driving" has been a problem for decades; why is such a law suddenly coming now, at nearly the same time in both the USA and the EU? The real reason is because there is an ongoing push to make driving cars intolerable. Self-driving cars have now reached the point where they are safer and more reliable than human drivers, but how can we get human drivers to give up driving cars? If you just outlaw driving cars, people will protest. Instead, regulators know that they can get people to stop driving cars if they just make driving so unappealing that people will willingly give it up. If you constantly feel like you're being watched while driving, this will make people more willing to hand over control of the car to a computer. Software companies, particularly Microsoft, have been using such tricks for years to push people away from locally-hosted computing. Why does every version of Windows get worse than the last one? Why does Microsoft, far from adding useful new features to new versions of Windows, seem to remove the features which people most used and replace them with advertising? Windows 11 is a joke. Its main "feature" seems to be that the Start button has been moved to the center of the taskbar instead of being in the bottom-left corner by default. The new Windows 11 Start menu, however, removed the ability to have folders embedded within the Start menu, which was such a basic functionality that removing it is beyond insane. It was widely reported around the time of Windows 11's release that the new Start menu was completely rewritten and uses React Native, which is a JavaScript-based platform that makes heavy demands on system resources. Why exactly would anyone remake the Start menu, one of the core components of the user interface, using an inefficient language meant for web scripting instead of just making it a simple menu which actually had more functionality before? This is embarrassingly stupid. It's readily apparent that Microsoft's "new features" in new versions of Windows are no longer actually new features which any person would use or benefit from in any way, but rather a form of user-response testing to see how users react to different software designs; Windows has stopped being a usable product and become a testbed for Microsoft to check how people react to whatever is the currently-popular trend in software-interface design. But thank goodness that Windows 11 comes with Teams as a "new feature", even though Teams is actually a business-oriented replacement for Skype which makes no sense to have on a home personal computer. Once again: Microsoft (and most other big software companies) design their software for corporate environments first, then try to fit these software products into home environments in a stripped-down form. Instead of getting a product that's designed for personal use, you're getting a product which has had features removed and which was designed for business users in a corporate environment in the first place. Why does Windows force constant and unbearable "updates" on its users when these updates never seem to do anything? In the middle of your work, Windows will often start bugging you about the need to restart your computer to install system updates, and if you ignore these notifications or close them, Windows will actually issue you an ultimatum, informing you that your computer will automatically restart at a given time later today if you don't restart it yourself. Not only do these updates interrupt your work and leave your computer unusable for long stretches of time while the computer installs the updates and restarts itself, they also sometimes hinder your work by removing features which people were actually using. Also, contrary to the software industry's claimed narrative that the latest software updates fix security vulnerabilities, there have been plenty of cases where a new software update actually introduced a security vulnerability which was later exploited, so this idea that you always need to install the latest updates to remain "secure" is nonsense; it is a flat-out lie. The software industry does not force updates onto users for their security; they do this to make local computing more unappealing. Then these software companies can sell the narrative of cloud computing, where you don't have to install updates because the software isn't running on your computer anyway, where all of these administrative and maintenance tasks are taken care of for you by someone else, and you just pay to have a constantly-available, constantly-usable computer, even though that's exactly what we had in the 1980s and 1990s before these constant and intrusive "updates" started being forced on us. It's only for our own good, we're told... but if you don't like it, you can give up your computer and switch to the cloud. In fact, Microsoft isn't only doing this with home-computer users. For years, Microsoft has been trying to force businesses which use locally-installed ("on-premises") versions of Microsoft Exchange to switch to the cloud-based Office 365, for approximately the same reasons. Many businesses made this switch, but many didn't, citing the greater control they have over their own in-house e-mail server, or compliance requirements which prohibit storing confidential data in the cloud (i.e. on shared remote servers). In response, Microsoft eliminated permanent on-premises Exchange licenses altogether; new versions of on-premises Exchange can only work with a subscription model, meaning you need to pay a recurring fee to use the software even though it's installed on your own computer. But wait, you're not just paying to use Exchange; current versions of Exchange require that you have a current paid subscription to what Microsoft calls "Software Assurance (SA)". This is Microsoft's "service" to make sure that your software is always up-to-date with the latest "fixes" and "feature packs". You see, you aren't actually paying to be able to use the software program, you are paying for "security", "stability", "usability", and "Software Assurance". Microsoft certainly isn't the only company to switch to such a model; already in 2013, Adobe introduced Photoshop CC, where the CC stands for "Creative Cloud", Adobe's online software-subscription service, and Photoshop CC only works with a current license, which of course you can't buy just once but must subscribe to on a regular recurring payment, because having people pay a one-time fee for a software program just wouldn't be viable. We're told that this is for our security, of course. So that bug fixes and security updates can be sent to users. Of course. It's nice that software developers think that it's a great service to force customers to pay for the developers' own mistakes; if software developers hadn't built bugs and security vulnerabilities into their products in the first place, we wouldn't have these problems. But no matter, surely it is worth paying a recurring service fee to use a software program in a world where there are other programs which do the same thing which you can download for free. Of course. In any other industry, "Quality Assurance" means "We check our products thoroughly for problems before release, because we want to make sure that the products which we release are in a finished state. If a problem is discovered in one of our products after it's been released, that's expensive for us, because we have to do a product recall, and we have to pay for the customer's costs of replacing the defective product or parts of the product." Only in the software industry does "Software Assurance" mean "We'll fix problems in our product after it's been released and users discover problems in the product. Also, customers need to pay for the privilege of getting fixes from us." Imagine if a major car company's car was discovered to have a design flaw which could kill passengers. Now imagine that that car company expects every customer to pay $500 to get the problem fixed. That would be the making of a massive class-action lawsuit. People would immediately recognize that this business model incentivizes car companies to build flaws into their products, since they can make even more money by selling fixes for flawed products. Why is this business model tolerated in the software industry? Why do you have to pay for a "service" that provides you with updates to fix security flaws which a software manufacturer released into their own product? Terry Davis was fond of the joke "What do you use Internet Explorer for? To download Chrome!" Unfortunately, today's operating systems are so poorly-designed and so lacking in functionality that one could transpose this question and answer thus: "What do you use an operating system for? To run a VM hypervisor within which you run the operating system you actually want to use." Why not just install the operating system you want instead of running it on a VM? Because there's no hardware support for that operating system; hardware manufacturers don't make drivers for good and useful operating systems, they only make drivers for operating systems which are built for business users and re-released in cut-down versions for home users. As I've said, software companies are trying to kill home computing, but hardware companies are complicit in this crusade: If you can't use your hardware with a real operating system because there are no drivers for it, then you'll be forced to use an operating system which requires you to pay a subscription fee to use it, or which is so onerous to use that its developer hopes to push you into just abandoning home computing altogether and switching to the cloud. In the end, software companies have nothing to gain from you being satisfied with their software, because if you are, then that means you won't buy anything more from them. Their business model today revolves around either making users so dissatisfied that they feel compelled to buy something else, or just eliminating people's ability to choose their own software altogether. Either way, if you are a computer user, then software companies are in an active war against your ability to use computer software, and this is not likely to ever change. Software companies are trying to kill home computing? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Software companies are trying to kill home computing?  EvanAnderson 20 hours ago | next [–] 
 I think enthusiast computing is dying. Home users will be able to buy packaged laptops and some desktop PCs, but I think the era of enthusiasts building "gaming rigs" and such is coming to an end. I think it's being ushered out by a feedback loop of high prices driving market contraction and, in turn, driving prices even higher as demand shrinks. Gaming will move to real-time streaming and there won't be a need or a market for GPUs and high performance CPUs in the enthusiast market. Home computing, in the context of having a marginally-powerful computer or phone / tablet with minimal storage and RAM in the home, will continue just fine. Subscriptions for storage and applications are already becoming the norm, and with the skyrocketing cost of storage the market for large capacity storage targeted at enthusiast and home users will dry up, too. The industry wants users to rent everything. Storage rental is particular pernicious, to me, because being able to store your personally-created works in a manner that maintains confidentiality is to cornerstone of digital sovereignty. Being forced to store your data in systems that will use your data for model training is definitely desired by the industry. If they can con users into renting that storage and giving up their data to model training so much the better. reply Exmoor 19 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 > I think the era of enthusiasts building "gaming rigs" and such is coming to an end. I've been hearing this for over two decades and yet gaming desktops are more mainstream than ever. Certainly the current market is negatively impacting pricing and availability, but those same factors are also pushing their competition just as hard. I'm not even sure cloud streamed games was a profitable idea when prices were sane, but it certainly isn't now. reply cyberrock 18 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I think gaming desktops are mainstream but have a longer lifespan now, as AM4 and RTX10xx hardware is perfectly fine for most gamers who play Big Walk or Queen's Domain rather than 8k 240fps Forza. In contrast when I bought a $600 GPU in 2013 (outrageous price back then) it wouldn't be able to handle a medium quality 1080p game in 3 years. So I think both assessments are right: an enthusiast top end rig is more expensive but most gamers simply need less top end rigs every year. reply dormento 4 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I was using a GTX1060 up until last year, and it still played pretty much everything on decent settings. PC hardware has been long lived for a while, in fact, I think this is one of the factors in the attacks on personal computing. reply EvanAnderson 19 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 I built my first PC in '94. The market today feels so much different than it ever has. We had some RAM and disk crunches in the past (and disk prices never really recovered from the Thai floods), but this market feels so different. Prices continue to spiral out of control. On the business side I've got Customers looking to replace servers purchased in 2020 and 2021 and they're not able to get anything reasonably similar for less than 4X what they paid for the old machines. They're turning, sometimes grudgingly, to renting storage and compute. The prices for off-lease "enterprise" gear are skyrocketing, too. There's no respite. reply lp92 15 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Those 2021 servers should still be quite capable. Why exactly are they looking to upgrade? reply NathanielK 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Their business is growing and needs more capacity presumably. reply account42 7 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 There was also a big shift from simply getting the best performance to also making the PC look "good" as a display piece on your desk. Everything has got to have RGB unicorn barf now, including RAM, your CPU cooler and other similar mundane components that have no business putting out any light. reply webstrand 19 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 I've never lived anywhere with low enough connection latency to accommodate real-time streaming of an action game, and my bare packet latency is 20ms to the nearest data-center (that I know of and can ping anyway). Add any latency in the input processing of the game, time to encode/transfer/decode the frame, and any local input latency on the client and you’re easily looking at an extra 50-100ms over playing locally, which is well into the range people can actually feel in anything twitchy. Turn-based or slower games would probably be fine, but I don’t see shooters or fighting games moving to streaming for anyone who doesn’t happen to live next door to a data center. There might be some unexploited latency-masking tricks in client-side cursors and client-side reprojection (the timewarp trick some VR uses to rotate the camera without receiving a new frame), but I suspect the legacy internet connectivity of rural and suburban homes in america will be a serious barrier to widespread adoption of real-time streaming. If local hardware gets priced out of reach, it could rather mean the end of gaming as a widely accessible hobby instead of a switch to real-time streaming? reply lmz 19 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Not everything has to be high res 3D requiring the newest GPUs. For twitchy games I guess they'll just stay low quality enough to be able to run on customer local devices. reply sublinear 16 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 It can be the worst of both worlds. It's both "local" and "in the cloud" if it's a subscription to a browser-based game. Bonus points if it's not even within a walled garden and you have to go out of your way to a specific publisher's website to play it. reply Aurornis 19 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 > I think it's being ushered out by a feedback loop of high prices driving market contraction and, in turn, driving prices even higher as demand shrinks. Shrinking demand makes prices go down, not up. Demand for gaming and consumer gear is higher than ever. Gaming GPUs were expensive before the AI boom. Remember when everyone was shocked that the 4090 was $1500 or the 5090 was $2000, but they were sold out anyway? Remember the extreme competition for 30 series GPUs and scalping before that? I have yet to hear a good explanation for these beliefs that consumer PCs and gaming are going away, because they’re all driven by incorrect economic ideas (like shrinking demand raising prices) or fear imported from some other ideas, while ignoring the ever expanding market for gaming and consumer PC gear reply Exmoor 19 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 > Shrinking demand makes prices go down, not up. In a simple supply/demand scenario, yes, but when shrinking demand causes manufacturers to spread costs across a smaller market it can lead to higher prices. A good example is hard disk drives. As the market moved to SSDs the constant cost decreases that had been reliable for decades started stabilizing or even rising. I paid $15/TB for 8TB drives in 2017 and that continued to be a good price for new drives until the AI boom drove costs way up recently. Similar trends have happened with lots of other products as they moved from mainstream to niche. reply Aurornis 19 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 > I paid $15/TB for 8TB drives in 2017 and that continued to be a good price for new drives until the AI boom drove costs way up recently. So prices were low when demand was low, then they increased when demand increased? For commodity items it’s expected to have some fluctuations, especially when prices are bottomed out and manufacturers are weighing the costs of competition in a cutthroat market with shrinking demand. However you don’t really escape the laws of supply and demand. That’s why you saw prices swing hard upward when demand increased, not when demand was the lowest. reply Arainach 18 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 It's not a simple curve. There has to be enough demand for any theoretical market effects to take place. If there isn't enough demand for something for multiple companies to find it worth building a factory and producing at industrial scale (and vendors to bother stocking, etc.), then you're faced with either monopoly pricing from the single vendor who sticks around or the dramatically higher cost of other manufacturing methods. reply EvanAnderson 19 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 My thesis is shrinking demand will cause specialty manufacturing lines to be used for more profitable hardware, driving down the supply. Why make enthusiast hardware when hyper-scalers need storage, RAM, and compute to rent to end users? reply m4rtink 11 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Well, you might also end up dead like SUN or SGI - they lived on expensive B2B workstations and one day, the companies just stopped buying & soon they were gone. Unlike the B2B market, consumer stuff is usually more stable and history has shown that companies supporting the consumer marked usually last longer. reply m4rtink 12 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Yeah, gaming demand is definitely here - unfortunately we need to wait a bit more for the AI bubble to fully collapse. Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app – Wilson Tovar (krthr) 
 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 Wilson Tovar (krthr)
 
 
 
 home • blog • poesía • photography • say hi 👋 

 
 
 
 

 

 
 Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app 

 
 
 
 19 Nov, 2026
 
 
 
 

 A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. 
 
 
 
 
 If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. 
 
 
 
 I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. 
 Why fanzines.app exists The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: 
 ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°)
├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up
└─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
 
 I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app . 
 In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server. 
 Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine. 
 Fixing how pages are paired In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover. 
 It looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left. 
 
 
 
 The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order. 
 I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it. 
 Smaller changes that make the editor less fussy When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them. 
 I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs ( X , Y , Width , Height ). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection. 
 The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text. 
 Before downloading the PDF, a Review step shows the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact. 
 A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish . Changing the language keeps your current pages. 
 Thanks for reading, Wil 
 
 You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app
